articles.title: EXPLAINED: Trump’s Threat to Halt Intelligence, Arms to Ukraine – 5 Things to Know
articles.body:
Over the weekend reports surfaced that the US was considering cutting off American intelligence feeds and arms sales to Ukraine. Kyiv Post broke that down into five things to know.
1. Did the Americans really threaten to cut Ukraine off from all US weaponry and military intelligence?
JOIN US ON TELEGRAM
Follow our coverage of the war on the @Kyivpost_official.
It looks that way. During Saturday talks in Miami between US and Ukrainian delegations on a possible halt to the Russo-Ukrainian War, members of the US delegation said Washington wants Ukraine to stop attacking Russian oil refineries, and if Kyiv refuses, then the US could suspend arms shipments to Ukraine and intelligence sharing with Ukraine’s military.
The threats reportedly were also made in calls on Saturday and Sunday from the State Department, Pentagon, and other US officials to Ukrainian leaders and European capitals. The Financial Times first reported the threats, citing European officials involved in the calls. Reuters and other outlets confirmed the FT account. Axios reported New York real estate mogul Steve Witkoff and Trump son-in-law Jared Kushner as heads of the US delegation in Miami made the threats directly to Kyrylo Budanov, head of Ukraine’s Office of the President and former head of Ukraine’s military intelligence. The Ukrainian delegation quit the planned talks one day early.
According to Western media reports Witkoff and Kushner warned the Budanov team that if Ukraine did not stop attacking Russian oil refineries then the US would consider halting all arms deliveries to Ukraine under the Prioritized Ukraine Requirements List (PURL), a mechanism by which Ukraine’s allies purchase US weapons for Ukraine at a 10 percent markup ordered by Trump. At the same time, reportedly, the US might cut off intelligence collected by the US on Russian military targets and activities, including real-time intelligence feeds.
EU Targets Russian Missiles and Drones in Biggest Sanctions Expansion Since 2022
The United States shut down practically all US arms donations and direct financial support to Ukraine in February 2025 and since then has not reinstated it. Since then, the Trump administration, according to Ukrainian sources, has cut off US military intelligence feeds at least once, for approximately a week in March 2025.
On Sunday, Budanov and the rest of the Ukrainian delegation walked out of the talks, cutting the negotiations short by a day.
2. What would a cut off of US intelligence feeds mean for Ukraine?
The key capacity Ukraine would lose is the earliest warning possible of Russian ballistic missile launches.
President Zelensky and other Ukrainian officials have said that, without that intelligence, Ukraine’s ability to respond to Russian missile strikes would be seriously weakened because alternate means of detecting Russian aircraft and missiles – primarily by Ukrainian and NATO-operated systems – are far less extensive and networked than the Americans’.
Most analysts say a Russian ballistic missile launch in western Russia is detected almost instantaneously by the US, giving residents of Kyiv three to five minutes to take cover before the missile impacts, thanks to US intelligence sharing. Without that warning targeted Ukrainians would have less than half that time, and possibly no time at all, to take cover.
Beyond missile early-warning for Ukraine, the US world-wide satellite and intelligence collection network is a possible gold mine of intelligence on Russia thanks to unique US capacities like super-computing power enabling interception and decoding of adversary communications and electronic emissions. In addition, hundreds of state-of-the-art imagery satellites give the US and its friends, at least theoretically, the ability to inspect every square centimeter of the planet thanks to satellites passing overhead.
For Ukraine, US collection of Russian radar data is especially important because US air war weapons like fighter jets and anti-aircraft missiles are regularly updated with changes in those radars detected by worldwide US electronic eavesdropping, and Ukraine uses both those weapons to defend itself against Russian air attacks.
Another unique US advantage Ukraine might lose is the giant analytical manpower and computer capacity of the CIA and NSA, which covertly suck in data through a worldwide collection effort and turn it into hard intelligence. For Ukraine this might mean not knowing Russian military plans, movements of units or key officers, or the precise location of major Russian weapons systems like warships, combat aircraft and ballistic missile launchers.
A key qualification is, of course, that no intelligence collection effort is perfect. Sometimes the US intelligence community gets it wrong, and like any big state bureaucracy the American intelligence community is fallible. So loss of US analytical capacity is not the same as loss of 100 percent accurate analysis.
3. What would a cut off of US arms and weapons assistance mean for Ukraine?
One of the most damaging effects of a cut off would be the loss of access to US military GPS networks which, in turn, would render “partially-dumb” US weapons operated by Ukraine that use GPS for precision guidance. The most important GPS-dependent weapons used by Ukraine are ATACMS missiles and GMLRS guided rockets fired by the HIMARS/M270 launch system.
Ukraine uses the system most often to hit high-value, fleeting targets, such as meetings at Russian military headquarters or heavy mobile anti-aircraft systems. Almost as important and similarly effective have been guided bomb kits called JDAMS, which, if the GPS works, allow a pilot to select a single point with five meter accuracy on a bridge or bunker line or a bomb strike.
The last time the Americans cut off GPS feeds to Ukraine, in March 2025, these systems effectively became “dumb” and only as accurate as unguided munitions. It is worth noting that Ukraine’s last confirmed ATACMS launch was in February 2026, so it’s possible a US cut off of ATACMS-specific guidance data to Ukraine is irrelevant, because Ukraine has shot off all its ATACMS and the US isn’t sending any more.
In terms of actual weaponry, by far the most important US weapon operated by Ukraine right now is the Patriot air defense system firing an interceptor missile called the PAC-3 MSE, which is the only weapon in Ukraine’s military that can, in practical terms, intercept a Russian ballistic missile. A July statement by Ukraine’s Defense Ministry said that 95 percent of Ukraine’s purchase from the US under PURL, are Patriot-system associated.
Besides Patriot-associated purchases needed to protect Ukrainian civilians and infrastructure from otherwise unstoppable Russian ballistic missiles, a US cut-off of arms sales could gradually make Ukraine’s 1990s-era F-16 fighter jet fleet unflyable because the jet and its spare parts and systems upgrades ultimately are from the American manufacturer Lockheed Martin. Ukrainian air defenses would suffer because the guided missiles fired by Ukraine’s aging F-16s – the long-range AIM-120 AMRAAM and the short-range AIM-9 Sidewinder – are both manufactured by the US company Raytheon.
Major US ground weapons operated by Ukraine, most visibly the M1A1 Abrams tank, the M3 Bradley Infantry Fighting Vehicle, and the M109 Paladin artillery system, similar to the F-16 would over time become more and more difficult for Ukraine to operate were the US to embargo arms sales, because parts needed for maintenance would be cut off.
4. If the Americans cut off intelligence feeds does Ukraine have other ways of getting information about Russia?
With the critical exception of ballistic missile early warning sufficient to let Ukrainians take shelter when the Russians launch a weapon at a city, the answer to that question is “yes.”
Most obviously, Ukraine has been at war with Russia since 2014 and Ukraine’s own spy and electronic eavesdropping networks have years of experience collecting war-critical information about Russia. Ukraine has the additional advantages of a population with millions of native Russian-speakers with millions more relatives in Russia, and a national security apparatus intimately familiar with Russian intelligence practices.
Lost US intelligence on Russia collected by satellites, to some extent, is compensated by Ukrainian agents on the ground. Most analysts say Ukrainian spy networks are probably best-developed in territory recently invaded by Russia, where the population is mostly hostile to the Kremlin.
European states with robust national intelligence efforts or just focusing largely on Russia – predominantly France but firmly including Britain, Finland, Poland, Sweden and the Baltic states – actively assist Ukraine with data collection. France’s CSO (Composante Spatiale Optique) military reconnaissance satellites provide high-resolution images of Russian bases, troop deployments and military infrastructure with resolution reportedly similar to the US’s, with the qualification that CSO passes a camera over a possible target once or twice a day, while a US satellite overpass can take place several times an hour.
The explosion of commercial satellite imagery, purchased by Ukraine or its allies, also helps fill in gaps left by US collection which, although capable, can be distracted away from Russia to other White House priorities like Iran, China, potential illegal migrants in Mexico or drug runners in the Caribbean or east Pacific. Among the commercial networks regularly feeding imagery into Ukrainian intelligence production are Finland’s ICEYE synthetic-aperture radar network, the US’s Maxar, Planet Labs, and BlackSky networks, and Canada’s RADARSAT-2 network.
A final intelligence collection effort that the Americans seem to have little ability to undermine is the NATO-led air defense operation along the Baltics, Poland, Romania and the Black and Baltic Seas that focuses on spotting Russian aircraft, drone and missile launches as early as possible, using ground- and air-based radars operating 24/7. NATO also regularly flies reconnaissance missions sometimes as close as a 100 km from Russian-occupied Crimea and Russia’s Black Sea coast, using electronic emission-sniffing spy planes, most often based in Crete, Romania, Turkey or Great Britain.
By doctrine the flights would search for precise locations of Russian air defense systems and military units so NATO could be prepared in case of war.
Russian officials and milbloggers have long accused NATO of sharing the intelligence with the Ukrainians, a charge NATO has steadfastly denied. In January 2026 President Emmanuel Macron told reporters France was providing about two-thirds of Ukraine’s intelligence needs. The Ukrainians say they have their own means of finding Russian targets.
5. If the Americans cut off arms supplies, does Ukraine have alternatives?
With exception of Patriot and Patriot-related equipment, the answer to that is not just “yes, in the future” but “yes, already.”
The most visible shift in Ukrainian arms needs has been tied to the revolution in ground warfare making drones the dominant weapons system on the ground battlefield and, parallel with that, legacy systems like tanks, infantry fighting vehicles and artillery less critical for fighting a war. Almost all members of the Ukrainian military, from private to general, will say that what Ukraine needs is more short-range tactical drones. However, compared to Ukrainian-made drones, American tactical drones are primitive and manufactured in scant quantities.
The situation is similar for Ukrainian air defense where, besides Patriot missiles to take on the Russian ballistic missiles, the Ukrainians need means of stopping recently developed Russian jet-powered drones. American anti-aircraft missiles are capable of engaging drones like that, but they cost more than the Russian drone. Meanwhile, Ukraine is fielding its own interceptor drones which have the benefit of having been tested not in laboratories and firing ranges, but in actual war against actual Russian weapons.
Germany has also already contributed in a big way to bulk up Ukrainian air defenses with donations of Cold War-era Gepard anti-aircraft cannon that have turned out to be ideal for blowing up Russian drones, an upgraded version of the Gepard, called the Skynex, and 11 IRIS-T SLM air defense systems whose advanced missiles have proved the most effective ground-based air defense system the Ukrainians have. A 12th system is reportedly en route to Ukraine by the end of the year.
Longer-term, France and Sweden have promised and begun pilot training for deliveries respectively of the fully modern Rafale and Gripen fighter jets for Ukraine’s air force, with the first aircraft planned to arrive in Ukraine in 2027.
In late September representatives from Lockheed Martin, the manufacturer of the competing US fighter jet, the F-16, were in Kyiv discussing with the Defense Ministry possible upgrades to Ukraine’s aging F-16 fleet, which without upgrades, compared to the incoming French and Swedish aircraft, would be obsolete. The Ukrainians said they would think about it.

articles.title: Can Turkey and Pakistan defend Saudi Arabia from the Houthis?
articles.body:
Breadcrumb
Can Turkey and Pakistan defend Saudi Arabia from the Houthis?
Turkey and Pakistan's promise of rapid military support for Saudi Arabia faces a more urgent test after weekend attacks on Riyadh’s international airport killed 12 people and forced its closure.
Turning that commitment into effective protection will depend on what its partners can spare, how their forces operate alongside Saudi units and how far Ankara and Islamabad are willing to enter the conflict.
At an emergency meeting in Riyadh on 5 October, the three countries pledged to implement their collective defence commitments and rapidly deploy agreed forces and capabilities to Saudi Arabia, subject to their national legislation.
The decision marked a significant step for the Mecca Joint Defence Agreement they signed in August, but left troop numbers, equipment, missions, and deployment schedules publicly unspecified.
Their contributions also begin from different positions. Pakistan already has an established military presence in the kingdom and has reportedly supplied weapons and advisers to Yemeni government forces.
Turkey is considering additional defensive assistance while explicitly ruling out offensive operations abroad under the pact.
The immediate test is whether these commitments can address Saudi vulnerabilities quickly enough to matter - and whether protecting the kingdom can remain separate from supporting its campaign in Yemen.
What Riyadh needs
Saudi Arabia’s requirement extends beyond additional troops. In September, drones struck the East-West Pipeline south of Medina, causing injuries and damage and prompting a precautionary shutdown of the route carrying crude to Red Sea export terminals.
Riyadh said the drones originated in Iraq, but no group claimed responsibility, and the Islamic Resistance in Iraq denied involvement. Earlier attacks on Eastern Province oil facilities had already raised concerns about Iran-aligned Iraqi factions, adding a northern threat to the Houthi challenge from Yemen.
The aviation threat escalated sharply over the weekend. An attack on King Khalid International Airport on 10 October killed 12 people and wounded more than 300, including Saudi and foreign nationals. On 11 October, the Saudi-led coalition said another projectile struck Terminal 4, causing a fire, while air defences intercepted a cruise missile nearby.
The airport remained closed that day. Neither weekend attack had been claimed at the time of reporting. The Houthis nevertheless renewed their warning against using Saudi airports and airspace, exempting Mecca and Medina.
The attacks followed earlier strikes that killed three Saudis, including a Saudia pilot, and a Sudanese national at Riyadh airport. Sustained protection of civilian infrastructure has become an immediate requirement.
“Saudi Arabia is primarily seeking to strengthen its air defences against Houthi drone strikes targeting critical infrastructure,” Sebastian Sons, an expert on Saudi Arabia, told The New Arab.
Sons expects Turkey to contribute equipment and technological expertise, while Pakistan could expand cooperation in training, capacity-building, and troop deployments. The potential division of labour reflects different strengths, although the governments have not publicly detailed their respective assignments.
For Riyadh, successful protection has economic as well as military consequences. Attacks on energy infrastructure and airports threaten business activity and complicate efforts to present the kingdom as a secure investment destination.
The WPC Energy Congress was still going ahead in Riyadh on 11 October, Saudi authorities said, despite the airport closure. Reinforcing defences could help Saudi Arabia sustain support for its Yemeni partners while reducing exposure at home.
The military campaign is also continuing. On 10 October, the Giants Brigades said they had repelled a Houthi attack north of Dhubab Airport near the Bab el-Mandeb, alongside Saudi-led airstrikes on Houthi reinforcements.
The coalition said it was working to dismantle the group’s ballistic missile network. Neither statement establishes that the Houthis’ ability to strike Saudi territory has been eliminated.
Turkey's available capabilities
Ankara’s contribution could initially draw on technical relationships already in place. According to reports, technical teams, air-defence systems, and electronic warfare equipment have been present in Saudi Arabia since last year. Turkish officials described plans for additional personnel and equipment, with further deployments dependent on parliamentary action.
Barın Kayaoğlu, a Turkish independent analyst and consultant, said the available options would depend on Saudi requirements. ASELSAN’s Korkut, an anti-aircraft gun system designed to intercept threats at close range, is one candidate.
“Some of those systems could be transferred over to the Kingdom,” he told The New Arab. Gun-based defences could help protect Saudi facilities against drones without relying solely on more expensive missile interceptors.
In early October, ASELSAN announced a $125 million export contract for weapon and electronic warfare systems. Saudi interest makes the Kingdom a possible buyer, although the announcement names neither the customer nor the delivery schedule. Ukraine is another potential destination, as Kyiv had received a small number of Korkut systems earlier this year for use against Russian attacks.
Kayaoğlu also identified MKE’s Tolga short-range air-defence system, as well as ASELSAN’s Gürz, which combines guns and missiles on a mobile platform like the Russian Pantsir-S1. For wider coverage, he suggested “the ALP-class radars and perhaps even the Hisar short-to-medium range air defence systems”.
The former would help detect and track threats, while the latter would provide interception beyond the reach of close-range guns. Such systems could reinforce lower defensive layers. Kayaoğlu cautioned that the longer-range Siper is not known to have anti-ballistic-missile capabilities.
Saudi interest in Turkish air defence also predates the current crisis. Around SAHA Expo 2026 in Istanbul, reports described Saudi interest in ASELSAN’s Korkut for low-altitude threats, proposed Kalkan surveillance radars linked to mobile command-and-control shelters, and a Roketsan proposal for six Hisar-O batteries to protect oil facilities and airbase corridors.
Availability also depends on personnel. “Some of it will relate to what and who can be spared to go to KSA,” Kayaoğlu told The New Arab. “Active-duty personnel are harder to spare; contractors or company personnel are much easier.”
Company technicians or recently retired personnel could support equipment sooner than a larger military contingent could undertake an operational mission. Still, in Kayaoğlu’s view, “showing the political commitment to a Mecca Pact partner is even more important than what and who is being sent”.
Kayaoğlu said a deployment of serving troops would require parliamentary approval, separately from ratification of the Mecca Pact. Existing bilateral agreements reportedly permit some technical assistance, while the unpublished pact’s implications for future authorisations remain unclear.
Ankara has drawn a public boundary around its involvement. Foreign Minister Hakan Fidan said on 8 October that military delegations were assessing Saudi needs, particularly air defence, electronic warfare, and technical support, while ruling out sending Turkish troops abroad to conduct attacks under the agreement.
“Unless the Houthis decide to target Turkish civilian vessels transiting the Red Sea and the Bab el-Mandeb, I do not see Ankara getting involved in Yemen’s civil war and opening a new front with Iran,” Kayaoğlu said.
The maritime domain could nevertheless offer scope for limited involvement. Surveillance, escort, intelligence-sharing and coalition coordination could support Red Sea security while maintaining a boundary between defensive assistance and offensive operations in Yemen.
Pakistan's head start - and its limits
Pakistan’s longstanding military relationship with Saudi Arabia gives it a different starting point. Reuters reported in May that Islamabad had deployed about 8,000 troops under the 2025 Strategic Mutual Defence Agreement, alongside a squadron of JF-17 light jet fighters, two squadrons of drones and a Chinese-made HQ-9 air-defence system. Sources told the agency that Pakistani personnel operated the equipment, financed by Saudi Arabia.
This gives Islamabad an existing air-combat, unmanned and ground-based air-defence presence, adding to those already stationed in the kingdom under earlier agreements. Reportedly, the pact could eventually allow for up to 80,000 Pakistani troops to support Saudi border security if required.
“Pakistan’s existing military presence gives it an established framework for cooperation, easing coordination and potentially allowing it to provide certain capabilities more quickly,” John Calabrese, a senior fellow at the Middle East Institute, told The New Arab.
“But an existing presence does not automatically translate into the capacity, much less the political authorisation, for a substantially larger deployment.”
Pakistan’s involvement reportedly extends to support for forces inside Yemen. In early October, Reuters reported four cargo-plane deliveries to Aden in September containing air-defence systems, light artillery, drones and counter-drone systems. A Pakistani official also said military advisers were working alongside Saudi counterparts supporting Yemeni troops.
The publicly reported categories do not establish models, quantities, readiness or the advisers’ precise duties. But assistance to Yemeni forces raises a question that a deployment confined to Saudi territorial defence does not: whether Islamabad’s contribution facilitates operations inside Yemen.
“I think the distinction could become blurred very quickly,” Calabrese said. Pakistan may describe its mission as protecting Saudi territory and infrastructure, he explained, while support to Yemeni forces risks drawing it into the conflict itself.
Domestic decision-making has also changed since 2015, when Pakistan’s parliament voted to remain neutral in the Saudi-led intervention while pledging to defend the kingdom. Reuters reported on 8 October that the latest commitment to rapid deployment had proceeded without a parliamentary vote. That political contrast does not, by itself, establish how quickly further units could become operational.
Islamabad must also preserve relations with neighbouring Iran, its diplomatic channels and capacity to manage its own security challenges. Calabrese expects those considerations to discourage an open-ended commitment, even as Pakistan seeks to demonstrate solidarity with Riyadh.
What rapid support can change
Across both contributions, speed depends on more than transporting equipment. Operators, maintenance, ammunition, communications and arrangements for coordinating engagements must be available. Protection of selected facilities may be achievable before a wider network is established, but the announced pledge gives no public basis for assigning a firm timetable.
For Saudi Arabia, additional support could improve protection and coordination without delivering a decisive battlefield outcome. “However, even with increased external support, a decisive military victory over the Houthis remains unlikely,” Sons said.
That makes the partnership’s political effect important alongside its operational contribution. “Beyond their practical value, Turkish and Pakistani support carries symbolic weight, allowing Riyadh to demonstrate regional unity and solidarity with non-Arab partners,” he added.
Sons sees these relationships as part of Saudi strategic diversification, complementing its ties with Washington. The kingdom, he said, will continue seeking greater US engagement against the Houthis. That possibility became more explicit over the weekend: on 10 October, Trump said the United States was considering joining Saudi strikes. This remained a possibility rather than an announced intervention.
The first measure of success will therefore be whether additional systems and personnel assume defined defensive missions and reduce Saudi exposure to attacks.
How much further the Mecca Pact alliance changes the war will depend on its partners’ willingness to sustain that support - and whether their efforts to limit involvement survive the demands of an expanding conflict.
Francesco Salesio Schiavi is an Italian specialist in the Middle East. His focus lies in the security architecture of the Levant and the Gulf, with a particular emphasis on Iraq, Iran, and the Arab Peninsula, as well as military and diplomatic interventions by international actors

articles.title: Kinzhal is 90% identical to Iskander-M: Ukraine’s intelligence identifies 58 companies in production chain
articles.body:
Ukraine’s Defense Intelligence (HUR) released information on the components of Russia’s Kinzhal air-launched ballistic missile and the companies involved in its production, according to a statement dated 12 October.
Russia has used Kinzhal missiles to strike targets across Ukraine since the start of its full-scale invasion. However, 22 of the 58 companies in Russia’s Kinzhal production network are not subject to sanctions, the intelligence agency noted.
Kinzhal missile: design, components, and production changes
Ukraine’s Defense Intelligence has published an interactive 3D model of the Russian Kinzhal missile on its War&Sanctions portal.
The 9-S-7760 missile, known as the Kh-47M2 Kinzhal, uses solid fuel and has a single stage. This means the missile does not consist of multiple stages that separate sequentially during flight. About 90% of its components are identical to those used in the 9M723 ballistic missile of the Iskander-M system, HUR noted.
The Kinzhal is equipped with a radar homing seeker, an active jamming station, and a decoy deployment system, according to the statement. The homing seeker helps the missile determine the direction to its target, while decoys are designed to make interception by air defense systems more difficult.
The missile can carry one of two types of warheads: a penetrating high-explosive warhead or a nuclear warhead. Russia is also developing a version with a high-explosive fragmentation warhead that strikes targets through an explosion and fragments. HUR believes this development may be linked to problems with the missile’s accuracy.
In 2026, Russia significantly reduced its state procurement order for Kinzhal missiles and redirected some production resources, components, and raw materials towards manufacturing Iskander-M missiles, HUR noted. Another reason is the limited number of MiG-31I and MiG-31K aircraft used to launch Kinzhal missiles, the intelligence agency reported.
Ukraine intercepts Kinzhal missiles, but has limited resources to do so
Despite their high speed, Russian Kinzhal missiles can be intercepted using US-made Patriot surface-to-air missile systems. In particular, PAC-3 interceptor missiles are designed to destroy ballistic targets and can be used against threats such as the Kinzhal and Zircon, Ukraine’s Ministry of Defense reported.
Ukraine is seeking additional Patriot interceptor missiles to defend against Russian ballistic attacks during the winter. 
Most of the approximately 1,000 missiles Kyiv has contracted for are not expected to arrive for several years, prompting Ukraine to ask its allies to supply missiles from their existing stockpiles, Defense News reported on 12 October 2026.
Sanctions loopholes allow Russia to obtain foreign components for Kinzhal missiles
Russia continues to use foreign components in missile production despite sanctions. For instance, the US-made Texas Instruments processors were found again in a newer version of the Kinzhal missile, Ukrainian presidential commissioner for sanctions policy Vladyslav Vlasiuk said in September, Interfax reported. According to him, foreign electronics continue to reach Russia through various supply channels.
Earlier, Ukraine had provided its partners with information on more than 100 Russian companies involved in ballistic missile production and urged them to impose sanctions on those entities, according to the President's Office.
On 12 October, the EU Council imposed sanctions on 1,569 individuals and entities linked to Russia’s military-industrial complex, including 826 Russian companies and 743 company CEOs.

articles.title: How would NATO defeat a Russian invasion? Its top commander envisions a wall of drones, a counteroffensive, and missile strikes deep behind Russian lines.
articles.body:
How would NATO defeat a Russian invasion? Its top commander envisions a wall of drones, a counteroffensive, and missile strikes deep behind Russian lines.
General Alexus Grynkewich, NATO’s Supreme Allied Commander Europe, said NATO forces would destroy “anything and everything” involved in any Russian attack on the alliance’s territory. He presented his “theory of victory” at a security conference in Warsaw.
Bloomberg reported a week earlier that Grynkewich would present a “quick victory” strategy for responding to a Russian advance on the alliance’s eastern flank. Reuters reported that he did not explicitly mention Russia in his speech, but his message was clearly directed at the Kremlin.
Grynkewich said NATO is a defensive alliance but will thwart, repel, and crush any attacks on its members:
If someone is foolish enough to attack us, we will fight. […] We will, in short, ensure any attack, against any ally, proves utterly futile.
In Reuters’ assessment, the general signaled to Moscow that, if necessary, NATO would launch large-scale retaliatory strikes against both the forces directly involved in the attack and facilities beyond the area under attack. “Should the adversary choose to press the attack or commit his reserves, we will break the warfighting system engaged against us,” Grynkewich said. “This includes not just the attacking force itself, but anything and everything that supports, sustains, and controls that force.”
He said that if NATO territory comes under attack, its forces would not allow the enemy to gain a foothold on the alliance’s territory. The aim, he said, is to reduce the enemy’s offensive capabilities until it can no longer continue fighting. Grynkewich believes this approach should underpin a deterrence strategy in which any escalation by the aggressor backfires.
Grynkewich said a key factor in deterring Russia is consistently and unambiguously showing that NATO is ready to repel any aggression.
The Wall Street Journal reported details of Grynkewich’s “theory of victory.” The plan calls for creating an extensive “autonomous zone” on the eastern flank, where drones and “ground robots” (probably ground drones) could hold back a Russian advance without heavy losses among NATO troops.
At the same time, long-range missiles would strike Russian command posts and air defense systems in the Kaliningrad region, near St. Petersburg, and in Belarus. The strikes are intended to undermine Russia’s ability to control the skies and allow the U.S. Army’s V Corps and other NATO ground forces to counterattack.
NATO aircraft would also need to strike Russian reinforcements quickly as they move toward the battlefield, along with other targets in the rear.
A system allowing NATO allies to share classified targeting data instantly through cloud infrastructure would make these strikes possible. Some elements of the system have already been tested in the Middle East during the U.S. attack on Iran.
The German tabloid Bild reported on a similar NATO plan in mid-August 2026. The article said NATO has a plan for a military response to a Russian attack on the Baltic states. Among other things, it calls for the alliance’s missiles and drones to disable Russian missile systems, including those in Kaliningrad.
The Wall Street Journal reported that while Grynkewich was speaking in Warsaw, more than 20,000 military personnel from various NATO countries were taking part in a 10-day command-post exercise called “Steadfast Duel.” The exercise was intended, among other things, to simulate one million NATO troops repelling an invasion from the east by an army of comparable size. The newspaper reported that other exercises also rehearsed strikes with ground-launched missiles to disable enemy command posts.
In late September, Russia’s embassy in Ireland claimed its diplomats were receiving information about NATO preparations for an air and naval blockade of the Kaliningrad region. The diplomats said that if this happened, Russia would be prepared to use any weapon, including nuclear weapons. The same warning appears in a document Russia sent to NATO that Reuters obtained. In it, Moscow accuses the alliance of pursuing a “dangerous and reckless course” that carries “high risks of the outbreak of a direct armed conflict.”
Vladimir Putin later made a similar statement:
If it comes to a direct attack on the Russian Federation — in this case, we mean Kaliningrad, perhaps other territories as well — then, of course, Russia’s use of all the weapons at our country’s disposal will inevitably and immediately be on the table. That is inevitable.
In its written response to the Kremlin, NATO said none of the alliance’s exercises or activities pose a threat to Russian territory.

articles.title: Ukraine Adapts Air Defense to Counter Faster Russian Jet Drones
articles.body:
Ukraine is fielding new ways to intercept Russia’s jet-powered drones, the country’s defense ministry said on Monday in its September air defense report.
The ministry said Russia is sending small groups of several jet drones into different regions, which Ukraine counters with aircraft and what it called innovative interception, according to RBC-Ukraine, though the ministry provided no specifics.
JOIN US ON TELEGRAM
Follow our coverage of the war on the @Kyivpost_official.
It added that ballistic missiles remain a challenge, while jet drones flying at about 400 kmh (249 mph) shorten the time available to detect and intercept them.
The new Russian drones are already having an effect. On Oct. 10, turbojet loitering munitions damaged power distribution facilities in the Kyiv region, injuring four people, causing voltage drops that shut down all three metro lines, and knocking out municipal water pumping stations.
How Kyiv is responding
While the ministry has been tight-lipped about its innovations, recent reports suggest a combination of efforts.
The most immediate is the F-16 fighter jets. Pilots have already used the jets’ 20mm cannons against jet drones, and Kyiv wants tens of thousands of rounds as a cheaper alternative to air-to-air missiles.
The second track focuses on dedicated interceptors, with the defense ministry testing and codifying various models that can down jet-powered drones. Arms makers are also working with the military to test new models, such as the Griffen jet-powered drone, which is said to have successfully intercepted a target in July.
Ukraine’s TENCORE Bundles 4 Ground Drones in Single AI-Powered Ecosystem
A third track is a small-missile program that President Volodymyr Zelensky said is expected to show results in the second half of the month, with production scaling up if it works.
The last would be AI-powered gun turrets, deployed around Kyiv in October after Russia began targeting bridges across the Dnipro River. Reports suggest 12 are in place, with eight more planned, though a defense adviser cautioned they are only a last line of defense and cannot protect the entire city, despite reported successes against jet-powered drones.
And scaling the new systems remains the main obstacle.
The Associated Press reported that ramping up interceptor production and training pilots could take three to six months, well beyond the end-of-October target. RBC-Ukraine has reported that technical complexity and high component costs, especially for engines Ukraine largely buys abroad, limit how quickly Ukraine can produce jet interceptors.
From experiment to mass use
Jet-powered drones are not new.
In February 2025, Ukraine’s military intelligence warned that Russia had begun domestic production of the jet-powered Geran-3, a variant of the Iranian Shahed design. Ukraine officially confirmed its inclusion in mass airstrikes in July 2025.
For months, use remained limited. Russia launched about 1,400 jet-powered Gerans in the first months of 2026, compared with 180 recorded in all of 2025, according to defense outlet Militarnyi.
Russia began launching the newer Geran-4 in May, and in August, the Ukrainian Air Force said up to two-thirds of the drones in some strikes were jet-powered, with around 2,850 launches documented in a single month, rising to nearly 3,500 by September.
Why they are harder to stop
Speed and altitude are the main advantages. Jet drones fly faster and higher than propeller-driven Shaheds, making them harder for mobile fire groups and existing interceptor drones to hit.
Defense Minister Yevhen Khmara has framed the shift as a change in the nature of the threat.
“The effectiveness of countering standard ‘Shahed’ drones already exceeds 90%,” he said. “The key challenge now is jet-powered drones, which require different interception speeds.”

articles.title: How many children have been killed in Russia’s full-scale invasion of Ukraine? A new Meduza investigation finds at least 940.
articles.body:
How many children have been killed in Russia’s full-scale invasion of Ukraine? A new Meduza investigation finds at least 940.
The war Russia launched has killed hundreds of thousands of people and harmed millions. Exactly how many are children is unknown. The two sides keep their own counts, but their methods differ, making comparisons difficult. Official U.N. figures also appear incomplete. Meduza examined all available information, checked it against as many public sources as possible, and established a minimum number of children who have died during the war. The answer is in the headline.
Caution: This article contains accounts of children’s deaths.
What Meduza counted
We counted everyone killed who was under 18. This matches the definition the U.N. uses to count casualties in international conflicts. Ukrainian and Russian law use the same age limit.
Our analysis drew on data from international organizations and Ukrainian and Russian authorities, as well as:
- Social media posts by people close to the child
- Posts by schools and hospitals
- Official statements from local authorities
- Law enforcement reports
- News articles and other public sources
Almost every death we counted was corroborated by two or more sources. In some cases involving occupied areas or hard-to-reach places near the front, a statement from local authorities was the only source. We recorded those deaths when the statement specified where and on what date the child died. We excluded reports lacking these details from our database.
We classified deaths by where the child died rather than by citizenship, because Russia forced people in occupied areas to obtain Russian documents. For Ukraine, we therefore counted children who died within the country’s 1991 borders — including annexed Crimea and Sevastopol, as well as occupied parts of the Donetsk, Luhansk, Zaporizhzhia, and Kherson regions. For Russia, we counted only deaths within its internationally recognized territory, excluding Ukrainian regions.
This distinction follows the U.N. General Assembly’s resolution on Crimea and the resolution adopted after the annexation of four Ukrainian regions.
It also prevents some deaths from being counted twice.
We do not give the children’s surnames in this article, but we used them in our analysis to ensure an accurate count. In all, we found the full names or first names of 409 children: 372 in Ukraine and 37 in Russia. We most often found their names in posts or statements from relatives, schools, hospitals, rescue services, prosecutors’ offices, courts, and local authorities, as well as news reports and memorial projects. International organizations such as the U.N. do not publish this information.
The war Russia launched has killed more than 940 children
As of early September 2026, at least 940 children had died because of the war:
- 873 in Ukraine
- 67 in Russia
For Ukraine, our count began with the figure published by the U.N. Human Rights Monitoring Mission: By August 31, 2026, the U.N. had confirmed the deaths of 835 children. Meduza’s count runs through October 9 and supplements the U.N. data with news reports and official statements about individual deaths. These account for another 38 deaths.
Using the same method, we confirmed 67 children’s deaths in Russia.
These figures differ from the countries’ own estimates. As of October 9, 2026, the Ukrainian government’s Children of War (Dity Viiny) website reported 755 children killed. Russia’s Foreign Ministry reported 264 as of June 30, 2026, in its latest statement on the subject.
There is a simple explanation for the gap. Ukraine’s figures include confirmed deaths across the country, including occupied parts of the Donetsk and Luhansk regions, but coverage of those areas is incomplete: Investigators often cannot obtain documents or reach the places where children died. Russia’s figures include victims in Crimea, Sevastopol, and other occupied areas as well as within Russia.
Our count is also a minimum estimate. The actual toll is almost certainly higher: The U.N. itself cautions that it cannot quickly verify every report of a child’s death, particularly in places where fighting has continued for a long time.
The number of child casualties began rising faster in 2026. In Ukraine this July, the number of children killed or injured reached its highest level since the first months of Russia’s full-scale invasion. In Russia, 32 children died between January and early October — more than in any previous full year of the war.
Ukraine: 873 killed
At least 873 children’s deaths have been confirmed within Ukraine’s internationally recognized borders. Ukrainian authorities’ data show that more than half of the children — 450 — died between February and December 2022.
Information about the first months of the invasion remains incomplete. In a report on children affected by war, the U.N. said at least 120 children died in Mariupol between February and April 2022. The actual number could be much higher: Independent researchers have been unable to enter the Russian-occupied city.
The exact number of people killed in the March 16, 2022, strike on the Mariupol Drama Theater remains unknown. Hundreds of civilians, including children, were sheltering inside. The word “CHILDREN” was written in enormous letters on the ground in front of and behind the building.
The Associated Press later estimated the death toll at around 600. That figure circulated widely but remained unconfirmed. Amnesty International confirmed at least 12 deaths. The human rights organization concluded that more than 12 people had died, but probably far fewer than 600.
How many of those killed in the theater were children is unknown. One of the few victims identified by name was 2-year-old Karolina. During the attack, she was on the theater’s second floor with her mother and older sister. Karolina and her parents died; her sister and grandparents survived. Karolina’s last words were: “Grandma, I’m with you.”
Children killed in other regions ranged in age from newborns to 17-year-olds. One of the youngest was 2-month-old Uliana. She died in Kryvyi Rih with her mother and two brothers, 2-year-old Demyd and 10-year-old Kyrylo, after a Russian ballistic missile hit their home.
On April 4, 2025, a missile exploded directly above a residential neighborhood in Kryvyi Rih, near a playground. Nine children, ages 3 to 17, were killed in that single attack; most were playing in the park when the missile struck. U.N. staff visited the site and saw marks left by hundreds of fragments on swings, slides, trees, and houses. “It’s an unimaginable horror,” said U.N. High Commissioner for Human Rights Volker Türk. The mission said the attack killed more children than any other since the war began.
On November 19 of that year, Russia attacked Ternopil with drones and cruise missiles. The missiles hit apartment buildings, killing at least 38 people, including eight children, and injuring another 99. In one building, 5-year-old Kamila and 18-month-old Nazar died with their mother. Their father was in another room during the strike and survived; he spent the next three days waiting by the ruins while rescuers searched for his family.
In another building, the same strike killed 17-year-olds Artem and Ruslan, who had been friends since kindergarten. After the first explosion, their families left the building and ran toward a shelter. The teenagers did not reach it in time and were killed by the next explosion.
Russia: 67 killed
Meduza confirmed 67 children’s deaths within Russia’s internationally recognized territory:
- Two in 2022
- Six in 2023
- 19 in 2024
- Eight in 2025
- 32 from January through September 2026
The children died in 13 regions. Almost half — 30 — died in the Belgorod region, near the front. Another 14 died in the Krasnodar region, seven in the Kursk region, five in the Bryansk region, and three in the Moscow region. These five regions account for 59 of the 67 deaths.
Russia’s Foreign Ministry previously reported 264 children killed. On October 1, it issued a separate estimate of 70 children killed since the beginning of 2026. One reason the counts differ is that the ministry includes figures from occupied areas: Crimea, Sevastopol, and captured parts of the Donetsk, Luhansk, Zaporizhzhia, and Kherson regions.
Of the 264 deaths reported by Russia, Meduza could link only 99 to specific events and corroborate them through other sources. Of these, 44 are already included in our count, while another 55 occurred within Ukraine’s internationally recognized territory.
For the remaining deaths, Russian authorities published no dates, specific locations, or other information that would allow us to check them. We feel obliged to cite this estimate here, but we cannot call it well founded.
The children’s ages are known in 58 cases. The youngest was 6 months old. His name was Yelisey. During the night of June 30, 2026, a Ukrainian drone hit his family’s house in the Moscow region. The second-floor bedroom, where the boy was with his mother, bore the brunt of the impact. Rescuers searched for Yelisey under the rubble for a long time. He suffered severe burns and died on the way to the hospital.
His 6-year-old brother, Matvey, was pulled out almost unharmed, but after the ordeal he did not speak for more than a day. Their parents were admitted to intensive care. Yelisey’s mother had one leg amputated, then the other after she was transferred to another hospital; his father underwent several complex operations.
Two-year-old Grisha died on June 12, 2025, in Borisovka in the Belgorod region. His grandmother was pushing him in a stroller around the building that day when a Ukrainian drone hit the apartment building. The child was taken to the hospital with a head injury. Doctors tried for several hours to save him.
In Novorossiysk, a Ukrainian drone fell onto a house. An 8-year-old boy died at the scene, while his mother and 6-year-old brother suffered severe injuries and burns. The child was buried in his school uniform: He was due to start second grade in a few weeks. His father is listed as missing in action.
Five-year-old Tolya suffered severe burns in a Ukrainian drone attack on a public beach in Kursk. Citing witnesses, Kursk Governor Alexander Khinshtein said the boy had tried to shield his mother with his body. The child died the next day while being transported to a Moscow hospital.
We found five other deaths that are unquestionably connected to the war but do not meet the international criteria for counting war casualties. We nevertheless believe they must be mentioned.
Three of these five deaths were murders committed by men who had returned from the war.
Former Wagner Group fighter Vladimir Vlasov struck his stepdaughter several times shortly after he was demobilized. The girl died at the scene.
Artem Buchin, who had previously been convicted of rape and murder and was pardoned so he could be sent to the front, raped his former wife after returning, then killed her and her 7-year-old daughter.
Vladimir Alexandrov of Nizhny Tagil, who had also returned from the war, raped and strangled his 11-year-old neighbor Anastasia Yakina.
Buchin and Alexandrov received life sentences. A court sentenced Vlasov to 14 years in a penal colony.
What Russia and Ukraine say about the children killed
Russian officials and state media regularly call those killed in Russia and occupied areas “victims of the Kyiv regime.” This narrative emerged long before the full-scale invasion.
In May 2015, a memorial opened in occupied Donetsk with the inscription “Alley of Angels. In memory of the children of Donbas who were killed.” A granite slab bore 66 names. Russia’s Investigative Committee later described the children as “girls and boys aged 1 to 18” and said they had died in Ukrainian shelling.
On the morning of February 24, 2022, when Putin announced the full-scale invasion, he said he was starting the war to protect people “who have been subjected to abuse and genocide by the Kyiv regime for eight years.” Three weeks later, he explicitly linked this argument to children’s deaths: Western countries, he said, “looked away for the past eight years while mothers in Donbas buried their children.”
Children’s deaths during the war in Donbas are not a propaganda fabrication. But the Alley of Angels memorial does not name every child killed during that period of the Russian-Ukrainian war: It includes only those whom authorities in the self-proclaimed Donetsk People’s Republic declared victims of Ukrainian shelling. Some children, however, died when mines or other munitions of unknown origin exploded. And children killed by shelling from separatists and Russian forces are simply absent from the list.
In all, the U.N. confirmed the deaths of 152 children between April 2014 and the end of 2021. Another 80 children died aboard MH17, which Russia shot down; the organization counts them separately. Since the full-scale invasion began, at least 940 children have died in Ukraine and Russia in a much shorter period — six times as many.
The Ukrainian government considers the deaths of children key evidence that the war is criminal. As early as March 7, 2022, Ukraine’s U.N. representative, Sergiy Kyslytsya, said at the U.N. Security Council that “Russian occupiers are killing Ukrainian children — deliberately and cynically.” At the time, Kyiv had reported 38 children killed and called on the U.N. to force Russia to agree to a ceasefire.
After the most severe attacks, Volodymyr Zelensky typically did not cite overall statistics but pointed to specific cases. When a Russian missile killed a 3-month-old girl in Odesa in April 2022, he said that killing children had become “the Russian Federation’s new national idea.” After nine children died in Kryvyi Rih in April 2025, he said: “It is wrong and dangerous to stay silent about the fact that it is Russia that is killing children with ballistic missiles.”
* * *
Russian propagandists, officials, and Putin himself still invoke the events of 2014–2022 to justify the attack on Ukraine. But once Ukrainian strikes on Russian cities became routine, they added several new arguments to this rhetoric.
At an emergency U.N. Security Council meeting following the shelling of Belgorod on December 30, 2023 — which killed five children — Vasily Nebenzya called the attack “a deliberate act of terrorism” and blamed not only Ukraine but also the United States, the United Kingdom, and European Union countries that supply it with weapons.
A new storyline emerged in this narrative in 2026, triggered by a Ukrainian strike on two colleges in Russian-occupied Starobilsk, where 21 people were killed. Some of those wounded were minors: The initial list of the wounded included 16 teenagers ages 15 to 17. All the teenagers who died were legal adults: the youngest had turned 18 four days before the strike. Russian human rights ombudswoman Yana Lantratova, and propagandists who followed her lead, pointedly described those injured or killed as children when discussing the attack.
Kremlin propaganda also claims that AI developed by the American company Palantir deliberately selected the college as a target. Vladimir Solovyov declared Palantir and its head, Alex Karp, directly responsible for the strike. He also blamed them for the deaths of children in Gaza and Iran, calling what was happening “the bloody harvests of Satanists,” and demanded “revenge for the children.” Military commentator Alexander Artamonov said that strikes on children supposedly constitute “a special method of warfare.”
Ukraine does cooperate with Palantir. Shortly before the attack, Ukraine’s Defense Ministry reported using AI to analyze combat data, identify targets, and plan operations. It has also been proven that Palantir’s technology was used in the strike on a school in Iran. But there is no independent confirmation that Palantir was involved in selecting the target in Starobilsk, let alone that it deliberately chose a student dormitory.
A few days later, rhetoric about those killed in Starobilsk turned into a direct call for revenge — specifically, according to the propagandists, revenge against children. Military commentator Yuri Baranchik said on the radio station of Komsomolskaya Pravda, the pro-Kremlin Russian tabloid, that in response “the children of Zelensky and Yermak should die.” Host Ivan Pankin pushed back, arguing that children should not be held accountable for their parents’ actions. Baranchik insisted that their deaths would strike a painful blow against Ukraine’s leadership.
Russian media have also justified, and even welcomed, strikes on Ukrainian cities that killed children. After a strike on a pizzeria in Kramatorsk in June 2023 killed, among others, two 14-year-old sisters and a 17-year-old girl, Andrei Kartapolov, head of the State Duma’s defense committee, said on propagandist Vladimir Solovyov’s show: “The strike on Kramatorsk was simply brilliant!” He added: “My old military heart rejoices.”
After nine children died in Kryvyi Rih in April 2025, military blogger Yuri Podolyaka called the dead civilians “accidental casualties” and blamed their deaths partly on their own carelessness.
The U.N., Russia’s Foreign Ministry, and the office of Ukraine’s prosecutor general did not respond to Meduza’s requests by the time this story was published.
List of the dead
Behind every number is a real child’s life.
The list below includes 518 of the dead children. We know the names of 409 of them. In another 93 cases, only the age is known, sometimes approximately. For 16 children, Meduza was able to establish only the place of death.
We included in this list only victims about whom we were able to learn at least something. The remaining 422 children in the overall count come from the U.N.’s list — we were unable to find enough information to describe each of them individually. The actual number of children killed is likely even higher.
Why do we trust the U.N.’s list but not the Russian Foreign Ministry’s?
It is worth explaining why Meduza includes U.N. statistics but not Russia’s Foreign Ministry figures.
Neither the U.N. nor Russia’s Foreign Ministry publishes a complete list naming the children killed. The difference is in how they verify information and how thoroughly they explain the basis for their overall death toll.
The U.N. monitoring mission describes its methodology in detail. Staff compare accounts from witnesses and relatives, medical and court documents, investigation records, photographs, videos, and official statements. Where possible, they visit the site. For a death to be included in the statistics, the combined evidence must provide “reasonable grounds to believe” that the event happened as described in the accounts and documents. This does not guarantee an error-free count, but it is a defined, publicly stated verification standard.
The U.N. mission operates under a mandate from the U.N. High Commissioner for Human Rights, rather than the Russian or Ukrainian government, and documents violations by both sides. Its count extends beyond territory controlled by Kyiv: For example, of the 669 children’s deaths confirmed for 2022–2024 in a thematic report, 148 occurred in Russian-occupied areas.
Russia’s Foreign Ministry is an agency of the state that launched the war. Its reports focus exclusively on victims of actions the Kremlin blames on Ukraine. This does not in itself make the reports of deaths false — the report’s compilers said they gather data from Russia’s Emergencies Ministry, Health Ministry, ambulance services, and regional authorities. But the U.N. explains how it verifies each death before including it in the count. The Foreign Ministry does not disclose how it checks reports or ensures that the same child has not been counted twice. We therefore cannot verify its overall figure.

articles.title: Europe has 11 ways to choke Russia’s war. It doesn’t need Trump’s permission for any of them
articles.body:
On 9 October, three weeks after signing the first major Russia oil sanctions in two years, Donald Trump agreed with Vladimir Putin to bring Russian diesel back to world markets. The US Treasury suspended its sanctions on that trade until April 2027 the same day. In the two days before, Russian strikes had killed more than 80 Ukrainian civilians.
Europe answered on 12 October with its largest sanctions package yet: nearly 1,600 new listings, almost all in Russia’s military-industrial complex. Its core, says Ukraine’s sanctions envoy Vladyslav Vlasiuk, is Russia’s missile program and the electronics inside it, from capacitors to semiconductors. Six in ten listings came from Ukrainian proposals, and Brussels adopted them within weeks.
That is the right reflex, and proof that Europe can move fast when it chooses. But the package names companies and people one by one. On the measures that cut whole sectors, the ones that would hurt Moscow most, Europe still waits for Washington.
It waits for Trump to decide whether to enforce the Graham Act he signed in September. It waits for him to decide whether to lean on Hungary and Slovakia or let them off. It waits for the G7 to rule on tanker services before touching its own ships. Europe keeps asking the Trump administration to decide things it is perfectly able to decide itself.
If the EU is serious about ending a war on its own continent, it does not need a miracle from Washington. It needs to pull the levers already in its hands. Here they are.
Strip Russian weapons of European parts
1. Fix export-control enforcement on dual-use goods. It is unacceptable that the newest Russian drones and missiles contain not only Chinese parts but American and European ones. The "War and Sanctions" portal logs what turns up. The EU should find and close the enforcement gaps in its own dual-use export law. Choking the supply to Russia's war industry serves Ukraine and Europe alike.
Cut Russia's energy money
2. Force Hungary and Slovakia off Russian oil. The EU banned Russian oil imports in 2022, with temporary exemptions for landlocked states: Czechia, Slovakia, Hungary. Czechia has since diversified and dropped Russian oil entirely. Slovakia and Hungary can do the same; the Czech case proves it is a question of will, not feasibility. Ending the exemptions would also make good on REPowerEU's central promise, phasing out Russian energy. The gas-import ban is already decided. Oil is the gap that remains.
3. Close the Greek and Maltese tanker loophole. Up to 40% of Russia's seaborne oil travels on European tankers, Greek and Maltese. The EU has banned maritime services for Russian oil since 2022, with one exception: cargoes sold below the price cap. This spring the Council discussed scrapping that exception, which would have meant a full ban, then made any change conditional on coordination with the G7. Once again, Europe is asking Washington to act for it. The EU should overcome Greek and Maltese resistance and ban every maritime service for Russian oil: transport, insurance, and the rest.
4. Stop the shadow fleet in European waters. Russia ships oil to India, China, and Türkiye through a shadow fleet of aging, often uninsured tankers. Europe can check their insurance and turn away any that lack EU or G7 cover, especially in the North Sea and the Baltic, where any spill would be an ecological disaster, and an uninsured operator would not pay for it.
Patrols in territorial waters and exclusive economic zones have to be reinforced. Russia also uses these ships for espionage, sabotage, and damage to undersea infrastructure. Strengthen NATO's Baltic Sentry. Consider adding a maritime operation by the UK-led Joint Expeditionary Force or the Coalition of the Willing across the North and Baltic Seas and the Skagerrak, before the Danish straits. If the Russian Baltic Fleet escalates, Europe should be ready for confrontation. Moscow should hear that it is not feared and that it will be stopped. At sea, it is weaker than even NATO's Baltic Sea states alone, never mind NATO's European members together.
5. Scrap the Lingen nuclear-fuel deal. In July, Lower Saxony approved a plan for the French state company Framatome to make nuclear fuel jointly with Rosatom, Russia's builder of nuclear weapons, at Lingen. It is dressed up as serving REPowerEU, since the venture lets Hungary, Slovakia, and Bulgaria buy fuel from a Franco-Russian joint operation instead of straight from Rosatom.
This is nonsense. Ukraine was once wholly dependent on Russian nuclear fuel and diversified fast; Finland and Czechia have done the same. Hungary, Slovakia, and Bulgaria can follow. Stretching the dependence out and hiding it behind a French partner is the opposite of what REPowerEU is for. Lower Saxony's own environment minister called the deal "grundfalsch," fundamentally wrong.
Fund Ukraine from Russia's own money
6. Build a Ukraine Fund from frozen Russian assets. Supporting Ukraine will cost more next year, not less, so it is time to get serious about Russia's frozen assets. Not confiscation, which European capitals still resist, and not a simple transfer to Kyiv, which amounts to the same thing, but a dedicated EU-run Ukraine Fund that could invest these assets and use them better than they are used now. ICUV has set it all out in a policy paper.
Isolate Russia further
7. Adopt the Graham-bill sanctions. Sanction every Russian state company (majority or controlling state stake) and every Russian oligarch who has not taken a public anti-war stand. Forbes counts 155 Russian billionaires.
8. Cut every Russian and Belarusian bank off SWIFT. Russia still has 301 operating banks, yet only 103 Russian banks and financial institutions sit under the EU's transaction ban, and just a handful of Belarusian ones. Gazprombank, which the US Treasury says pays Russia's soldiers, is still not on the EU list. Stop listing banks one by one: disconnect the entire Russian and Belarusian banking systems and put them under a full transaction ban, with narrow exceptions for food, medicine, and humanitarian trade.
9. End land transit to and from Russia, Kaliningrad included. Stop all overland freight, rail and road, between the EU and Russia. Baltic ports should carry no Russian trade at all, not just grain. Halt the gas transit to Kaliningrad through Lithuania's pipelines, too; let it arrive by sea, where Russia already runs an LNG terminal. Winters are mild now, so the real effect is mostly higher costs, and even that is worth doing.
10. Ban visas for Russian (ex-)servicemen and their families. The EU's 21st sanctions package laid the legal basis in July and then set no start date. Bring it into force, and extend it to the families.
Deliver accountability
11. Launch the Tribunal for the Crime of Aggression and the Claims Commission. Speed up the creation of, and accession to, the tribunal for the crime of aggression against Ukraine, and the convention establishing a Claims Commission.
The point
Europe cannot escape this burden. A Russian victory, even a partial one such as a peace on Moscow's terms, would cost it far more than helping Ukraine to a partial victory of its own, a peace along the line of contact. If Europe wants the war to end, it has to lead, alongside Ukraine, instead of waiting on a miracle from the Trump administration. The tools are already in its hands.

articles.title: Second Day of Houthi Strikes Hits Riyadh and Dammam Airports
articles.body:
A second consecutive day of attacks on Saudi Arabia's airports left one person dead and 11 injured at Riyadh's King Khalid International Airport on Sunday, according to Saudi civil aviation authorities, as Yemen's Iran-backed Houthi rebels claimed responsibility for a series of strikes.
An unidentified projectile struck Terminal 4 at the Riyadh airport and sparked a fire, while air defenses intercepted a cruise missile nearby. Saudi authorities later identified the person killed in Sunday's attack as a Pakistani national. The airport has faced several attacks over the past week.
The new strike came a day after a Houthi missile attack killed 13 people and injured more than 300, according to one account, making it the deadliest attack on a Gulf country since the US-Iran war began in March. Another report put Saturday's death toll at 12. The attacks marked an apparent escalation in the Houthis' conflict with Saudi Arabia and the Yemeni government backed by Riyadh.
Following Saturday's strike, Saudi authorities extended the airport closure and announced that schools would switch to online learning until Thursday.
The Houthis claimed to have carried out several attacks on Saudi airports and other targets. A spokesman said the group had "carried out four qualitative operations in the past 24 hours using ballistic and cruise missiles and drones." The targets included Riyadh airport, Dammam airport in eastern Saudi Arabia and two facilities belonging to state oil company Aramco.
Saudi authorities confirmed on Sunday evening that King Fahd International Airport in Dammam had also been attacked. The General Authority of Civil Aviation said on X that "The assessment of the damage and verification of the safety of airport facilities were still under way, in coordination with the relevant authorities."
The Houthis warned airlines, passengers and airport workers to stay away from Saudi airports and airspace, saying further attacks would follow if Saudi military operations in Yemen continued. In a statement circulated on social media, the group said airports in Mecca and Medina would not be targeted and urged people to heed its warnings, adding that Saudi Arabia would bear responsibility for failed interceptions.
Videos shared on social media showed travelers moving across debris-strewn areas of Riyadh airport as sirens sounded. Those killed in Saturday's missile strike included four Saudi citizens, two Bangladeshis, a Palestinian, a US citizen, an Egyptian, a Jordanian, a Syrian and a Sudanese national. The Indian embassy in Saudi Arabia said an Indian citizen who had been wounded in Saturday's attack died on Sunday.
Egyptian state television identified the Egyptian woman killed in the attack as 28-year-old flight attendant Azza Ramzy, who worked for Saudi airline Flynas. A relative told the Associated Press that the Syrian victim, Buthaina Ahmad Oweida, was a widowed mother of four who had lived in Saudi Arabia for five years. Her niece, Nisreen Oweida, said the 56-year-old came from Syria's northern Idlib province and had left during the country's civil war. She lived in Mecca and was returning from visiting her sister in Riyadh when she was killed.
On Saturday night, Maj. Gen. Turki al-Maliki, spokesman for the Saudi-led coalition fighting the Houthis in Yemen, pledged that the coalition would "respond firmly" to the attack, without providing further details. The coalition has also described the Houthi strikes as a "full-fledged war crime."
The Houthis said a Saudi airstrike hit a house in Sana'a, Yemen's rebel-held capital, on Sunday, killing a child and wounding six others. The Houthi-run health authority said coalition airstrikes had killed 91 Yemenis and injured 168 over the previous six weeks, with women and children accounting for 60% of the casualties. Saudi authorities did not immediately comment on the claims. Houthi-run Al Masirah TV also reported a Saudi strike on Sana'a's international airport on Sunday afternoon.
The British embassy in Saudi Arabia advised people on X to avoid all but essential travel to Jeddah and Dammam and to stay away from almost all airports. Australia urged its citizens in Riyadh to shelter in place as the attacks intensified.
The strikes have raised concerns that more countries could be drawn into the Yemen conflict, further widening the regional consequences of the US-Iran war, which has already spread to Lebanon and Iraq. The increasing intensity of Houthi attacks on Riyadh and Saudi energy infrastructure has brought additional foreign involvement in the conflict, as governments face pressure over oil prices already elevated by the war with Iran.
US President Donald Trump said on Saturday that he would speak with Saudi Crown Prince Mohammed bin Salman after the airport attack. Trump told reporters the strike was "not acceptable" and said Washington was considering whether to join Saudi military operations against the Houthis, adding, "We're going to look into it."
The United States has provided intelligence cooperation and targeting assistance, with about 200 US military advisers stationed in Saudi Arabia to support the campaign, but has not directly participated in fighting the Houthis. Direct US involvement could prompt the group to resume attacks on ships passing through the Bab al-Mandab Strait, a route used by about 10% of global maritime goods. It could also deepen US involvement in Middle Eastern conflicts as American public frustration with the ongoing war with Iran grows. Trump faces November midterm elections as an unpopular war and rising prices threaten his party's performance.
Saudi Arabia has increased its military operations against the Houthis in recent weeks, backing a Yemeni government counteroffensive after the rebels seized strategic territory along the Red Sea coast last month. The Houthis launched a campaign to capture Yemen's Red Sea coast in early September, following months of escalating tensions with the government and its Saudi patron. The offensive ended years of relative calm after a UN-brokered ceasefire in 2022 froze the front lines.
Saudi-backed government forces have sought to retake areas seized by the Houthis over the past month. Despite reporting initial gains, the government forces have not dislodged the rebels from positions near the Bab al-Mandab Strait, including Perim Island. The Houthis appear to have retained their recent gains, and it remains unclear what further Saudi action against the group would involve. The rebels previously withstood years of airstrikes by an international coalition and the United States.
Saudi Arabia led an international coalition that intervened in Yemen in 2015 after the Houthis captured Sana'a and toppled the government. Recent Houthi attacks on Saudi energy infrastructure and the group's military advances have drawn Riyadh back into the war.
The attacks prompted international condemnation, including from UN Secretary-General António Guterres and European Commission President Ursula von der Leyen. Von der Leyen wrote on X that "Attacks by Iran's proxies are pushing the region into a spiral of violence," adding that they were destabilizing major global transport and energy hubs.
German Foreign Minister Johann Wadephul firmly condemned what he called a "terrorist act against Saudi Arabia and civil aviation," and sent condolences to the victims' relatives. UK Defense Secretary Wes Streeting described the attacks as "contemptible" and a "dangerous escalation." France's Foreign Ministry condemned the "heinous attack" and expressed its "total solidarity" with Saudi Arabia. Russia also condemned the Houthi attack and called for hostilities to end through "political and diplomatic means."
On Monday, Saudi Arabia, Pakistan and Turkey issued a joint statement pledging to accelerate implementation of their mutual defense pact, including by speeding up the deployment of military forces in the kingdom. The United Kingdom said it would provide defensive military support to Riyadh by refueling aircraft involved in intercepting Houthi missiles. Saudi Arabia has also sought additional assistance from France, Egypt, the UK and Pakistan as its stocks of interceptor missiles run low.

articles.title: Accuracy Problems: Russia Developing New Kinzhal Missile Warhead
articles.body:
Russia is developing a new version of its air-launched Kinzhal ballistic missile with a high-explosive fragmentation warhead, potentially in response to problems with its accuracy, Ukraine’s military intelligence agency (HUR) said.
On Monday, Oct. 12, HUR disclosed the assessment alongside an interactive 3D model of the missile and information about its components and manufacturers published on its War & Sanctions website.
JOIN US ON TELEGRAM
Follow our coverage of the war on the @Kyivpost_official.
The Kinzhal, designated 9-S-7760 and widely known as the Kh-47M2, currently has two warhead configurations: a penetrating high-explosive warhead designed to breach reinforced structures and a nuclear warhead. Its published specifications list a warhead weight of 450 kilograms (992 pounds).
The proposed modification would add a high-explosive fragmentation warhead, which causes damage through both blast and fragments.
HUR said the development could be directly linked to guidance problems, noting that precision is particularly important for a penetrating warhead intended to strike hardened targets.
Russia significantly reduced its state defense orders for Kinzhal missiles in 2026, redirecting manufacturing capacity, components, and raw materials toward the ground-launched 9M723 Iskander-M ballistic missile, HUR said.
The agency attributed that shift to the Kinzhal’s accuracy problems and limitations affecting the aircraft used to launch it.
Kinzhal missiles are carried by modified MiG-31I and MiG-31K interceptor aircraft. HUR said those aircraft have a limited remaining service life and are no longer manufactured by Russia’s aviation industry.

The Kinzhal is a single-stage, solid-fuel missile, with an integrated warhead. According to HUR, about 90% of its components are common to the Iskander-M’s 9M723 missile.
Key differences include a tail fairing that separates after the engine starts, a radar seeker described by Russia as capable of operating in all weather, and an active jamming system alongside equipment that releases decoys.
HUR’s online model identifies components including the missile’s radar seeker, navigation equipment, solid-fuel engine, and penetrating warhead, as well as the companies involved in their manufacture.
