France Enters Sixth-Generation Fighter Race Solo, Unveils “Super Rafale” Plans
France is moving ahead with its own sixth-generation fighter jet after the collapse of its joint aviation project with Germany, while preparing an advanced “Super Rafale” equipped with artificial intelligence, upgraded engines, and next-generation weapons.
French Air and Space Force Chief of Staff General Jérôme Bellanger outlined plans to accelerate the country’s independent fighter development program and modernize its existing combat aircraft fleet, according to French newspaper Les Echos on October 11.
We bring you stories from the ground. Your support keeps our team in the field.
The move follows the breakdown of the Franco-German Future Combat Air System (FCAS) program, which was intended to produce a next-generation European fighter. France is now pursuing its own aircraft, designated ACF (Avion de Combat du Futur), replacing the previously planned New Generation Fighter (NGF) concept.
Development of the ACF is expected to enter a phase leading to a flying prototype in 2027, with work on an operational version scheduled to begin in 2029. Meanwhile, France plans to officially launch development of the Rafale F5, known as the “Super Rafale,” in December 2026.
The upgraded fighter will feature a new engine, advanced sensors, artificial intelligence, and a high-speed missile designed for France’s airborne nuclear deterrent. It will also serve as a technological foundation for the future sixth-generation aircraft.
France prepares AI-powered fighter and drone operations
France is also developing technology that will allow fighter jets to operate alongside unmanned aircraft.
Under the HypAIRion program, two Mirage 2000 fighters have been converted into flying laboratories to test artificial intelligence systems. The initiative aims to conduct its first coordinated flight involving a Rafale and an accompanying drone in 2028.
According to Les Echos, Dassault Aviation has already tested two AI algorithms aboard a Rafale and simulated a firing engagement involving a Harmattan AI drone.
The technology is intended to improve threat detection, targeting, and coordination between crewed aircraft and drones, allowing them to operate together against enemy air defenses.
France plans 60 more fighter jets by 2035
France also intends to expand its fighter fleet from approximately 170 aircraft to at least 230 by 2035—an increase of more than 35%.
Bellanger said the existing fleet is already being operated at a rate more than 15% above normal utilization levels, reflecting growing demands on French airpower.
The French Air and Space Force is also establishing two new squadrons at Cazaux Air Base. One will operate reconnaissance and strike drones, while the other will focus on high-altitude threats, including ballistic missiles and surveillance balloons.
According to Les Echos, France’s proposed 2027 defense budget includes up to €3 billion in procurement authorizations for the Rafale F5 program and another €2.7 billion for the ACF fighter. Both programs remain dependent on parliamentary budget approval.
The modernization effort comes as European air forces adapt to threats highlighted by Russia’s war against Ukraine, including the widespread use of attack drones and missiles.
The Franco-German Future Combat Air System (FCAS) had previously faced repeated delays due to conflicting national priorities and disagreements over industrial cooperation. Similar challenges affected the joint Main Ground Combat System (MGCS) tank project, raising broader concerns about the future of Franco-German defense cooperation.

Ukraine Reveals Russia’s Kinzhal Missile Secrets—From Nuclear Warheads to 22 Unsanctioned Manufacturers
Ukraine’s Defense Intelligence Directorate (HUR) has revealed new details about Russia’s Kh-47M2 Kinzhal aeroballistic missile, identifying 58 Russian companies involved in its production, 22 of which remain outside international sanctions.
The findings were published on HUR’s War&Sanctions portal, alongside an interactive 3D model of the missile, detailed information about its components, and a list of Russian enterprises involved in its manufacturing.
We bring you stories from the ground. Your support keeps our team in the field.
According to Ukrainian intelligence, the Kinzhal, officially designated 9-S-7760, is a single-stage, solid-fuel missile with an integrated warhead. Approximately 90% of its components are shared with the 9M723 ballistic missile used in Russia’s Iskander-M operational-tactical missile system.
Despite these similarities, the Kinzhal has several distinguishing features, including a tail aerodynamic fairing that separates after engine ignition and a radar seeker that Russia describes as capable of operating in all weather conditions.
HUR noted that while an active radar seeker has been proposed for the Iskander missile, its use in strikes against Ukraine has not been documented. The Kinzhal also features an active electronic jamming system alongside its S-200 decoy deployment system.
Ukrainian intelligence identified two types of warheads currently used in the Kinzhal: a penetrating high-explosive warhead and a specialized nuclear warhead. The penetrating version has a thick metal casing designed to breach reinforced concrete and other fortified structures.
Russia is also reportedly developing a new modification equipped with a high-explosive fragmentation warhead. According to HUR, this development could be linked to problems with the missile’s guidance accuracy, as penetrating warheads require greater precision to effectively strike hardened targets.
These reported limitations have also coincided with a shift in Russia’s missile production priorities. HUR said Moscow significantly reduced its state defense orders for Kinzhal missiles in 2026, redirecting manufacturing capacity, components, and raw materials toward producing 9M723 Iskander-M ballistic missiles.
Another factor behind this shift is the limited availability of aircraft capable of carrying Kinzhal missiles. These include modified MiG-31I interceptor aircraft and their predecessors, the MiG-31K, neither of which is currently being produced by Russia’s aviation industry.
HUR said it plans to release a separate list of Russian companies responsible for modernizing and maintaining these aircraft.
Beyond the missile’s technical characteristics, Ukrainian intelligence also highlighted gaps in international sanctions targeting Russia’s defense industry.
Of the 58 Russian enterprises identified as participants in Kinzhal production, 22 have not been sanctioned by any country in the international sanctions coalition.
“Despite certain shortcomings, Russia continues its efforts to modernize its Kinzhal missiles. To counter the aggressor’s plans, it is necessary to coordinate sanctions against all companies involved in their production and strengthen controls over technologies actively used by the Russian Federation,” HUR added.
The disclosure comes amid Ukrainian efforts to target Russian facilities associated with the production of missile systems, including the Kinzhal. Satellite imagery previously revealed significant damage to Russia’s Volgogradpromproekt chemical plant, a facility linked to the production of Iskander, Kinzhal, and Kalibr missiles, following a Ukrainian strike involving an FP-5 Flamingo cruise missile.

articles.title: Zelenskyy vows to retaliate if Russian strikes on Ukraine’s power grid continue
articles.body:
Volodymyr Zelenskyy has vowed to respond to Russia’s continuing attacks on the Ukrainian power grid as European leaders rally around Kyiv amid a feud with Donald Trump over Ukraine’s strikes on oil refineries.
Speaking to a gathering of European security officials in Warsaw on Monday, the Ukrainian president said Kyiv would retaliate if strikes on its power grid continued: “If Russia does not agree to an energy ceasefire this winter, we will respond.”
On Sunday, Trump announced an “energy ceasefire” between Kyiv and Moscow that Zelenskyy said neither side had agreed to. On Monday, Zelenskyy said he was “surprised” by the post, which went online while Kyiv was being attacked by Russian Shahed drones.
Russia then launched a “targeted attack” on a Kharkiv power station hours later, as much of Kyiv was plunged into darkness. “It’s clear that Putin does not read Truth Social,” Zelenskyy said.
Russia bombed six energy facilities on Monday, injuring 33 people, the Ukrainian president said. “It is becoming increasingly clear that Russia does not want to agree to the energy ceasefire proposed by the US and intends to continue its terrorist air attacks against our communities,” he added.
Zelenskyy also suggested that Ukraine’s recent counter-strikes on datacentres belonging to the Russian technology company Yandex had reduced the number of bots posting messages in Europe and the US. “It suddenly became a little easier to breathe on many social platforms. There was less hate, less division and fewer provocations,” he said.
The Kremlin refused to say on Monday whether it agreed with Trump’s Truth Social post, which claimed a ceasefire was “effective immediately”. It also rejected Zelenskyy’s proposal that Russia stop bombing for 60 days so Ukraine could hold a presidential election. Moscow wanted an overall peace deal first, it said, which, for the Kremlin, means Kyiv’s capitulation.
The fast-moving row between Washington and Kyiv began on Friday, when Trump announced he was lifting sanctions on Russian diesel exports. He said the move would reduce global and domestic fuel prices before next month’s US midterm elections.
Both Republican and Democratic politicians have criticised the move, pointing out that the deal violates a US law that blocks Russian energy imports. On Monday Trump defended it. “I made the right choice for the American People – ALWAYS, AMERICA FIRST!” he wrote in a social media post.
Earlier a furious Zelenskyy called the decision “weak” and said it would generate “billions” in extra revenue for Putin, enabling him to wage war “even more intensely”. An equally irate Trump said Zelenskyy should “damn well stop” hitting Russian refineries. Ukraine needed a “new leader”, he said on Saturday.
Ukraine has said it is ready to negotiate an energy ceasefire that would take the pressure off its electricity grid before the winter. European leaders have voiced support for Kyiv in its dispute with Washington, saying Russia was responsible for the continuing strikes on energy infrastructure in both countries.
“We welcome the energy ceasefire when it holds,” the EU foreign policy chief, Kaja Kallas, said at a meeting of European foreign ministers on Monday. “We haven’t yet seen that also Russia will stick to it.”
Ministers from the Baltic states criticised a US decision to lift sanctions on imports of Russian diesel, which had been blocked as part of punishment for Putin launching the full-scale invasion of Ukraine in 2022.
“This deal doesn’t help, neither the crisis of the oil products, nor the unity within the transatlantic community when it concerns Russia,” said Lithuania’s foreign minister, Keʂtutis Budrys. “And it is not the European way. Our way is to increase pressure because we already see how it works.”
Russia has increased its attacks on Ukrainian infrastructure, using jet-powered drones and ballistic missiles ahead of the cold winter months, leading to blackouts and water shortages far earlier in the season than has been usual during the war.
Trump’s proposal was for both sides to halt strikes on oil refineries but Kallas said that deal favoured Russia, which has far more refineries.
The US president has blamed the high price of diesel on Ukraine’s attacks, rather than the global shock to energy markets from the US war in Iran and the subsequent closure of the strait of Hormuz.
According to the Financial Times, the US has threatened to stop the procurement system that provides Ukraine with weapons, paid for by its European allies. The White House has also said it could turn off intelligence sharing unless Kyiv halts its long-range strikes on Russian oil refineries.
The Kyiv Independent newspaper said Ukraine’s commander in chief, Mykhailo Drapatyi, had received a call from the US telling him to stop bombing. “They called all the top military officials with threats,” a Ukrainian official told the newspaper.
Ben Hodges, the former head of US forces in Europe, described the energy ceasefire “deal” as a fantasy and “a classic ‘Trumpian’ announcement of something not based on any facts.”
“No one should be misled,” he said, adding that Russia “never adheres to any agreements unless forced to do so”.
He urged Ukraine’s military to ignore Trump and “ramp up” their attacks on Russian oil and gas complexes. “Clearly, this is having a very significant effect. Otherwise, you wouldn’t be hearing all this pressure from the Kremlin on the White House demanding that it stop. Of course, it is having a huge impact.”

articles.title: North Korea Fires Multiple Ballistic Missiles as Tensions with South Korea Rise
articles.body:
North Korea fired multiple ballistic missiles toward the sea off its east coast on Monday, South Korea’s military said, marking Pyongyang’s fourth launch in a month and following Seoul’s recent test of a hypersonic missile.
The ballistic missiles, which appeared to be of different types, were fired at around 9:20 a.m. local time (0020 GMT) from near Pyongyang, and one type flew more than 900 km (559 miles), South Korea’s Joint Chiefs of Staff said.

Follow our coverage of the war on the @Kyivpost_official.
Earlier, Japan’s coast guard said North Korea had fired two unidentified projectiles, believed to be ballistic missiles, adding that both appeared to have already fallen.
South Korea’s National Security Office convened an emergency meeting, where it condemned the missile launches as violations of United Nations Security Council resolutions and urged an immediate stop.
North Korea has been under UN sanctions since 2006, aimed at halting Pyongyang’s development of nuclear weapons and ballistic missiles.
North vs South: Power play
The latest launches come at a time when tensions have been rising between the two Koreas in recent weeks amid weapons tests by both countries.
Last week, South Korean President Lee Jae Myung oversaw the country’s first test-firing of a hypersonic missile, a rare public showcasing of a missile test by a South Korean president.
Monday’s missile launches by North Korea appeared to be “a show of force in response to the successful test launch of our hypersonic missile, as well as an intentional demonstration of missile capabilities,” a spokesperson for South Korea’s Joint Chiefs of Staff said.

North Korea last fired a ballistic missile on October 3, with state media KCNA saying it was a hypersonic missile tested under the supervision of leader Kim Jong Un.
The tests followed a border mine blast last month that wounded three South Korean soldiers. Seoul said the landmines had been planted by North Korea and demanded an apology, but Pyongyang has dismissed this and accused South Korea of provocation.
Pyongyang has conducted missile tests on more than 10 occasions this year, including four in the last month.
The unusually frequent tests indicate Pyongyang wanted to increase its leverage ahead of a potential summit between leader Kim and US President Donald Trump, said Song Seong-jong, a professor at Daejeon University in Seoul and a former South Korean Defence Ministry official.
“They definitely need to raise the value of their status before meeting Trump,” Song said.

articles.title: EU blacklists 1,569 Russian arms suppliers and their bosses in its biggest sanctions round ever, as Trump eases up on Moscow
articles.body:
The EU adopted its largest-ever round of sanctions listings on 12 October, targeting the suppliers behind Russia’s war industry, the Council of the EU announced. The bloc acted as Russia keeps killing Ukrainian civilians every day, while US President Donald Trump eases sanctions on Russian diesel.
Russia’s planned winter campaign against Ukraine’s infrastructure depends on arms factories fed by a web of component suppliers and on oil revenue that still flows despite Ukraine’s refinery strikes, so every supplier cut off from that web raises the cost of waging it. As Washington eases off, Europe’s own pressure has a gap: its ports still take record volumes of Russian Arctic gas, and a full ban on long-term contracts starts only in 2027.
Missile suppliers top the list
More than half of the new listings hit the supply chain for ballistic missiles that Russia “uses to kill Ukrainian civilians every day,” EU foreign policy chief Kaja Kallas said in the statement. Russian attacks killed more than 150 people in the past week, Ukrainian President Volodymyr Zelenskyy said on 11 October.
The list names 826 Russian companies, mid-level firms the Council calls the “core” of Russia’s arms industry, with at least €20 billion in yearly turnover, and 743 people who run them. They make parts for missiles, drones, and military aircraft, from semiconductors and radars to explosives and navigation systems. Their assets are frozen, EU firms may not finance them, and the executives may not enter the EU.
Foreign ministers ratified a deal EU envoys reached on 7 October. Ukraine’s sanctions commissioner Vladyslav Vlasiuk said 60% of the listings came from Ukrainian proposals.
Ministers reject the diesel deal
EU foreign ministers in Luxembourg vowed to keep the sanctions despite Trump’s diesel deal with Russian President Vladimir Putin, Euronews reported. Kallas addressed Washington directly as she arrived.
“The US is our biggest ally, but our message is clear: if we want to end this war, the only way we can do this is (by) putting more pressure on Russia,” Kallas said.
Irish Foreign Minister Helen McEntee called the deal “concerning,” and Lithuanian Foreign Minister Kęstutis Budrys said it was “not the European way.” Kallas warned that an energy truce covering only refineries would favor Russia, since Ukraine has one refinery and Russia “plenty.”
Trump announced the diesel deal on 9 October, and the US Treasury waived sanctions on Russian diesel until April 2027. Zelenskyy said the EU would provide about €3 billion more in military aid this week.
Washington presses Kyiv
Trump expects Ukraine to stop hitting Russian refineries under his proposed energy ceasefire, a White House official told Axios. Zelenskyy said Kyiv would halt such strikes if Moscow did the same. On 10 October, Trump told reporters it was time for Ukraine to get a new president. Germany’s foreign minister, Britain’s defense secretary, and a senior lawmaker from Chancellor Friedrich Merz’s party backed Zelenskyy, while the Kremlin sided with Trump.
Zelenskyy offered to hold elections after a 60-day ceasefire, and Kallas said elections are impossible while the war goes on. The Institute for the Study of War assessed that Russia exploits Ukraine’s legal ban on wartime elections to drag out the war.

NATO believes Europe must step up support for Ukraine to deter Putin – Bloomberg
General Alexus Grynkewich, NATO Supreme Allied Commander Europe, has stated that Europe must step up its support for Ukraine in response to Russian hybrid attacks.
Source: Grynkewich at the Warsaw Security Forum in a comment to Bloomberg
Details: Commenting on the intensifying wave of Russian aggression against Europe, which includes NATO airspace violations, arson, sabotage and cyberattacks, Grynkewich noted: "They're trying to break our collective will."
He cited Denmark and Germany as examples, which increased their aid to Ukraine after hybrid attacks were carried out on their territories.
Quote from Grynkewich: "Those are appropriate responses that show Russia that the objectives that they're seeking to attain are unobtainable."
Details: Bloomberg notes that these attacks occurred against the backdrop of Russian leader Vladimir Putin's forces continuing to suffer significant losses in Ukraine. Meanwhile, the publication says, Ukrainians are inflicting ever-greater economic damage on the Russian occupiers by conducting numerous attacks on oil refineries and data centres deep inside Russia.
NATO, as before, largely leaves it to individual countries to respond to such incidents independently. Last month, Germany, for the first time, officially accused Russia of attempting to attack Leipzig Airport using a drone laden with explosives.
Quote from Grynkewich: "I'm certainly not afraid to attribute it [to Russia]. If a nation wants me to, I'm happy to talk about it."
Details: The news platform notes that although political forces criticising further support for Ukraine are gaining traction in Europe and decisive elections are set to take place in 2027, Grynkewich expressed his conviction that they will be "subsumed" by Ukraine's "centrality" to European security.
Quote from Grynkewich: "I think it will become very obvious to them very quickly what the right thing to do is, and why it's necessary for their own national security."
Details: Bloomberg explains that Grynkewich is in Poland to present his plans on how to swiftly defeat Russia should it invade NATO territory amid rising tensions between the military alliance and Russia.
The disclosure of the "theory of victory" is intended to deter Russia by demonstrating what would happen if it seized NATO territory, he noted.
Grynkewich added that drones and artificial intelligence technologies are an integral part of this strategy, primarily augmenting the advantages NATO already holds over Russia, such as F-35 fighter jets.
When asked whether these efforts might be hampered by US President Donald Trump's agreement with Putin on diesel fuel imports from Russia to the US, he replied that he was focusing exclusively on military matters.
"Windows of opportunity come and go. We have to look for those windows of opportunity and seize them when they're available," he said regarding the establishment a dialogue aimed at ending the war between Ukraine and Russia.

Ukrainian marines cleared about 6 km² near Pokrovsk without losses. The Russians they faced got a can of meat a week. The deputy commander says the operation also yielded a lot of intelligence—and that more surprises await Russia.
Ten casualties to one, by a NATO official’s count: Russia’s September in Ukraine’s kill zones. Russia kept sending troops into drone-packed kill zones in September, and up to 28,000 died, a senior NATO official told Bloomberg.
Russia’s supply base in occupied Luhansk Oblast burned overnight—NASA’s fire map caught it. The fires broke out together and grew within the hour, satellite data show, and Ukrainian monitoring channel Exilenova+ reported heavy Ukrainian strikes in the area.
Short on interceptors, Ukraine goes after the launchers: eight Russian ballistic systems hit, three destroyed since September, a minister says. Ukraine's Defense Minister says the hits made Moscow rework planned barrages, as he presses partners for anti-ballistic missiles in bulk instead of one-off deliveries.
Intelligence and technology
Russia’s sabotage of Europe should bring Ukraine more weapons through US purchase scheme, with clear statement of where its red lines lie, NATO’s top European commander says. The PURL program lets allies fund US-made weapons for Ukraine and drew nearly $5.5 billion in pledges before May.
Built by Ukraine’s ex-defense minister and unit that wrecked $12 billion of Russian gear, new interceptor downs two jet drones over Kyiv. Mykhailo Fedorov and Lasar’s Group commander Pavlo Yelizarov developed the drone in a month, Fedorov says.
Russia is building satellite network that could put all of Europe in reach, defense executive warns. Oleksandr Danyliuk, head of the European defense-tech firm Destinus, called Russia’s Rassvet system an extraordinary threat, first to Ukraine and then to Europe.
Russia is hacking cameras across Europe to track arms bound for Ukraine. At home, Ukraine has secured about 40,000 that could guide strikes — WSJ. In 2024, Russian hackers seized residential webcams in Kyiv, according to Ukraine’s Security Service.
International
“Zelenskyy is helping Democrats”: Trump’s MAGA base accuses Ukraine of trying to swing US midterms, says journalist in US. The narrative runs across all levels of the US information space, from anonymous accounts to national television.
Bipartisan US senators say Trump’s Russian diesel deal conflicts with 2022 ban, as he presses Kyiv to spare Russian refineries. The administration says the deal will lower fuel prices, but lawmakers warn it could help finance Russia's war against Ukraine.
Ten years on, Britain’s prime minister says Russia meddled in the Brexit vote—and warns Germany and France. In 2020, London said it saw “no evidence of successful interference.” Now Andy Burnham says Merz told him the AfD is linked to Russia.
Political and legal developments
For years, Hungary tied Ukraine’s whole EU course to ethnic Hungarians’ language rights. Kyiv has now passed the schooling law meant to lift the block. Hungary had blocked four stages of Ukraine’s membership process over the matter.
EU blacklists 1,569 Russian arms suppliers and their bosses in its biggest sanctions round ever, as Trump eases up on Moscow. Most of the listed firms feed the supply chain behind the ballistic missiles Russia fires at Ukrainian cities, and EU ministers vowed to keep up the pressure despite the US-Russia fuel arrangement.
Zelenskyy says Ukraine could hold elections if Russia agrees to 60-day ceasefire. Moscow counters with truce lasting only voting day. Spokesperson Dmitry Peskov says Ukraine needs the 60 days not to hold elections but to heal its wounds and keep fighting.
New developments
Peacekeepers, riot police, and drone crews: Russia’s bloc rehearses an operation in a Belarusian oblast bordering two NATO states. Police and national guard units train alongside soldiers from five former Soviet states, under priorities Russia set as the bloc’s chair this year.
Germany stays in Russia’s sabotage crosshairs, and its industry now braces for the long haul. Companies are no random targets, the country’s main industry lobby warns, a week after the foreign intelligence chief said Germany had become a main obstacle to Russian power in Europe.

articles.title: Ukraine war latest: Russian drones strike Kyiv morning and evening, kill woman, injure 14
articles.body:
Ukraine war latest: Russian drones strike Kyiv morning and evening, kill woman, injure 14
Key developments on Oct. 12:
- Russian drone attacks throughout the day strike Kyiv apartment block, kill woman, injure 14
- Russia strikes Roshen confectionery factory in Vinnytsia
- New interceptor drone destroys two Russian Geran-5 drones in first week, Fedorov says
- SBU detains 19-year-old suspected of plotting bomb attack on bus full of soldiers
- Fire Point trolls Russia's Yandex after drone attack on data center
- Russia-led military bloc launches joint military drills in Belarus
Russian drone attacks hit Kyiv twice on Oct. 12, killing one person and injuring at least 14 others, city authorities said.
During an evening attack, a Russian drone struck a 25-story residential building in Kyiv's Darnytskyi District, according to the Kyiv City Military Administration.
A woman was killed in the strike, while 11 people were injured, Mayor Vitali Klitschko said.
Earlier in the day, Russia launched a drone attack on Kyiv, injuring three people, including an elderly woman.
Klitschko first said at 11:32 a.m. local time that air defenses were operating in the city.
Drone debris fell in an open area near residential buildings in the Solomyanskyi District of Kyiv and on a house in Darnytskyi District, while in the Pecherskyi District, a fire caused by wreckage of a drone that had crashed near a building was brought under control, Klitschko said.
Yuliia Sheremet, 38, the owner of the house that was damaged in Darnytskyi District, told the Kyiv Independent that her elderly, disabled father was at home when the attack occurred.
Sheremet was working not far away at the time, so she "immediately ran" to her house when she heard explosions and saw the smoke rise.
"And I saw there was no home anymore..."
Her father was injured but survived. Neighbors helped her to get him out. "It's nothing short of a miracle that Dad didn't die today," Sheremet said.
"I'm in shock... It's impossible to live like that, and I don't know how to carry on. We're all exhausted. We need help so that we can defend Ukraine."
Kyiv resident Yana Mohal, 25, woke up to a "horrible and loud" sound in Darnytskyi District, she told the Kyiv Independent. She went outside to see whether she could help Sheremet's father, an "elderly man with a dog," who was trapped in a damaged house.
Mohal added that it was the first time that the Russian attack had struck so close to her.
Russia is regularly attacking Kyiv and other cities across Ukraine. At least 16 people were killed and more than 100 others injured in Kyiv and the surrounding region between Sept. 25 and Oct. 2, according to a Kyiv Independent count based on official reports.

Russia strikes Roshen confectionery factory in Vinnytsia
Russia struck a production complex belonging to Ukrainian confectionery company Roshen in Vinnytsia on Oct. 12, the company said.
"Thanks to the timely activation of the warning system and the prompt evacuation, the lives of employees were saved," Roshen said in a statement.
Vinnytsia Oblast authorities earlier reported that a Russian attack had hit a civilian infrastructure facility in the city and caused a fire. More than 50 rescuers and 13 pieces of emergency equipment were deployed to the site, while explosive ordnance specialists inspected the surrounding area. No injuries were reported.
Roshen later confirmed that its Vinnytsia production complex had been hit.
The company rejected claims circulating in Russian media that its facilities were being used to manufacture drones.
"The corporation's enterprises produce confectionery products and do not manufacture drones or other products for military purposes. The production complex in Vinnytsia is a civilian facility," the company said.
The company did not immediately disclose the extent of the damage to the plant.
"Strikes on food industry facilities endanger the lives of civilian workers, destroy production capacity and jobs, and disrupt the supply of goods," Roshen added.
read also
New interceptor drone destroys two Russian Geran-5 drones in first week, Fedorov says
A new model of interceptor drone developed by former Ukrainian Defense Minister Mykhailo Fedorov has been tested successfully, Fedorov himself claimed on social media, posting video footage of the drone successfully intercepting two Russian Geran-5 drones.
"Our new interceptor is already taking down jet-powered Shaheds over Kyiv. Two Geran-5s down in its first week," Fedorov said.
The development time from conception to the first successful tests was just one month, Fedorov claimed, while the new interceptor was deployed by "Lasar's Group," a special forces unit within the 27th Separate Brigade of Ukraine's National Guard.
The successful test comes as Ukrainian cities are under repeated assault from Russia's new generation of jet-powered drones, especially the Geran-5, which blurs the line between a drone and a cruise missile, according to experts.
"The Geran-5 much more resembles a low-cost cruise missile than a long-range drone like the original Shahed derivatives," Fabian Hoffmann, a senior research fellow at the Norwegian Institute for Defence Studies, told the Kyiv Independent.
The Geran-5 is particularly difficult to engage, flying significantly higher and faster than any of Russia's older drone models, with a maximum speed of 600 km/h (370 mph).
read also
SBU detains 19-year-old suspected of plotting bomb attack on bus full of soldiers
Ukraine's Security Service (SBU) has foiled an alleged Russian plot to bomb a bus carrying Ukrainian soldiers in the northwestern city of Rivne, detaining a 19-year-old student suspected of preparing the attack, the SBU and Rivne Regional Prosecutor's Office said on Oct. 12.
According to the SBU, the suspect planted an improvised explosive device under a bus transporting "an entire unit" of Ukrainian soldiers and installed a remotely accessible camera disguised in a juice box opposite the parking area to monitor the vehicle.
Russian intelligence operatives planned to detonate the bomb once the soldiers boarded the bus and were moving to their permanent deployment location, the SBU said.
The suspect acted in exchange for money after being recruited by Russian intelligence services through Telegram channels offering quick earnings, according to the SBU.
After arriving in Rivne, he allegedly collected the explosives from a hiding place designated by his Russian handler and planted the device under the military vehicle. The explosive device was reinforced with two glass bottles containing flammable liquid, the SBU said.
SBU officers discovered the plot, neutralized the explosives, and detained the suspect at the city's bus station when he attempted to leave for Kyiv. Investigators also seized his phone, which the SBU said he had used to report the planted device to his Russian handler.
The Rivne Regional Prosecutor's Office said the suspect had been formally notified of suspicion of an attempted terrorist attack. A court ordered his detention without bail. If convicted, he faces up to eight years in prison and possible confiscation of property.

Fire Point trolls Russia's Yandex after drone attack on data center
Ukrainian defense company Fire Point trolled Russian tech giant Yandex on Oct. 12, after the company reported damage to another of its data centers, disrupting access to its financial services.
"Today, another Yandex data center was damaged," Dima Pirogov, head of Yandex's fintech division, wrote on X on Oct. 11.
Pirogov said the disruption had left many users unable to check their balances, pay for purchases, or transfer money.
"Dima, have you tried turning it off and on again?" Fire Point replied.
The incident follows a series of reported drone strikes on Russian data centers that have disrupted Yandex services.
Yandex's data center in Russia's Vladimir Oblast was completely shut down on Oct. 11 following a reported drone attack, Russian state news agency TASS said, citing the company.

Russia-led military bloc launches joint military drills in Belarus
Russia and four other members of the Russian-led Collective Security Treaty Organization (CSTO) have begun joint military exercises in Belarus on Oct. 12, the organization said.
The drills will run from Oct. 12 until Oct. 16 at two training grounds on Belarusian territory, involving more than 1,500 military personnel, over 300 pieces of military equipment, and around 80 drones, according to the CSTO.
Military contingents from Belarus, Russia, Kazakhstan, Kyrgyzstan, and Tajikistan are participating in the exercises.
The drills focus on training CSTO "peacekeeping forces" and involve exercises to respond to biological threats, the organization said.
CSTO Deputy Secretary-General Mirlan Turgunbekov said in an Oct. 11 statement that the exercise is "particularly relevant given the escalating military and political situation."
The CSTO, which was established in 2002, includes Russia, Armenia, Belarus, Kazakhstan, Tajikistan, and Kyrgyzstan. Russia is by far the most powerful member of the alliance. Armenia is not particpating in the drills.
Belarus has supported Russia's full-scale war against Ukraine by allowing Moscow to use its territory as a staging ground for the full-scale invasion of Ukraine in 2022.

articles.title: NATO's top US commander warns Russia that any 'foolish' attack on allies would be 'futile'
articles.body:
NATO's top US commander warns Russia that any 'foolish' attack on allies would be 'futile'
NATO's top US military commander in Europe said Monday that any "foolish" attack on the alliance would be "utterly futile", a warning to Russia as European fears grow over the threat from Moscow that includes "hybrid" warfare and cyberattacks.
"If someone is foolish enough to attack us, we will fight. We will stop the attack and deny them the ability to achieve their objectives, whatever those may be," US General Alexus Grynkewich, NATO's Supreme Allied Commander Europe, said in a speech in Warsaw.
"We will, in short, ensure any attack against any ally proves utterly futile."
Grynkewich elaborated what he called his "theory of victory" to defeat an armed attack on the alliance as worries surge over what Western officials call a "hybrid" campaign of sabotage and interference by Moscow, including cyberattacks.
"Let me make one point very clear: I do not assess that conflict is imminent or inevitable. It isn't," Grynkewich said.

Worries have grown in recent months that the Kremlin is stepping up actions in Europe after high-profile incidents including the discovery of an explosive-laden drone at a German airport.
Grynkewich said that NATO allies needed to quickly attribute blame to Russia once they have proof and should let Moscow know clearly it cannot push too far.
"It's important that allies continue to consult, think about how we might respond, and make sure that we message clearly and concisely to the Russians where our red lines are," he said.
NATO insists it is a purely defensive alliance and is not seeking to invade Russia.
Read moreHybrid warfare: The threat of Russia looms over the Mediterranean
Grynkewich said that if there were a larger attack, NATO would act decisively to halt its foes and then destroy their ability to keep fighting if needed.
"My theory of victory is simple: we will block the initial attack. If the attack persists, we will blunt it and prevent enemy advance," he said.
"And if required, we will break the enemy's forces and the operational warfighting system that is arrayed against us."
French President Emmanuel Macron in September said measures were being taken to protect France's critical infrastructure and defence industry sites from "Russian hybrid attacks", adding that the threat from Moscow had intensified in recent weeks.
Read moreDrones, sabotage, surveillance: Moscow’s hybrid warfare takes to the high seas
'Burden of escalation'
The commander said that NATO would then not seek to "escalate" – in an apparent reference to the use of nuclear weapons.
"The burden of escalation would rest squarely upon the aggressor; they and they alone would bear the full moral, political, and strategic weight of deciding whether to do so," he said.
The strong message from NATO's top commander comes at a time of potential vulnerability for Europe.
The uptick in Russian activity comes as allies are bracing for possible cuts to US forces in Europe as the US administration reviews its deployments on the continent.
The results of the process are expected to be announced towards the end of the year.
European countries are already rushing to bolster their militaries as doubts have soared over the reliability of the United States under President Donald Trump.
Grynkewich insisted that Washington remained firmly behind the alliance's mutual self-defence pledge.
"I think no one should question the commitment of the United States to this alliance," he said.
He said the European push to take more responsibility for its defence was making the alliance tougher and more capable.
"We're in the implementation phase, and that is driving a stronger and more united alliance than I've seen in a long, long time," he said.
(FRANCE 24 with AFP)

articles.title: Russia is hacking cameras across Europe to track arms bound for Ukraine. At home, Ukraine has secured about 40,000 that could guide strikes — WSJ
articles.body:
The ordinary security camera watching a street or a parking lot has quietly become a weapon of war. Ukraine’s Security Service has identified about 40,000 surveillance cameras since Russia’s 2022 invasion that Russian forces and spy agencies could have used to snoop, find targets and correct strikes, and has protected, reoriented or blocked them, The Wall Street Journal reported.
The discovered threat reaches well beyond Ukraine: Dutch intelligence warned in July that Russian state actors are systematically hacking cameras across Europe to track arms deliveries to Ukraine and the whereabouts of Ukrainian troops.
AI makes it faster
About 1.2 billion internet-connected cameras now watch the world, in doorbells, traffic lights, and baby monitors, and almost any of them can be hacked, the journalists found.
In Ukraine, the danger is lethal. In 2024, Russian hackers took over residential webcams in Kyiv, including one that a condominium association had installed, to find targets and adjust missile strikes on the capital, Ukraine's Security Service says.
Spying on Europe’s edge
Evidence of European reach keeps surfacing. Cybersecurity firm CloudSEK has recently uncovered an exposed server it suspects belongs to a Russian-speaking hacker, containing hundreds of webcam images of Ukrainian defense, government, energy, and communications sites, as well as scenes of daily life.
Many of the images came from locations near Ukraine’s border with NATO member Romania, CloudSEK says.
The Dutch warning and the server point the same way: cameras far from the front line are feeding Russia data on how the West arms Ukraine.
Ukraine turns the lens back on Russia
Ukraine also uses the same tactic inside the occupied territory. The international hacker group Team OneFist took control of a camera in Sevastopol, in occupied Crimea, and used it to watch Russian ships, submarines, and helicopters, spotting a previously unknown air base that Ukraine later struck, damaging planes and air defenses.
Team OneFist also reached cameras on the Kerch Strait Bridge, learning that Russia had installed motion sensors beneath the bridge to guard against waterborne attacks. Penetrating a well-placed camera gets analysts closer to targets at less risk than any secret agent.

articles.title: Russia’s New 6,500-Km Missiles Could Target NATO as Moscow Prepares 32 for Strategic Bombers
articles.body:

Russia’s New 6,500-Km Missiles Could Target NATO as Moscow Prepares 32 for Strategic Bombers
Russia is expanding its long-range strike capabilities with plans to acquire 32 Kh-BD cruise missiles, each capable of traveling up to 6,500 kilometers (4,039 miles).
The weapons could allow Russian strategic bombers to target NATO countries from launch areas in the Arctic, potentially expanding Moscow’s long-range strike capabilities while raising questions about whether the missiles are intended for use against Ukraine or reserved for a possible confrontation with the Alliance.
We bring you stories from the ground. Your support keeps our team in the field.
According to Defense Express on October 11, citing a new report by the Royal United Services Institute (RUSI), the Kh-BD missiles are intended for Russia’s Tu-160M and Tu-95MS strategic bombers. The report, authored by defense researcher Sidharth Kaushal, examines Russia’s nuclear arsenal and its efforts to modernize strategic delivery systems.
The Kh-BD, also known as Izdeliye 506, is designed to extend the strike range of Russia’s existing bomber fleet. Its development comes as Moscow continues to struggle with its next-generation PAK DA bomber program, originally intended to replace the aging Tu-95MS and Tu-160 aircraft.
Russia’s Kh-BD could strike US from the Arctic
According to Kaushal, the missile’s claimed 6,500-kilometer range could allow Russian bombers to launch attacks against US territory from the Arctic, potentially using Alexandra Land Island in Russia’s far north as a launch area.
Such a capability could expand Moscow’s strategic strike options and complicate American air defense planning. However, the Kh-BD’s actual performance and ability to penetrate US missile defenses have not been independently verified.
The RUSI report also highlights a significant vulnerability in Russia’s strategic aviation operations.
US intelligence capabilities reportedly allow Washington to detect preparations for missile strikes involving Russian Tu-95MS and Tu-160 bombers. In a scenario involving direct nuclear escalation, this could leave major Russian strategic aviation bases, including Engels and Olenya, vulnerable to potential preemptive NATO strikes.
Defense Express noted that Russia first publicly unveiled the Kh-BD in September 2023, when Russian officials disclosed its claimed range and identified the modernized Tu-160 as a potential launch platform.
The missile is reportedly larger than Russia’s existing Kh-101 air-launched cruise missile, requiring additional modifications to the Tu-95MS and Tu-160 bombers before they can carry it.
32 Kh-BD missiles for Ukraine or NATO?
Details about Moscow’s procurement plans emerged in 2025, when Ukrainian defense outlet Militarnyi published leaked Russian documents indicating that the Russian military was scheduled to receive 16 Kh-BD missiles in 2024 and another 16 in 2026.
Each missile was reportedly valued at approximately $4.5 million, bringing the estimated cost of the planned 32-missile acquisition to $144 million.
If Russia fulfilled the procurement schedule, its military could have received up to 32 Kh-BD missiles by 2026. However, there is no independent confirmation that all planned deliveries have been completed.
According to Defense Express, Moscow faces two potential options for deploying the new weapons.
One possibility is that Russia could use the Kh-BD in strikes against Ukraine, testing the missile under actual combat conditions. Alternatively, the Russian military could retain the limited stockpile as a strategic reserve for a possible direct confrontation with NATO.
The development reflects Moscow’s broader effort to modernize its strategic aviation capabilities without introducing an entirely new bomber platform.
With the PAK DA program still unrealized, Russia remains dependent on upgraded versions of its existing long-range aircraft, making advanced cruise missiles such as the Kh-BD an important component of its future strike capabilities.
Earlier, Russian officials and state propagandists issued a series of threats against NATO countries, including Poland, Lithuania, Germany, and Norway. Russian state television host Vladimir Solovyov declared, “We don’t need their love. We need their fear,” while European officials warned that Moscow was attempting to intimidate NATO allies and weaken their support for Ukraine.

articles.title: Imagined threat: How Europe learned to manufacture enemies from Israel
articles.body:
The rhetoric of “existential threat” has become the dominant currency of political legitimacy in both Israel and Europe. In Israel, this rhetoric is deeply entrenched—a well-documented doctrine of “permanent war” that frames every adversary as an existential danger requiring eradication rather than negotiation or a possible settlement. In recent years, Europe appeared to have adopted the same Israeli playbook, with leaders warning of an imminent Russian attack on NATO territory despite their own intelligence agencies admitting they see no evidence of such a threat. This is not paranoia; it is a calculated rhetoric, deliberately cultivated by warmongering politicians who benefit from sustaining a permanent threat – real or imagined – whether in Israel, Europe, or anywhere else.
The most striking recent exposure of this manufactured threat came not from Moscow, but from a NATO member state on the front line. On 30th September 2026, Lithuanian Prime Minister Mindaugas Sinkevičius stated plainly after meeting NATO Secretary General Mark Rutte in Brussels: “Is there any proof, real proof intelligence services are providing, something on the table, that Russia is getting ready for something? And there is actually none.” If any country had reason to sound the alarm, it would be Lithuania due to its bordering of the Russian territory. Yet its prime minister explicitly warned against exaggeration, stating: “You can’t exaggerate and say, Oh, something is happening in the upcoming months or weeks.” When a leader of a frontline state with Russia is publicly dismissing the narrative of an imminent Russian attack, the question becomes unavoidable: who benefits from insisting otherwise?
Israel’s playbook: The doctrine of permanent war and victimhood
Israel’s use of the existential threat narrative is not a reaction to genuine peril but a deliberate strategy. To justify its open-ended military occupation, aggressive and expansionist agenda, Israeli leaders for decades played the victimhood card that it is being under constant existential threats, invoking the Holocaust and the spectre of annihilation.
Imagine how this playbook is blatantly applied, Israeli leaders, after committing a genocide and almost totally destroying Gaza, still say about dangers and threats coming from Gaza.
In both southern Syria and Lebanon, Israel occupies vast areas of both countries while still pretending to be under the threat and danger.
Israeli Army Chief of Staff Eyal Zamir has framed the current confrontation as a “decisive battle” against existential threats that emerged after 7th October, opening the door to continuous fighting that will not stop until the “imagined threat” to the security establishment disappears. David Barnea, while in power as Mossad chief, similarly re-proposed the goal of “overthrowing the Iranian regime” as an existential imperative.
This doctrine serves multiple functions. Domestically, it suppresses any discussion of political alternatives or peaceful settlements, and allows to move ahead with its expansionist agenda in the region, making war the only option on the table.
Externally, it exploits Europe’s guilt over the Holocaust to extract unconditional support for such policies, with Netanyahu claiming Israel is defending “Western civilisation” against “evil regimes.”
The result is a permanent rhetoric that legitimises aggression as self-defence and portrays Israel as a victim.
Europe follows: The Russian threat that isn’t
Over the past years, it became clearer that Europe adopted this same tactic toward Russia. In mid-September, Polish Prime Minister Donald Tusk told parliament that intelligence assessments suggest Russia may be preparing a drone or missile attack on NATO territory in the near future. However, he did not identify the intelligence services behind his assessment, according news reports. French President Emmanuel Macron backed Tusk’s assessment, calling the warnings “sound and well documented,” and convened an emergency meeting in Paris to discuss “the threat.”
Yet the evidence for this imminent threat is strikingly thin. A senior EU official, speaking anonymously, stated in August 2026 that “European intelligence services generally do not currently see the risk of a Russian attack on European countries, and this assessment has not changed.” The official added that regarding potential threats to NATO members, “we see nothing indicating that anything is currently being prepared.” Estonian Foreign Ministry Secretary General Jonatan Vseviov went further, criticizing what he called “panic on social media.” These official denials are not isolated remarks; they reveal a systematic effort by certain European circles to cultivate a state of enmity with Russia and to keep the narrative of an imagined threat alive on the table—not because the threat is real, but because it serves their political agenda.
Russian President Vladimir Putin has repeatedly denied any intention to attack Europe. “I want to emphasise once again: we are not preparing any military action against Europe, we have no such plans. Most importantly, there is no reason to do so.” Kremlin spokesman Dmitry Peskov also dismissed the warnings as “alarmist stories” that “of course have nothing to do with reality.”
The function of manufactured threats
Why would European leaders manufacture a threat that their own intelligence services say does not exist? The answer lies in the same functions the tactic serves in Israel, which is to advance a political agenda over any other one, domestic control, military budgets, and justification of aggressive policies.
Slovak Prime Minister Robert Fico warned in September 2026 that some Western politicians are trying to provoke a direct NATO-Russia conflict after their strategy of defeating Moscow via Ukraine failed, calling it a “deadly danger.” The logic is clear: when military and political strategies fail, a new threat must be invented to justify continued militarisation and the suppression of any opposition.
Europe’s adoption of Israel’s playbook is not merely an imitation; it is a shared strategy of governance through permanent emergency. Both Israel and Europe have found that an imagined enemy is more useful than a real one. A real enemy can be negotiated with, contained, or defeated. An imagined enemy is eternal, requiring eternal vigilance, eternal militarisation, and eternal obedience.
The danger of this approach is not just that it manufactures war. It also manufactures the conditions for the erosion of democracy. When every critic becomes a potential traitor and every question becomes a security threat, the space for genuine political debate collapses. The playbook that Israel perfected in its treatment of Palestinians — dehumanisation, permanent emergency, and the criminalisation of dissent — is now being applied to Europe’s relationship with Russia. A stark example on this imitation was documented in early October when Belgian Defense Minister Theo Francken publicly claimed that Russian drones had been detected over Belgian military barracks, presenting it as proof of Russia’s hostile intentions. However, the Belgian public broadcaster VRT investigated and found that the drones never existed. The report revealed that Francken had invented the threats to obtain additional budget funds for his ministry.
While a genuine conflict and dispute do exist between Europe and Russia, Moscow has consistently called for dialogue to resolve their differences. It did so in the context of the war in Ukraine, only to find that Zelensky was provoked – or perhaps even ordered – to reject a negotiated settlement and to continue his endless war with Russia. This serves the interests of some European circles and leaders who persist in portraying an imagined Russian threat, revealing themselves as warmongers as their Israeli counterparts; more committed to prolonging the conflict than to seeking its settlement.

articles.title: Zelensky Warns China Is Helping Russia Develop Starlink Rival
articles.body:
President Volodymyr Zelensky told the Financial Times in an interview published on Oct. 3 that Beijing was helping Moscow build Rassvet, Russia’s version of SpaceX’s Starlink.
“We know that China works on satellites, works on the possibility of helping Russia with a system similar to Starlink,” he said, adding that “they are getting closer, and they are passing it on to Russia.”
JOIN US ON TELEGRAM
Follow our coverage of the war on the @Kyivpost_official.
What is the threat from Rassvet?
The system is being built by Moscow’s “Bureau 1440” and is designed to operate at an orbit height of around 800 kilometers (500 miles). It will include laser links between satellites and a ground based 5G network.
Following initial launches in July and August, milbloggers said the system was suffering from widescale technical difficulties. In September, Bureau 1440 said it was working on improved systems which Intellinews said was likely being done using Chinese assistance.
Zelensky said that Rassvet could be operational by early 2027, warning US President Donald Trump several times. Most recently, during September’s UN General Assembly in New York, Zelensky called for sanctions to be imposed on Russian and Chinese companies involved in its development.
Intellinews also reported that the satellite system could be part of the military technical cooperation as part of the “CRINK alliance” – an informal grouping between China, Russia, Iran, and North Korea. According to them, CRINK is an attempt to keep ahead of Western weapons systems development.
Ukraine’s TENCORE Bundles 4 Ground Drones in Single AI-Powered Ecosystem
The report suggested that such cooperation could see the fusion between Moscow’s missiles, drones, and other materials with China’s electronics capability.
In January 2023, Yury Borisov, then head of Roscosmos, said Russia had agreed to buy electronic components for rocket and space technology from China after Western sanctions prevented the import of critical supplies, saying that electronics was Russia’s “Achilles’ heel,” as per Interfax.
According to Reuters on Oct. 1, Denys Sienik, deputy chief of mission at the Ukrainian embassy in Washington, said that Russia was rapidly expanding the Rassvet satellite network, aiming to start operations in 2027, which would pose grave risks to Ukraine.
“They will be able to target Ukrainian targets in real time anywhere on our territory,” Sienik said.
Rassvet has currently deployed a relatively small number of satellites compared with the thousands that make up the Starlink constellation. Its capabilities over Ukraine were erratic as connectivity was dependent on the satellite being overhead. Its aim was to establish sufficient numbers that would allow continuous coverage of Russia’s military communications.
Satellite communications are critical
The war in Ukraine has shown that reliable satellite communications are an indispensable component of modern warfare to support command networks, reconnaissance, logistics, and operation of unmanned weapons systems.
Starlink has provided connectivity in areas where conventional communications infrastructure has been destroyed or disrupted – a facility of which was deprived in February 2026 when Elon Musk implemented a “whitelist” system that deactivated terminals not registered and verified by Ukrainian authorities.
The US has also limited Ukrainian access to Starlink for deep strikes into Russia. Meanwhile, China’s defense sector is said to be developing countermeasures to Starlink that could include laser weapons in order to attack and destroy satellites.
Previously on X, Anton Gerashchenko said that 2027 could see Rassvet move from experimental to fully operational, adding that the threat could extend to factories, airfields, ports, and energy sites in Europe where air defense systems would be unable to repel against Russian long-range drone swarms.

articles.title: Ukraine Will Stop Hitting Russian Oil Only if Putin Ends Energy Strikes, Zelenskyy Says

Ukraine Will Stop Hitting Russian Oil Only if Putin Ends Energy Strikes, Zelenskyy Says
As Washington pushes Kyiv to end its campaign against Russia’s oil industry, Ukrainian President Volodymyr Zelenskyy has made clear that any pause in refinery strikes must come with a price for Moscow—a reciprocal end to attacks on Ukraine’s energy infrastructure.
Ukraine is ready to halt strikes on Russian oil refineries—but only if Russian leader Vladimir Putin stops attacking Ukrainian energy infrastructure, President Volodymyr Zelenskyy said on October 11, rejecting any unilateral suspension of attacks amid growing pressure from US President Donald Trump.
We bring you stories from the ground. Your support keeps our team in the field.
According to Zelenskyy’s official statement on October 11, Kyiv is prepared to consider a reciprocal halt to energy-related strikes, provided Moscow ends its attacks on Ukraine’s power infrastructure and both sides receive credible guarantees.
“Ukraine will be ready to stop strikes on Russian oil refineries if Russia stops attacking our energy infrastructure. Any de-escalation measures must be reciprocal and backed by real guarantees,” Zelenskyy said.
The Ukrainian president emphasized that Moscow could end attacks on energy facilities immediately but that Putin has shown no willingness to do so.
The proposal follows another week of large-scale Russian attacks on Ukraine. According to Zelenskyy, Russian forces launched approximately 1,450 guided aerial bombs, 75 missiles of various types, and more than 1,640 attack drones over the past seven days. He said approximately 60% of the drones were jet-powered.
The strikes included an attack on Zaporizhzhia that killed 23 people, including four children, according to Ukrainian authorities.
Russian forces also targeted a medical facility in Kharkiv and struck a five-story residential building in Sloviansk, destroying an entire section of the structure and potentially leaving civilians trapped beneath the rubble.
Zelenskyy said Ukraine was continuing discussions with European leaders to secure additional military assistance, particularly air defense systems and ammunition for combat aircraft.
His latest proposal comes amid mounting tensions between Kyiv and Washington over Ukraine’s campaign against Russian oil infrastructure.
On October 9, Trump announced an agreement with Putin to supply Russian diesel fuel to American and international markets, despite existing US sanctions targeting Moscow’s energy revenues.
Trump decided to pursue the diesel agreement after Zelenskyy refused Washington’s demand to unilaterally suspend Ukrainian strikes on Russian oil refineries.
Trump subsequently criticized Zelenskyy over his willingness to negotiate, while Ukrainian officials maintained that attacks on Russian oil facilities would continue unless Moscow agreed to stop targeting Ukraine’s energy infrastructure.
Zelenskyy has also warned that easing sanctions on Russia without a credible and lasting de-escalation agreement could provide Moscow with additional billions of dollars to finance its war against Ukraine.

The Defence Intelligence of Ukraine revealed details about the Russian Kinzhal aeroballistic missile
Kyiv • UNN
The Defence Intelligence of Ukraine released the technical specifications of the Kinzhal and data on 58 enterprises involved in its production. 22 companies are not subject to sanctions.
The Main Directorate of Intelligence of the Ministry of Defense of Ukraine has revealed the technical features of the Russian Kinzhal missile and published data on 58 enterprises involved in its production. Twenty-two of them are still not under sanctions imposed by any country in the sanctions coalition. The data were published on the War&Sanctions portal, UNN reports.
The Kinzhal is a single-stage solid-fuel missile with an integrated warhead. In terms of its components, the missile is 90% unified with the 9M723 ballistic missile of the Iskander-M OTRK
The main differences of the Kinzhal include a tail aerodynamic fairing that separates after the engine is started, a radar homing head (in the Iskander, the ARGSN currently exists only on paper, and its use in strikes against the territory of Ukraine has not been recorded), which the enemy calls "all-weather," and an active jamming station, in addition to the S-200 decoy-launching system.
The Kinzhal has two types of warheads: a penetrating high-explosive warhead (PrFBCh) in a thick metal casing for breaching ceilings, concrete and hardened structures, and a special nuclear warhead.
The DIU has revealed details of a new modification of Russia’s "Geran-4"05.10.26, 11:22 • 4224 views
The enemy is currently working on a modification with a fragmentation high-explosive warhead (OFBCh). Such changes may be directly related to problems with the missile's guidance accuracy, since high accuracy is more important specifically for a penetrating warhead.
For this very reason, in 2026 the enemy significantly reduced the volume of the state defense order for these missiles, directing production capacities, component supplies and raw-material resources toward the production of 9M723 Iskander-M ballistic missiles.
The second reason for this prioritization is the limited service life of the Kinzhal carriers — MiG-31I interceptor fighters and their predecessors, the MiG-31K, which the Russian aviation industry is not currently manufacturing.
The GUR of the Ministry of Defense of Ukraine also published data on 58 Russian enterprises involved in the cooperative production of Kh-47M2 Kinzhal aeroballistic missiles. It is telling that 22 of them are still not under sanctions imposed by any country in the sanctions coalition.
Despite certain shortcomings, Russia continues work to modernize the Kinzhal missiles. And to thwart the aggressor's plans, it is necessary to synchronize sanctions against all the enterprises involved and strengthen control over the technologies actively used by the Russian Federation

articles.title: Peacekeepers, riot police, and drone crews: Russia’s bloc rehearses an operation in a Belarusian oblast bordering two NATO states
articles.body:
Russia and four allies began five-day military drills in Belarus on 12 October, the Russia-led Collective Security Treaty Organization (CSTO) said. The troops are rehearsing peacekeeping and a biological-threat response. Minsk insists the drills target no one, while Belarus’s army chief calls them deterrence against hostile states.
Russian troops crossed Belarus to advance on Kyiv in 2022, and it now hosts Russian units with Oreshnik missiles and equipment guiding attack drones into Ukraine. Every foreign deployment there worries Kyiv and neighboring NATO members, which blame Minsk and Moscow for border pressure.
Riot police and drone crews in a “peacekeeping” drill
Belarus, Kazakhstan, Kyrgyzstan, Russia, and Tajikistan brought more than 1,500 troops and over 300 weapons and vehicles, including about 80 drones, The Moscow Times reported, citing the bloc. Armenia, the sixth member, is not among them. The peacekeeping drill runs in Vitsebsk Oblast, bordering Latvia and Lithuania, with Belarusian riot police and internal troops joining, the bloc’s command said.
Russia sent motorized rifle, reconnaissance, electronic warfare, and drone units from its Central Military District, the CSTO said. Russia, this year’s chair, prioritized peacekeeping readiness and the joint biological protection and medical unit, a bloc general said.
Belarus’s military insisted the drills are planned, yet its army chief called them “one of the measures of strategic deterrence against aggressively minded states” and claimed the West is “effectively preparing for a new hot war.”
Pressure on Belarus’s neighbors
In Latvia, armed, masked escorts from Belarus tried to force migrants across this month, the military said, and raiders stole border cameras hours later. Estonia’s police and border guard chief warned migration pressure could jump before winter, as Russia eases entry from countries like Ethiopia and Belarus passes migrants on to the EU. Lithuania posted up to 100 soldiers on its border with Russia’s Kaliningrad, and in September NATO’s Italian jets downed a drone that crossed in from Belarus. On 9 October, Minsk summoned Ukraine’s envoy over an alleged drone strike on a Belarusian truck in Russia, and Kyiv rejected the “absurd accusations” of “an accomplice in the crime of aggression against Ukraine.”
Belarus keeps its army on alert
In September, Belarusian armor drilled near the Suwałki Gap, NATO’s land link to the Baltic states, and Lukashenka said the whole army would be checked, up to mobilization. On 12 October, he ordered a snap check of a 6th Separate Guards Mechanized Brigade battalion, state news agency BelTA reported. European spy agencies also warn of more Russian assassination plots against defense executives.
Ukraine’s intelligence still rates the threat from Belarus as low, but each new contingent, missile unit, and airborne brigade there widens what Kyiv and NATO’s eastern flank must watch.

articles.title: North Korea fires multiple ballistic missiles towards S Korea, Seoul urges Pyongyang to stop ‘UN violations’
articles.body:
North Korea fires missiles towards sea, escalating tensions on Korean Peninsula (Reuters image)
North Korea fired multiple ballistic missiles towards its eastern waters on Monday, South Korea’s military said, as Pyongyang continued its weapons testing amid heightened tensions and a prolonged freeze in diplomatic engagement.South Korea’s Joint Chiefs of Staff said the missiles were launched from an area near the North Korean capital, Pyongyang. Japan’s Defence Ministry detected at least two missiles and assessed that they had landed in waters outside the country’s exclusive economic zone.
South Korea’s presidential office condemned the repeated launches, saying they violated United Nations Security Council resolutions and urging Pyongyang to stop such activities immediately.The latest launches came days after South Korea flight-tested its first domestically developed hypersonic weapon on Friday. Designed to travel at least five times the speed of sound and evade missile defence systems, the weapon was described by President Lee Jae Myung as an important step towards strengthening the country’s conventional defence capabilities.North Korea has intensified its weapons development as leader Kim Jong Un seeks to expand the country’s arsenal of nuclear-capable systems.
On October 3, Pyongyang conducted a test of what it described as a hypersonic intermediate-range missile designed to penetrate missile defence systems in South Korea and Japan.The country has also carried out missile tests and live-fire drills and commissioned a new warship, underscoring Kim’s push to strengthen its military capabilities despite repeated US and South Korean offers to resume diplomatic engagement.Tensions on the Korean Peninsula have also been aggravated by a series of land mine explosions near the heavily militarised inter-Korean border last month that injured three South Korean soldiers. South Korea’s military and the US-led United Nations Command concluded that the blasts were caused by mines planted by North Korea. Pyongyang has denied responsibility and dismissed Seoul’s demands for an apology.
Kim has halted diplomatic engagement and cooperation with South Korea in recent years, describing the neighbouring country as a permanent enemy. Nuclear negotiations with Washington have also remained stalled since 2019, when talks broke down during US President Donald Trump’s first term.Kim has so far rejected Trump’s overtures to revive dialogue. Pyongyang has demanded that Washington abandon what it calls its “hostile” policy and drop denuclearisation demands as a precondition for negotiations.The impasse has complicated Lee’s efforts to pursue engagement with North Korea. While advocating dialogue and adopting a more conciliatory tone, the South Korean president has also called for stronger conventional defence capabilities and reduced reliance on the United States.Washington unilaterally scaled back a major military exercise with South Korea in August, with Trump citing his “very good relationship” with Kim.

His reporting focuses on elections, national security, and institutional affairs, tracking the decisions and conflicts that shape public life. articles.title: Zelenskyy: Russia struck Ukrainian power plant 'immediately after' Trump declared energy ceasefire
articles.body:
Russia continued attacking Ukraine's energy infrastructure after US President Donald Trump announced an immediate ceasefire covering energy facilities, Ukrainian President Volodymyr Zelenskyy said on Monday, raising questions about whether Moscow had agreed to the arrangement.
Speaking by video link at the Warsaw Security Forum, Zelenskyy said Russian forces struck a power plant in Kharkiv shortly after Trump's announcement on Sunday.
Add Helsinki Times as a preferred source on Google (opens Google in a new tab)
He also confirmed attacks on energy facilities in Kyiv and other regions.
"Immediately after the post, Russia launched a targeted strike on a power plant in Kharkiv, causing further damage to our energy system," Zelenskyy told the conference.
"It's clear Putin doesn't read Truth Social," he added, referring to the platform where Trump announced the agreement.
Trump claimed on Sunday that Russia and Ukraine had accepted an immediate halt to attacks on each other's energy infrastructure.
"Both parties have agreed. Do not break it!" he wrote.
Zelenskyy said Ukrainian officials learnt about the announcement through media reports rather than diplomatic channels. The Kremlin had not publicly confirmed its participation by Monday morning.
Despite the confusion, Zelenskyy said Ukraine would honour an agreement covering energy infrastructure if Russia followed the same terms.
"We are ready to respect an energy ceasefire if Russia is ready to do the same. We agree, if they agree," he said.
The Ukrainian president insisted that any arrangement must protect electricity generation, transmission networks and gas facilities rather than focus exclusively on oil refineries.
Ukraine has one refinery, in Kremenchuk, which Russian attacks have damaged. Russia operates a network of refineries that Ukrainian drones have targeted to disrupt fuel supplies and reduce Moscow's energy revenues.
"If Russia wants us to stop our long-range strikes against its oil refineries and oil exports, then Russia must stop its strikes against our energy system and critical infrastructure, and stop killing our people," Zelenskyy said.
According to Axios, an unnamed White House official said Trump's announcement concerned oil refineries, with a wider agreement covering electricity infrastructure potentially following later.
Ukrainian authorities reported further attacks overnight. Kharkiv's CHP-5 power plant came under fire on Sunday, while strikes damaged electricity networks in Izyum and energy and railway facilities in the Zhytomyr region.
A missile attack on a grocery store near Kharkiv killed three people and injured at least 22, including two children, according to regional governor Oleh Syniehubov.
Zelenskyy said Russia had carried out more than 200 strikes against Ukrainian electricity facilities during the preceding week, alongside 17 attacks on oil and gas infrastructure.
European officials questioned the ceasefire announcement.
"We welcome the energy ceasefire when it holds. We haven't yet seen that also Russia will stick to it," EU foreign policy chief Kaja Kallas said ahead of a meeting of foreign ministers.
Polish Prime Minister Donald Tusk called for further sanctions against Moscow and said Russia's continued attacks demonstrated its response to ceasefire proposals.
The dispute follows Trump's decision on Friday to ease restrictions on Russian diesel exports under an agreement intended to increase fuel supplies.
Zelenskyy criticised the arrangement, arguing that additional energy revenue would help finance Russia's war.
The Financial Times, citing unnamed European officials, reported that Washington had threatened to restrict intelligence sharing and weapons procurement arrangements unless Kyiv stopped attacking Russian refineries.
Trump also called for Ukraine to elect a new president. Zelenskyy responded that elections required a full ceasefire, citing martial law and the difficulty of allowing frontline troops to vote.
He said a 60-day halt to fighting would provide an opportunity to prepare elections and address the legislative obstacles.
Ukraine has suspended national elections under martial law since Russia launched its full-scale invasion in February 2022.
