articles.title: Europe at back of US arms queue – NATO envoy
articles.body:
Europe at back of US arms queue – NATO envoy
European countries should expand their own arms production because American factories will largely be occupied with supplying the US military, Washington’s envoy to NATO, Matthew Whitaker, has said.
US defense spending could reach $1–1.5 trillion in 2026, leaving limited manufacturing capacity for foreign buyers, Whitaker said at the Warsaw Security Forum on Monday. “The US needs friends with manufacturing capacity,” Whitaker said, urging Europe to increase output to meet its own growing weapons demand.
The warning comes as Washington struggles to replenish missile stocks depleted by its war against Iran. The Center for Strategic and International Studies estimated that US forces had fired over 1,000 Tomahawk cruise missiles by late May, representing nearly a third of its stockpiles. It also used over 1,500 high-end Patriot interceptors, or about 65% of its reserves, as of late July. Reuters also reported in August that the US army had used “virtually all” of its high-precision long-range missiles.
Bloomberg reported last month that NATO members faced delivery delays of up to several years as Washington prioritized rebuilding its own inventories. Germany’s requests for accelerated Tomahawk deliveries were unlikely to be fulfilled within five years, according to the report.
Europe has continued to suffer weapon shortages after donating billions worth of arms to Ukraine. A European Defence Agency assessment presented in September identified significant shortages in air and missile defense, ammunition and other essential capabilities. Efforts to manufacture Patriot interceptors in Germany have also yet to bear fruit.
Whitaker said that Europe ranks fourth among Washington’s security priorities, behind homeland security, the Western Hemisphere and the Pacific. Nevertheless, he reassured European officials that “we still love you,” and that the US “isn’t stepping back” but “just asking you to step forward.”
He also urged NATO to modernize bases, supply chains for fuel, and deployment arrangements to move forces and equipment from Western to Eastern Europe, “where we would expect any future conflict.” He announced no new relocation decisions.
Since returning to office, President Donald Trump has moved to reduce US military commitments in Europe. He has repeatedly criticized NATO members for insufficient spending and demanded that they assume greater responsibility for their own defense.
European governments have meanwhile been ramping up military spending, citing allegations that Russia could attack a NATO country by the end of the decade. Moscow has repeatedly rejected claims that it plans to attack Europe, but has warned that NATO would face a full military response if it attacked Russia first.

articles.title: Ukrainian drones hit three of Russian tech giant Yandex’s data centers in four days. Ukraine’s president says the bots thinned out too
articles.body:
Ukraine’s drone strikes on Russian tech giant Yandex thinned out social media bots, Ukrainian President Volodymyr Zelenskyy said on 12 October. Network data do show Yandex’s automated traffic collapsing after the strikes. Disinformation researchers say that traffic is search crawling, not trolls. A Ukrainian social media monitor told Euromaidan Press its own data show no clear drop in bot activity either.
Russian influence operations are a live threat to European votes. In August, the Matryoshka network fabricated news clips aimed at Sweden’s general election. German and French authorities flagged the same network targeting Germany’s local votes and French presidential hopeful Gabriel Attal. A way to switch such networks off would hand allies a new tool, which is why the claim needs testing.
The president’s claim
Addressing the Warsaw Security Forum by video link, Zelenskyy said that once Ukraine began answering Russia’s operation against Ukrainian data centers and its strikes reached Yandex, many social media platforms suddenly became a little easier to breathe on.
Many people noticed less hatred, discord, and provocation because there were fewer bots, he said. It was quite clear where those bots came from, he noted. Their disappearance once Yandex went down proves again that Europe is not the source of the problems, he added.
Lithuanian Prime Minister Mindaugas Sinkevičius said at the same forum that allies should ask Zelenskyy to strike more data centers in Russia, answering a question on how to protect their elections from interference.
Three data centers in four days
Drones first hit Yandex’s data center in Sasovo, Ryazan Oblast, on 8 October. Yandex said it shut the site down completely. The next day, a strike on its Kaluga site completely disabled several modules, the company said. Yandex calls Kaluga its largest data center, Russian science outlet T-Invariant noted.
Ukrainian drone maker Fire Point said its FP-1 long-range drones carried out that strike.
After the first strike, on Sasovo, a source at Yandex summed up the mood for The Bell: “Things are rotten. We keep working.”
Overnight on 11 October, drones hit the third site, in Vladimir. Yandex said it fully halted that data center too. Vladimir Oblast Governor Aleksandr Avdeev acknowledged an attack on “infrastructure” near the city. It started a fire and cut power to two substations serving 5,000 residents, he claimed.
What the traffic data show
Automated web requests from Yandex’s network fell to 0.4% of their two-week peak after the third strike, Cloudflare Radar data showed, Cybernews reported. That chart counts automated requests to websites, mostly from Yandex’s own search crawlers. It does not count social media posts.
The chart “has nothing to do with social media,” the Russian opposition analysis group Antibot4navalny wrote.
Russia’s overall bot traffic last week looked much like any other week. Yandex’s own figure began recovering on Sunday. Covert troll farms usually hide behind residential proxies, hacked devices, virtual private networks (VPNs), and Western cloud providers, the outlet added.
What Ukrainian social media shows so far
Yevhen Luzan tracks Ukrainian social media sentiment as an analyst at the Ukrainian nonprofit CAT-UA. Its daily reviews sample about 500 random posts. On 11 October, that sample showed an unusually small share of posts criticizing Ukraine’s authorities, he told Euromaidan Press. Accounts showing signs of bot activity made up only a few tenths of a percent of that criticism. That is within the margin of error.
The same day, though, US President Donald Trump’s deal for Russian diesel supplies dominated Ukrainian feeds. Luzan said a rally-around-the-flag effect could explain the shift, as outrage at Washington crowded out domestic stories.
“To state it definitively and draw a cause-and-effect link from this correlation would be too bold,” he said.
Across the wider pool of about 10,000 daily mentions, CAT-UA sees no significant drop in posting activity in recent days. The curve shows only the usual rises and dips around the start and end of the week, Luzan said.
“For now, even a hypothetical drop in bot farm activity dissolves entirely in the natural fluctuations of the information space,” he said.
How a crawler chart became a bot story
The claim that Russian social media bots fell by half is unproven and built on a misread chart, disinformation analyst Joohn Choe concluded in a fact-check. It traces back to an 8 October post by security researcher Jeremiah Fowler. That post said Russian bot traffic had dropped to 49%. On 11 October, radio reporter Jamie Dupree spread it on X. Tom’s Hardware then ran it under a headline calling the crawler traffic “Russian disinformation bot traffic,” wording it has since changed.
Ukrainian military analyst Tatarigami claimed that Texas separatist accounts with identical “Veteran, Christian, Father, MAGA” bios had gone quiet. He said Quebec separatists and Polish anti-EU accounts went quiet alongside them.
Polish military analyst Jarosław Wolski claimed that AfD’s online support fell 56%, posting a chart without naming its source. Another X user said “Polish” bots had vanished.

articles.title: Short on interceptors, Ukraine goes after the launchers: eight Russian ballistic systems hit, three destroyed since September, a minister says
articles.body:
Ukraine has been striking the launchers Russia uses to fire ballistic missiles at its cities, Ukrainian Defense Minister Yevhenii Khmara told journalists. He said the strikes have already disrupted some Russian attack plans, but supplies of anti-ballistic interceptors still fall short of the threat.
Russia strikes Ukraine’s cities and power grid with drones and missiles every day as it prepares to leave civilians without power and heat this winter. Ballistic missiles are the part of that barrage Ukraine still struggles to stop, so every launcher put out of action before it fires means fewer missiles to intercept.
Iskander and S-400 launchers hit since September
Ukrainian forces hit eight launchers used for ballistic strikes on Ukraine in September and early October, destroying three and damaging five, Khmara said. They belonged to Russia’s Iskander tactical missile systems and S-400 air defense systems, he added. Such strikes have already forced Russia to cancel or change planned ballistic attacks, the minister said.
The S-400 was designed to shoot down aircraft and missiles, but Russia also uses it to fire ballistic missiles at Ukrainian cities, including Kyiv. In mid-September, Ukraine reported hitting two S-400 launchers near Vygonichi in Russia’s Bryansk Oblast. Russia had used the same systems against Kyiv the night before.
Can’t intercept the missiles? Hit the factories—Ukraine’s other way to stop Russia’s ballistic missiles
On 23 August, Ukrainian President Volodymyr Zelenskyy said Ukrainian forces had hit an Iskander launcher near the border. He described it as part of a separate operation to hunt nearby launch positions and linked the tactic to low stocks of anti-ballistic missiles.
Strikes on launchers while interceptors stay scarce
Khmara called the launcher strikes Ukraine’s asymmetric response to a ballistic threat that remains critical.
“Existing and potential supplies of missiles for anti-ballistic defense are not enough to fully cover this threat,” he said.
Instead of waiting for large long-term contracts, the Defense Ministry is looking for missiles in partners’ available stocks to speed up transfers, Khmara added. “We need dozens and hundreds of missiles, not one-off deliveries,” he stressed.
Meanwhile, Russia significantly cut its 2026 state orders for Kinzhal air-launched ballistic missiles, Ukraine’s military intelligence said on 12 October. It redirected the production capacity, components, and raw materials to Iskander-M ballistic missiles, the agency added.
Russia’s missile and drone attacks continue
Overnight on 12 October, Russia attacked Ukraine with a Kh-59 guided missile and 121 attack drones, 76 of them jet-powered, Ukraine’s Air Force reported. Air defenses downed or suppressed 89 drones, but strikes hit 15 locations, and the attack was still going on in the morning.
Russia’s new ballistic missile could reach western Ukraine—and it may be tested there within months
In the week to 11 October, Russia hit Ukraine’s power generation and transmission facilities more than 200 times and its gas and oil sites 17 times, Zelenskyy said. Russian attacks that week killed more than 150 people and injured more than 700, he added.
Jet-powered drones are still the main problem for Ukraine’s air defense. It stops more than 90% of slower propeller-driven Shaheds, compared with about 55% for the jet ones.
Ballistic missiles have struck Kyiv repeatedly this autumn. On 24 September, Russian ballistic and hypersonic missiles damaged a maternity hospital in the capital. On 7 October, a Russian missile barrage killed 22 people in Pryluky, Chernihiv Oblast.

articles.body:
Zelenskyy says 'increasingly clear' Russia does not want energy ceasefire after strikes
Ukrainian president Volodymyr Zelenskyy said it was “increasingly clear” that Russia was unwilling to accept a US-proposed ceasefire on energy strikes, as Moscow hit six Ukrainian energy facilities on Monday.
“This is what happens when Russia sees the prospect of higher revenues for its war machine,” he wrote in a post on X.
Ukrainian president Volodymyr Zelenskyy said it was “increasingly clear” that Russia was unwilling to accept a US-proposed ceasefire on energy strikes, as Moscow hit six Ukrainian energy facilities on Monday. “This is what happens when Russia sees the prospect of higher revenues for its war machine,” he wrote in a post on X.
German chancellor Friedrich Merz said that Russia would only negotiate “seriously” under pressure, days after president Donald Trump announced a temporary easing of US sanctions on Russian diesel. “For Germany and for Europe, such a decision is out of the question,” said Merz, referring to the US-Russia diesel deal.
Nato should signal its “red lines” to Russia over sabotage attacks in Europe, the alliance’s top military commander said. “It’s important that allies continue to consult, think about how we might respond, and make sure that we message clearly and concisely to the Russians where our red lines are,” Nato commander Alexus Grynkewich said in Warsaw.
Russia carried out drone strikes on various targets in Ukraine on Monday, including on vessels carrying military cargo, Russia’s defence ministry said. The ministry said it had struck three cargo vessels which it said were being used to transport military cargo to Ukraine’s Black Sea ports - two bound for Odesa and one heading to Mykolaiv.
A 13-year-old girl was among three people killed in a Russian strike on a house near the frontline city of Kramatorsk in eastern Ukraine on Monday, the authorities said. The head of the Donetsk regional military administration, Vadym Filashkin, said a house in the Cherkaske area was hit with cluster munitions, accusing Russia of “a deliberate attempt” to maximise civilian casualties.
The Kremlin spokesperson, Dmitry Peskov, has said Russia rejects the idea of a temporary ceasefire, telling reporters that Moscow wanted a long-term peace deal instead. “In the Kremlin, both President Putin and officials at other levels have repeatedly stated that we do not want a ceasefire,” said Peskov. “We want long-term peace and are prepared to do everything possible to achieve it.“
Ukraine has passed legislation protecting the rights of national minorities, in a move expected to remove a major stumbling block to the country’s EU ambitions. Hungary had been blocking the opening of so-called negotiation “clusters” – policy areas with which EU candidates must align their laws – accusing Kyiv of failing to protect the rights of Ukraine’s Hungarian minority.
European Union foreign ministers have a clear understanding that now is not the moment to ease pressure on Russia, Kaja Kallas, the bloc’s foreign policy chief, told reporters on Monday. “Pressure on Moscow, not concessions, is the fastest way to end the war,” she said following a gathering of European foreign ministers in Luxembourg.
EU countries back barring entry to Russians who fought in Ukraine, but need to work out how to implement the measure, Kallas added. “The political agreement is there. We just need to work out the technicalities,” she said after a meeting of EU foreign ministers.
Russia presents a long-term threat to Europe regardless of the outcome of the war in Ukraine, the head of Germany’s domestic intelligence agency said. Warning that Moscow wanted to upend Europe’s international order, Sina Sellen, president of the BfV, said Russian-orchestrated attacks would “continue to come”.
France’s high school students will stage new protests on Tuesday, the Agence France-Presse (AFP) news agency is reporting. A government source told journalists last week that the cost for damage caused by the demonstrations, which have shaken an unpopular government trying to reduce a ballooning budget deficit, was already “at least 30 million euros”.
An “unprecedented” cyber-attack is behind the shutdown of refrigerator units in multiple French supermarkets, according to the chief executive of Cooperative U, one of the chains affected. At least 150 Intermarche shops were targeted, along with almost 100 Cooperative U outlets, AFP reports. Paris prosecutors confirmed the attack, with media reporting that hackers were “managing to remotely trigger the forced defrosting of the refrigeration systems in numerous stores.”
EU countries back barring entry to Russians who fought in Ukraine, but need to work out how to implement the measure, Kallas added.
“The political agreement is there. We just need to work out the technicalities,” she said after a meeting of EU foreign ministers.
The EU has been mulling introducing the ban for months – but has faced questions over how it could be enforced.
The push has gained traction as fears have risen over what Western officials describe as Moscow’s “hybrid” campaign of sabotage and interference in Europe.
Alongside that there are also discussions on limiting travel for Moscow’s diplomats and tightening criteria for tourist visas for Russians.
“One important element is to reduce the security risks inside our borders,” Kallas said.
European Union foreign ministers have a clear understanding that now is not the moment to ease pressure on Russia, Kaja Kallas, the bloc’s foreign policy chief, told reporters on Monday.
“Pressure on Moscow, not concessions, is the fastest way to end the war,” she said following a gathering of European foreign ministers in Luxembourg.
Ukraine has passed legislation protecting the rights of national minorities, in a move expected to remove a major stumbling block to the country’s EU ambitions.
Hungary had been blocking the opening of so-called negotiation “clusters” – policy areas with which EU candidates must align their laws – accusing Kyiv of failing to protect the rights of Ukraine’s Hungarian minority.
Ukraine has long said it respected minority rights but nonetheless negotiated with Budapest over a possible law in a bid to accelerate its EU bid.
Kyiv’s parliament voted Monday to pass the legislation, which president Volodymyr Zelenskyy then signed into law, his office said.
“A Ukrainian law has been passed that ensures the rights of national minorities without compromising the status of the Ukrainian language,” the parliamentary press service said.
Russia carried out drone strikes on various targets in Ukraine on Monday, including on vessels carrying military cargo, Russia’s defence ministry said.
The ministry said it had struck three cargo vessels which it said were being used to transport military cargo to Ukraine’s Black Sea ports - two bound for Odesa and one heading to Mykolaiv.
It also reported a strike on a logistics centre in the Mykolaiv region.
One person was killed in a drone attack on a car in the village of Kupino, in Russia’s Belgorod region that borders Ukraine, local authorities said.
Reuters could not independently verify the report.
Zelenskyy says 'increasingly clear' Russia does not want energy ceasefire after strikes
Ukrainian president Volodymyr Zelenskyy said it was “increasingly clear” that Russia was unwilling to accept a US-proposed ceasefire on energy strikes, as Moscow hit six Ukrainian energy facilities on Monday.
“This is what happens when Russia sees the prospect of higher revenues for its war machine,” he wrote in a post on X.
Russia presents a long-term threat to Europe regardless of the outcome of the war in Ukraine, the head of Germany’s domestic intelligence agency said.
Warning that Moscow wanted to upend Europe’s international order, Sina Sellen, president of the BfV, said Russian-orchestrated attacks would “continue to come”.
“The hybrid threat is here, and it has long been decoupled from the situation in Ukraine,” he said at a Berlin conference organised by the BfV.
“For Russia, [the goal] is a fundamentally new map of Europe and of its role within Europe and in geopolitics.”
A 13-year-old girl was among three people killed in a Russian strike on a house near the frontline city of Kramatorsk in eastern Ukraine on Monday, the authorities said.
The head of the Donetsk regional military administration, Vadym Filashkin, said a house in the Cherkaske area was hit with cluster munitions, accusing Russia of “a deliberate attempt” to maximise civilian casualties.
German chancellor Friedrich Merz said that Russia would only negotiate “seriously” under pressure, days after president Donald Trump announced a temporary easing of US sanctions on Russian diesel.
“For Germany and for Europe, such a decision is out of the question,” said Merz, referring to the US-Russia diesel deal.
“Russia will only negotiate seriously under pressure and that is why we are maintaining our sanctions against Russia.”
Nato should signal its “red lines” to Russia over sabotage attacks in Europe, the alliance’s top military commander said.
“It’s important that allies continue to consult, think about how we might respond, and make sure that we message clearly and concisely to the Russians where our red lines are,” Nato commander Alexus Grynkewich said in Warsaw.
Ukrainian officials said Russian attacks killed six people in two Ukrainian cities yesterday.
In Kharkiv, Ukraine’s second-largest city, a strike on a grocery store killed three people and injured 20 others, including two children, the regional governor, Oleh Syniehubov, said.
Footage released by the Kharkiv prosecutor’s office captured the moment of the strike, showing debris flying through the air and fires breaking out as car alarms sounded.
An “unprecedented” cyber-attack is behind the shutdown of refrigerator units in multiple French supermarkets, according to the chief executive of Cooperative U, one of the chains affected.
At least 150 Intermarche shops were targeted, along with almost 100 Cooperative U outlets, AFP reports. Paris prosecutors confirmed the attack, with media reporting that hackers were “managing to remotely trigger the forced defrosting of the refrigeration systems in numerous stores.”
Reuters is carrying some further quotes from Nato’s supreme allied commander for Europe, Gen Alexus Grynkewich, about how the alliance says it would deal with an attack on Nato territory. He told the audience at the Warsaw Security Forum:
If someone is foolish enough to attack us, we will fight. We will stop the attack and deny them the ability to achieve their objectives, whatever those might be. We will, in short, ensure any attack, against any ally, proves utterly futile.
Should the adversary choose to press the attack or commit his reserves, we will break the warfighting system engaged against us. This includes not just the attacking force itself, but anything and everything that supports, sustains, and controls that force.
Nato’s supreme allied commander for Europe, Gen Alexus Grynkewich has been outlining what he describes as the Nato “theory of victory”, in which he says Nato forces would block, then blunt, then break any aggressive move against the alliance.
While stressing that he did not see conflict as “inevitable”, he said at the Warsaw Security Forum it was a plan to “prepare us to execute our most sacred task – the defence of our people and our territory.”
Nato’s supreme allied commander for Europe, Gen Alexus Grynkewich, is speaking now at the Warsaw Security Forum. We will bring you any key lines that emerge.
A little more from Kremlin spokesperson Dmitry Peskov here on the prospects of a limited truce agreement. He says that Russia would potentially offer a one-day truce if Ukraine were to hold elections. He said:
If they truly want to hold elections in Kyiv, then the president of Russia, the commander-in-chief, will be ready to give an order not to launch strikes on Ukraine on election day, specifically on election day.
France’s high school students will stage new protests on Tuesday, the Agence France-Presse (AFP) news agency is reporting,
A government source told journalists last week that the cost for damage caused by the demonstrations, which have shaken an unpopular government trying to reduce a ballooning budget deficit, was already “at least 30 million euros”.
Widespread disillusionment has seen young people protest over recent weeks against what they say is underfunding and neglect of the education system, with the demonstrations marred by often violent clashes that have injured hundreds.
Trying to appease the student’s demands, the government announced last week that about 3,000 substitute teachers would be deployed in the coming days to replace absent staff at the 114 worst-affected high schools.
But the Union of High School students described the initial announcements as “crumbs” and maintain their demand for an extra €10m (£8.4m) to be invested in the country’s lycees, where students – most between 15 and 18 – complete their high school education.
On Friday, the government noted a drop in the number of blockades and meetings outside the country’s lycees. More than 96% were opening on Friday, the education ministry said, but now a new stage of the campaign for improved conditions could mark a turning point in the protests.

articles.title: “Zelenskyy is helping Democrats”: Trump’s MAGA base accuses Ukraine of trying to swing US midterms, says journalist in US
articles.body:
Three weeks before the US elections, the American right has a new villain for high fuel prices: Ukraine. Ukrainian journalist in the US, Ostap Yarysh, says the MAGA wing of US conservatives is pushing a claim that Ukraine deliberately strikes Russian oil refineries to raise fuel prices, trick US President Donald Trump, and help the Democratic Party before the November congressional vote.
The accusation casts Kyiv’s refinery strikes as a planned political move against Republicans, and it has spread from anonymous social media accounts to national television and members of Congress, Yarysh notes. Yet experts tie the fuel-price spike mainly to the US war with Iran, and the closure of the Strait of Hormuz, not to Ukraine, and even Russia’s promised 300,000 tons of diesel would barely cover a day's US demand.
The messaging runs through influential American figures. Utah Senator Mike Lee wrote on X that “Zelenskyy is working overtime. To help Democrats in November.”
Fox News host Rachel Campos-Duffy called Zelenskyy ungrateful for continuing to bomb refineries and complicate the president’s position before the midterms, according to Yarysh’s account.
Blogger Jack Posobiec, who has a multimillion audience, has urged Washington to immediately stop sharing intelligence with Ukraine and cut off its funding, framing the strikes as an attempt to hurt Trump before the vote.
When you cannot fix the problem, try to control the story
Yarysh reads the campaign as damage control. The Republicans’ weak position before the vote stems mainly from the economy and a jump in domestic fuel prices, he says, a problem the promised Russian diesel cannot solve.
Blaming Ukraine serves two purposes, Yarysh argues: it channels voter anger toward an outside culprit, and it gives Trump a ready explanation if Republicans lose in November, that Zelenskyy set him up to help the Democrats.
Not everyone on the right is buying the blame
Even inside MAGA, some push back on that rhetoric. Yarysh points to far-right activist Laura Loomer, who argued that buying Russian oil fills the coffers of Iran’s regime, which she said "chants death to America."
With three weeks to the vote, Yarysh warns that Ukraine should expect many more such accusations, as the information attack is likely to intensify rather than fade before election day.

articles.title: European allies publicly back Zelensky after Trump says Ukraine needs a new president
articles.body:
European allies publicly back Zelensky after Trump says Ukraine needs a new president
Europe’s largest countries rallied behind Ukrainian President Volodymyr Zelensky after U.S. President Donald Trump said Ukraine needs a new leader.
German Foreign Minister Johann Wadephul said that Germany remains on the side of Ukraine and its government and “fully support the President as he carries out his difficult duties.”
British Defense Secretary Wes Streeting said: “We stand with President Zelensky.” He stressed that London would like to see “strong Western unity in resolve and support for Ukraine” and said he considered it his duty to help bring that about.
French President Emmanuel Macron also said that Paris “will continue to stand by Ukraine and President Zelensky.”
On Saturday, Trump said Zelensky “could’ve made many deals and for some reason he never does,” and said he believed it was “time for Ukraine to get a new President.”
In response, Zelensky said he’s ready to hold new presidential elections without waiting for the war to end, though he said that would require a 60-day ceasefire. He said he would accept whatever choice the Ukrainian people make. “If President Trump really wants to have some changes in — during elections, I also shared it with his team. So please tell Putin, give us two months, 60 days off. Total ceasefire, 60 days, and we will organize elections,” Zelensky said.
The rift between Trump and Zelensky became public amid Trump’s demands that Kyiv stop striking Russian oil refineries and a deal between Moscow and Washington to ease U.S. sanctions on Russian diesel exports.
On Sunday, Trump announced that Russia and Ukraine had agreed to an energy ceasefire, though what exactly this meant was unclear. Zelensky first said Trump’s statement came as news to him, but later said Ukraine’s Armed Forces “had received all the relevant orders,” without specifying what he meant.
This morning, Zelensky said that Russian drones struck a power plant in Kharkiv immediately after Trump’s statement. He said he was confident that “Putin does not read Truth Social, and his Shaheds drones follow a different set of instructions.” Zelensky warned that Ukraine would respond to Russian strikes.
“This winter, if Russia does not agree to an energy ceasefire, we will respond. That is why yesterday the American president’s post drew real interest and real hope that the energy ceasefire could actually work. We in Ukraine immediately supported this idea,” Zelensky added.
Moscow did not officially comment on Trump’s remarks about the ceasefire. Regarding Trump’s comments about replacing the Ukrainian president, Kremlin spokesperson Dmitry Peskov said:
Trump said he believes it’s time for a new president. Why? Because the president of Ukraine needs to make very responsible and very difficult decisions to stop this war. Either Zelensky takes on that responsibility, shows that political will, or he doesn’t. So far, he hasn’t.
Regarding the 60-day ceasefire to hold elections, Peskov said he believed Ukraine’s president needed that time not for elections, but “to regroup, heal wounds, and continue the war.” He did not rule out that Putin “would be prepared to order that no strikes be carried out against Ukraine on election day, specifically on election day.”

articles.title: Estonia Considers Light Fighter Jets to Intercept Jet-Powered Drones
articles.body:
Estonian Defense Minister Martin Herem said the country should consider acquiring its own light jet aircraft to counter Russian jet-powered drones.
He made the remarks to The Baltic Sentinel after visiting Ukraine.
Herem linked the need for this capability to the rapid development of jet-powered attack drones, which are harder to intercept with conventional counter-drone systems because of their high speed and altitude.
According to an official statement from Estonia’s Ministry of Defense, Martin Herem met with Volodymyr Zelensky and Defense Minister Yevhen Khmara on October 11.
Topics discussed included strengthening Ukraine’s air defense, defense-industrial cooperation, and leveraging Ukraine’s combat experience to develop Estonia’s defense capabilities.
Estonia currently has no fighter jets of its own and relies on NATO allies for air policing under the Baltic Air Policing mission. However, the Estonian Air Force leases two L-39 jet trainers from private company Aerohooldus OÜ for tactical air controller training.
Estonia has previously discussed developing a domestic light combat aviation capability. A former Estonian Air Force commander told ERR that the L-39s could theoretically be armed, but their civilian status and lease terms prevent this.
The drone threat has also directly affected Estonia. In May, a fighter jet deployed as part of Baltic Air Policing shot down a drone over Estonian territory for the first time.
Meanwhile, Tallinn is strengthening its ground-based air defense capabilities. In June, Estonia received the first components of the medium-range IRIS-T SLM air defense system and is also considering procuring longer-range systems capable of countering ballistic missiles.

articles.title: France Launches Development of Its Own 6th-Generation Fighter and ‘Super Rafale’
articles.body:
After withdrawing from the joint Franco-German FCAS fighter program, France is launching its own project to develop a next-generation fighter and modernize its air force.
Chief of Staff of the French Air and Space Force Jérôme Bellanger made the statement, Les Echos reports.
France has definitively parted ways with Germany and is accelerating the development of its own aircraft, designated ACF (Avion de combat du futur).
The new fighter jet will replace the NGF (New Generation Fighter) concept and succeed the Rafale F4 aircraft.
Meanwhile, in December, France’s Ministry of the Armed Forces and Veterans Affairs is expected to officially launch the development phase of the ‘Super Rafale’ fighter F5 version.
This version will feature new engines, artificial intelligence, electro-optical systems, and a hypersonic missile for nuclear deterrence.
The development phase for the ACF prototype is scheduled to begin in 2027, with creation of the production variant set to start in 2029.
To integrate combat AI, the French Air and Space Force is launching the HypAIRion project, which converts two Mirage 2000 aircraft into flying laboratories.
The project’s main goal is to conduct the first joint flight of a Rafale fighter in tandem with a guided wingman drone in 2028.
France plans to expand its fighter jet fleet to at least 230 aircraft by 2035, up from the current 170.
The Air Force is also establishing two new squadrons at Cazaux Air Base, one specializing in reconnaissance and strike drones.
The second squadron will focus on high-altitude threats, including ballistic missiles and reconnaissance balloons.

articles.title: EU Blacklists Nearly 1,600 in Russian Defense Firms and Executives
articles.body:
The European Union adopted its largest-ever single set of sanctions against Russia to date on Monday, blacklisting 1,569 individuals and companies within the country's military-industrial complex.
The measures blacklist 826 Russian companies and 743 chief executives, bringing the total number of listings under the EU sanctions regime protecting Ukraine’s territorial integrity to nearly 4,600. The designated entities face immediate asset freezes and funding blocks, while the targeted individuals are now barred from entering the bloc.
The package specifically targets mid-level suppliers that form the "core" of Russia's defense sector, which together generate an annual turnover of at least 20 billion euros ($22.32 billion) and employ more than 250,000 people.
According to the European Council, the designated companies supply critical components for advanced weapons systems, including semiconductors, radars, satellite systems, explosives, and optics. Notably, more than half of the new listings address the production chain for the ballistic missiles Russia uses in its daily strikes against Ukrainian infrastructure.
"Bombing Kyiv’s bridges, ships transporting grain, and the National Academy of Sciences are not the actions of a country seeking peace," said Kaja Kallas, the EU's High Representative for Foreign Affairs and Security Policy.
The sweeping European measures come just three days after U.S. President Donald Trump announced an agreement on Truth Social with Russian President Vladimir Putin for Moscow to supply millions of tons of diesel fuel to American and global markets in an effort to lower domestic fuel costs.
Further commenting on the latest EU sanctions, Kallas, however, stressed: "This is not the time to ease pressure on Moscow but to increase it."
The new listings follow the European Council's June 2026 directive to intensify pressure on Moscow in response to an escalating military campaign that has deliberately targeted civilian infrastructure and, according to the Council, aims to undermineUkraine's resilience.

articles.title: Lithuanian prime minister says more Ukrainian strikes on Russian data centers could help safeguard European elections from interference

Lithuanian prime minister says more Ukrainian strikes on Russian data centers could help safeguard European elections from interference

I think we should ask Mr. Zelensky to strike more data centers in Russia, and that might help.

Sinkevičius said the top priorities for both Lithuania and NATO as a whole were air defense, protection against drones, and countering hybrid threats.
Over four days, Ukrainian drones struck three Yandex data centers in Russia. The company’s services are still down. Replacing the damaged equipment will take about six months and will be expensive because of sanctions and a global shortage of computing capacity.

articles.title: Republicans Denounce Trump’s Diesel Deal With Russia’s Putin Amid Mounting Backlash
articles.body:
President Donald Trump on Monday defended his plan to import diesel from Russia amid mounting calls from within his own party to reverse course on the controversial deal. "I made the right choice for the American People—always America first," Trump said of the move.
Lawmakers across party aisles, however, argue that the deal goes against a 2022 law which banned Russian oil imports and is not in the best interests of the American public.
“Congress explicitly banned Russian energy imports in 2022 to prevent American dollars from financing Putin’s brutal war against Ukraine. Congress was clear: The U.S. should not import oil from Russia until it ends its aggression against Ukraine and ceases threats against our NATO allies,” read a joint bipartisan statement released Sunday by four Republican Senators and three Democrats.
The lawmakers argued that Trump’s decision to allow Russian diesel imports to the U.S. “runs directly counter to that law” and criticized the lack of congressional overview, insisting that the Administration had failed to consult with Congress or submit any explanation over its decision. “The United States should not provide [Russian President Vladimir] Putin with a financial lifeline while Russia continues to kill Ukrainian civilians. The Administration must immediately reverse course,” they urged.
The statement was co-signed by GOP Senators Lisa Murkowski of Alaska, Susan Collins of Maine, Thom Tillis of North Carolina, and John Curtis of Utah, alongside Democratic Senators Jeanne Shaheen of New Hampshire, Ron Wyden of Oregon, and Richard Blumenthal of Connecticut.
Trump said Friday he had reached an agreement with Putin for Moscow to "immediately" supply 300,000 tons of diesel to American and global markets. The move comes amid a renewed push by the Administration to lower energy prices for Americans, which have skyrocketed since the Iran war began in February. The increased diesel fuel prices have shaken the loyalties of some of Trump’s most ardent support groups, with farmers telling TIME their day-to-day operations are being severely impacted.
In the wake of the diesel supply deal, Trump on Sunday claimed Russia and Ukraine had “agreed” to an energy cease-fire “effective immediately.” However, Ukrainian President Volodymyr Zelensky on Monday said Russian strikes overnight—which reportedly killed several people and wounded dozens—had included attacks on energy facilities.
“So there were Russian violations of the energy cease-fire announced by President Trump,” said Zelensky. “For now, this is Putin’s answer to Trump—Russian attacks. But we are waiting. We are waiting for the details of the conversation between the Americans and the Russians. We are waiting to see what specific steps the Americans are ready to take.” Trump over the weekend responded to Zelensky's initial criticism of the diesel deal by telling reporters "it's time for Ukraine to get a new President."
U.S. lawmakers pushing back against Trump’s Russia diesel plan had sternly warned against putting trust in Putin.
Sen. Tillis, during an appearance on NBC’s Meet the Press, expressed concern that the diesel deal could place American lives at risk. “These are bad people hanging out with bad people, putting American lives at risk—particularly our Special Operators and forward-deployed personnel,” Tillis said, insisting that Putin “cannot be trusted.”
He also doubled down on his argument that the President’s deal may violate the law passed by Congress four years ago, as it outright banned Russian oil imports unless specific criteria were met, including a full Russian withdrawal from Ukraine.
“I do believe there’s a legitimate case for saying the President’s not following the law,” Tillis said. “We were very clear that Russia is the aggressor. Russia is the one who can end this war by backing out of [the] territory they occupied.”
Just three weeks ago, Trump signed a sweeping Russia sanctions bill, intended to target the country's financial institutions and the energy industry, which has largely financed the assault on Ukraine. The bill was named after Sen. Lindsey O. Graham, the late Republican Senator who spent the final year of his life building support for the measure.
Some Republican lawmakers mentioned this legislation as they criticized the diesel plan. “The President should be using those authorities instead of allowing Russia to export diesel, rake in revenues, and continue its catastrophic war in Ukraine,” said Murkowski.
“I oppose President Trump’s decision to lift sanctions on the purchase of diesel from Russia,” said Collins. “I was a co-sponsor of the Russian sanctions law, which the President recently signed, but is now not following.”
TIME has reached out to the White House for comment.
Republican Rep. Brian Fitzpatrick of Pennsylvania announced Saturday he plans to introduce a bipartisan bill intended to stop Trump from lifting sanctions on Russian oil.
“We will be introducing bipartisan legislation to block any and all purchases of Russian oil. It will be called the ‘Ronald Reagan Peace Through Strength Act,’” said Fitzpatrick.
Rep. Don Bacon of Nebraska, a Republican who has clashed with Trump on other high-profile issues, said he has already agreed to be a co-sponsor of the bill, insisting that “Congress must make a stand.”
Treasury Secretary Scott Bessent has defended the move, insisting the agreement with Russia will work through existing legal channels the U.S. has to help bring prices down.
“We’re doing it with all the legal authorities we have, so anyone in Congress who says that—whether it’s an old bill or the current Lindsey Graham bill—prohibits us from doing it, is wrong,” he told Fox News.
Republican Sen. John Barrasso of Wyoming has also defended the diesel deal, telling CBS' Face the Nation that the President “has to make tough decisions.”
U.S. allies warn Trump's diesel deal could bolster Russia's war
Zelensky described Trump's initial announcement as a “gift to Putin” and said easing sanctions on Russia was “an obvious weakness” that “plays into Russia’s hands—allowing it to kill more, wage war for longer, have even less respect for America, and inflict even greater losses and damage on the world.”
The agreement has also drawn criticism from international leaders, particularly in Europe, where governments have played a central role in supporting Ukraine's defense against Russia.
Swedish Prime Minister Ulf Kristersson expressed his “regret” over the U.S. agreement with Russia, warning that “energy revenues are central to the Russian war chest.” Estonian Prime Minister Kristen Michal similarly said the agreement was a “big miscalculation,” arguing that it “is opposite to the long-term activities of the western world to limit the flow of energy carriers to Putin.” Both Sweden and Estonia were among the top 10 countries providing aid to Ukraine as a share of their GDP between January 2022 and February 2026.
Kaja Kallas, the E.U.'s foreign policy chief, said that “suspending sanctions on Russian diesel provides Moscow with more revenues to wage war.”
On Monday, Kallas announced that European foreign ministers had adopted nearly 1,600 new sanctions targeting Russia's military-industrial complex, underscoring the contrast between Washington's decision and Europe's continued push to economically isolate Moscow.
The U.K. has also opposed Trump's agreement. Defense Secretary Wes Streeting said Sunday that Britain did not support the deal with Putin and would instead look to "strengthen sanctions” against Russia. Prime Minister Andy Burnham acknowledged that “the last 24 hours had been difficult for Ukraine and reiterated his complete solidarity” during a phone call with Zelensky.
Canadian Prime Minister Mark Carney also spoke with Zelensky on Sunday, and expressed his view that the “agreement is in direct opposition to the efforts of Ukraine, Canada, and our allies to create peace and stability in Europe.”

articles.title: EU to Provide Ukraine with Nearly €3 Billion in Additional Military Aid
articles.body:
The European Union plans to allocate around €3 billion in military aid to Ukraine next week.
Ukrainian President Volodymyr Zelensky announced this on October 11 following a phone call with European Commission President Ursula von der Leyen.
According to von der Leyen, the new funding will be directed towards drones and missiles to strengthen Ukraine’s defense and protect its airspace.
The funding is being provided under the EU’s Ukraine Support Loan programme, which totals €90 billion for 2026–2027.
Of this amount, €60 billion has been allocated for defense needs, while the remaining €30 billion will go towards budgetary support for Ukraine.
We had a very detailed discussion with @vonderleyen on virtually all the current areas of our work with the European Union and the decisions needed to support Ukraine. I thanked Ursula for the recent €1.24 billion tranche for defense, which Ukraine has already received. I am grateful for the confirmation that another approximately €3 billion in military support will be allocated as early as next week. These funds will strengthen us.
Of course, I briefed the President on the brutal Russian strikes that continue unabated. Just before our conversation, the Russians struck a power plant in Kyiv with a “shahed” drone, and many districts experienced power outages. Later, there were strikes on energy facilities in the Kharkiv region. And all of this happened AFTER the President of the United States made his statement about an energy ceasefire.
Under these circumstances, reliable support from our partners means real protection for people’s lives and a guarantee that the Russians will not be able to break Ukraine. We deeply appreciate all the tangible steps taken to support our defense and our people.
Ursula and I agreed that our teams will have detailed discussions on our next joint actions and the coordination of our steps. We are also preparing to open the negotiating clusters – so that all the remaining clusters are opened by the end of the year. Ukraine’s European path is also a path toward strengthening Europe itself. Thank you!
— Volodymyr Zelenskyy / Володимир Зеленський (@ZelenskyyUa) October 11, 2026
Zelensky also thanked the European Commission president for the previous tranche of €1.24 billion, which Ukraine has already received, and for confirming further funding.
On October 7, the European Commission transferred €1.24 billion to Ukraine to purchase Ukrainian-made unmanned aerial vehicles (UAVs), interceptor drones, ammunition for them, and missiles.
By the end of 2026, a further €28.1 billion will remain available to Ukraine under the Ukraine Support Loan programme.
Of this amount, €15.4 billion has been allocated to the defense industry, while €12.7 billion will go towards budgetary support.
A further €4.4 billion in budgetary assistance remains available under the Ukraine Facility programme.
Militarnyi previously reported that Germany would provide Ukraine with €1 billion in military aid and €350 million to repair energy infrastructure.
The two sides also plan to finalize an agreement on the joint production of various types of drones.

articles.body:
EU foreign ministers have approved over 1,600 new sanctions listings targeting Russia’s military-industrial complex, with more than half linked to the production chain for ballistic missiles, EU foreign policy chief Kaja Kallas said.
“This is the single largest expansion of our sanctions list since Russia started its war,” Kallas wrote on X.
JOIN US ON TELEGRAM
Follow our coverage of the war on the @Kyivpost_official.
The 22nd sanctions package covers 1,646 entities and individuals, according to The Moscow Times. With the new listings, nearly 4,650 entities and individuals are now under EU sanctions over Russia’s war against Ukraine.
The measures target people and companies involved in missile development, testing, and manufacturing, as well as the production of fuel, engines, and specialized materials used in missile systems.
“More than half are connected to the production chain for ballistic missiles,” Kallas said.
Reuters reported that the blacklist also includes manufacturers of specialized textiles, synthetic fibers, and carbon fibers used in weapons production.
The package further targets drone manufacturers and shipyards that service submarines, while 77 individuals are being sanctioned for participating in State Duma elections held in Russian-occupied Ukrainian territories.
The EU has also added seven North Korean entities and individuals accused of helping Russia’s war effort, amid growing concern over military cooperation between Moscow and Pyongyang.
Russia Suffers 50,000 Casualties in 1 Month – NATO
Kallas said the new measures were intended to disrupt Russia’s ability to manufacture weapons used against Ukraine.
“We are making it significantly harder, slower and more expensive for Russia to produce the weapons it uses to kill Ukrainians.”

articles.title: Ten casualties to one, by a NATO official’s count: Russia’s September in Ukraine’s kill zones
articles.body:
Russia suffered vastly more casualties than Ukraine in September, a senior NATO military official told Bloomberg. Ukraine’s General Staff put the month’s Russian toll only slightly lower.
September’s toll lands on a recruitment system that was already falling short. Ukraine’s military intelligence (HUR) estimated that Russian losses outran new contracts in June and July, when monthly losses ran lower. In August, Ukrainian President Volodymyr Zelenskyy, citing military intelligence, warned that Russia is preparing a mass call-up after its parliamentary elections. That vote ended on 20 September.
Where the numbers come from
Russian casualties passed 50,000 in September, up to 28,000 of them killed, the official said. Ukraine’s losses over the same month came to about 5,000, according to the official, who spoke on condition of anonymity. Russia does not release casualty figures, Bloomberg noted. In late August, Pavlo Palisa, deputy head of Ukraine’s Presidential Office, put Russia’s July losses at 43,000 killed and wounded. Bloomberg could not confirm his figures.
To push forward, Russia keeps feeding troops into “kill zones,” the official said. These are stretches of ground saturated with armed drones, mines, and artillery fire. Maksym, call sign Rumyn, is a deputy company commander in the 46th Airmobile Brigade’s drone battalion. In April, he said the zone once ran 3–5 km deep and is now several times larger.
Ukraine suffered 10 times fewer casualties than Russia in Vivaldi counteroffensive, veteran says. Ukraine’s innovations in drone and ground robot tactics are changing frontline warfare
Rising stakes for Moscow
Russia’s defense spending is expected to near $199 billion this year, Bloomberg reported, citing two sources close to the government. That is about 40% above the plan the government set in late 2025.
Russian President Vladimir Putin would struggle to wind down the invasion without a political cost, Martin Jäger said last week. He heads Germany’s Federal Intelligence Service (BND).

articles.title: Trump ‘really mad’ at Zelensky – media
articles.body:
Trump ‘really mad’ at Zelensky – media
US President Donald Trump is furious with Vladimir Zelensky over Kiev’s continued attacks on Russian oil refineries, with Washington reportedly threatening to cut off weapons supplies and intelligence sharing unless Ukraine stops the strikes, according to Axios and the Financial Times.
The confrontation comes after Trump struck a diesel deal with Russian President Vladimir Putin to ease a global fuel shortage that has sent American energy prices soaring.
Kiev has continued to target Russian refining facilities despite repeated warnings, with Trump accusing Zelensky of deliberately hurting American consumers and farmers while refusing opportunities to end the conflict.
“Trump is really mad. He feels Zelensky is taking the US for granted,” a White House official told Axios on Sunday. The source argued that Kiev’s attacks on Russian refineries are doing more damage to its relationship with Washington than to Russia.
US officials contacted Kiev and several European capitals over the weekend, threatening to suspend intelligence sharing and the NATO-backed Prioritized Ukraine Requirements List (PURL) mechanism, through which European countries purchase American weapons for Ukraine, according to the Financial Times, which cited officials familiar with the discussions.
Trump envoys Steve Witkoff and Jared Kushner also reportedly warned Ukrainian representatives during talks in Miami on Friday that Washington could stop sharing intelligence if Kiev continues to ignore the president’s demands, according to a Ukrainian official cited by Axios.
A US official, however, denied making direct threats, saying the negotiators instead reminded Kiev of Washington’s extensive military and intelligence support and urged it to stop taking actions that hurt American consumers.
The confrontation has threatened to derail broader negotiations aimed at ending the Ukraine conflict. Witkoff and Kushner have reportedly put their planned trip to Moscow on hold until Kiev and its leading European backers clarify whether they are prepared to support a unified peace proposal.
Trump reached a diesel deal with Putin on Friday after Zelensky ignored at least half a dozen requests to stop striking Russian refineries, according to earlier Axios reporting. The US Treasury subsequently eased sanctions on Russian diesel exports until April 2027, while Moscow pledged substantial fuel deliveries to help alleviate global shortages.
Zelensky called the move a “weak decision,” arguing that the agreement will provide Russia with additional revenue. Trump hit back, accusing the Ukrainian leader of creating problems for the world and suggesting that it is time for Ukraine to elect a new leader capable of reaching a deal.
On Sunday, Trump unexpectedly announced that Moscow and Kiev agreed to an immediate ceasefire covering attacks on energy infrastructure. “Effective immediately, there is an ENERGY CEASEFIRE in the War between Russia and Ukraine. Both parties have agreed. Do not break it!” he wrote on Truth Social.
The announcement caught Kiev by surprise, with Zelensky saying it “was news for me.” Moscow has also yet to confirm the agreement.
A White House official described the proposed agreement as a “refinery for refinery” arrangement, under which both sides would stop attacking oil refineries, but not necessarily other energy infrastructure, according to Axios. Kiev has said the deal would disproportionately benefit Russia, since Ukraine has only one largely nonfunctional refinery and fully relies on imported fuel.

articles.title: Russia could strike NATO territory within months, Czech intelligence chief warns
articles.body:
Russia could carry out increasingly dangerous operations on NATO territory within the coming months, including sabotage attacks and strikes against weapons depots supplying Ukraine, the head of the Czech Republic's intelligence service warned Monday.
Michal Koudelka, director general of the Czech Security Information Service, told a parliamentary security conference that Moscow appeared to be adopting a strategy of "escalation for de-escalation," potentially taking greater risks to pressure Western countries supporting Ukraine.
"This could involve sabotage attacks on the territory of a NATO member state against a facility connected to aid for Ukraine, a drone or missile attack on a weapons depot intended for Ukraine, or, in an extreme case, even a limited military action against one of the neighbouring member states of the Alliance," Koudelka said.
However, he emphasized that the most extreme scenario, a direct Russian military operation against a NATO member state, was not an immediate threat.
"Russia has all its forces concentrated in Ukraine," he explained.
Koudelka said his agency had no specific intelligence indicating an imminent direct threat to the Czech Republic but was closely monitoring Russian activities targeting the country and its NATO allies.
According to the intelligence chief, Moscow's hybrid operations, which can include sabotage, cyberattacks and other disruptive activities, are designed to undermine cohesion within NATO and weaken the alliance's collective response to Russia's war in Ukraine.
His assessment comes amid growing concerns over the possibility that Russia could expand its confrontation with Western countries beyond Ukraine without launching a full-scale military attack against NATO.
Russian President Vladimir Putin said earlier this month that Moscow had no plans to attack any European country and wanted peaceful coexistence with its neighbors.
Russia has also repeatedly denied allegations that it is responsible for sabotage operations or other forms of hybrid warfare targeting European countries.

articles.title: Russia Suffers 50,000 Casualties in 1 Month – NATO
articles.body:
Russia suffered more than 50,000 military casualties in Ukraine during September, including as many as 28,000 troops killed, according to an assessment by a senior NATO military official.
The figure covers both killed and wounded personnel and represents one of Russia’s heaviest months of the war, Bloomberg reported on Sunday, Oct. 11.
JOIN US ON TELEGRAM
Follow our coverage of the war on the @Kyivpost_official.
The unnamed official, who discussed the assessment on condition of anonymity, estimated that Ukrainian forces suffered approximately 5,000 casualties over the same period.
That would put Russia’s total monthly losses at roughly 10 times Ukraine’s. Neither estimate could be independently verified, and Ukrainian authorities rarely disclose comprehensive figures for their own military casualties.
Russian troops sent into “kill zones”
The NATO official attributed Russia’s heavy losses partly to its continued attempts to advance through heavily defended Ukrainian positions.
Russian commanders have been sending troops into what the official described as “kill zones” covered by armed drones, landmines, artillery, and other defensive systems.
Despite the cost in personnel, Moscow continues offensive operations along several sections of the front.
At the same time, Ukrainian forces have intensified long-range strikes against Russian oil refineries, data centers, and other facilities supporting Moscow’s war effort. Ukrainian ground operations have also reportedly returned more than 125 square kilometers (48 square miles) of territory to Kyiv’s control.
Russia Needs Just 5 Drones to Test NATO, Kuleba Says
The NATO assessment broadly corresponds with figures released by Ukraine’s General Staff, which estimated that Russia lost 46,230 personnel in September. The Ukrainian military did not specify how many were killed and how many were wounded.
Russia’s total losses near 1.55 million
By Wednesday, Oct. 7, Ukraine’s military estimated that Russia’s total personnel losses since the beginning of the full-scale invasion had reached nearly 1.55 million.
That figure also combines troops killed and wounded and has not been independently confirmed.
Russia does not publish comprehensive information about military casualties or recruitment. Moscow’s last detailed official death toll was released during the early months of the invasion and is widely considered outdated.
Estimates from Ukraine, NATO, and Western intelligence agencies vary because they use different sources and methodologies, while distinguishing between deaths, injuries, and troops who later return to service remains difficult.
War places growing pressure on Moscow
The rising casualties come as the Kremlin spends heavily to recruit personnel and sustain offensive operations.
Russia’s defense expenditure is expected to approach 17 trillion rubles, or approximately $199 billion, in 2026 – around 40% higher than the government’s original plan announced at the end of 2025, according to Bloomberg.
German Federal Intelligence Service Chief Martin Jäger said last week that President Vladimir Putin’s war had created a situation in which ending the invasion without paying a domestic political price was becoming increasingly difficult.
The Kremlin has continued relying on large enlistment bonuses, regional recruitment campaigns, and pressure on vulnerable groups to replace battlefield losses while avoiding another publicly declared nationwide mobilization.

articles.title: North Korea fires multiple ballistic missiles toward Sea of Japan
articles.body:
North Korea fired multiple ballistic missiles toward the Sea of Japan on Monday, said South Korea's military, a little over a week after Pyongyang tested a suspected hypersonic missile.
The Joint Chiefs of Staff (JCS) detected the launches around 9.20 am local time (0020GMT) from the Pyongyang area, with the missiles traveling more than 900 kilometres (559 miles), according to Yonhap News Agency.
South Korea's military said it had intensified surveillance for additional launches and was sharing intelligence with the United States and Japan while maintaining heightened readiness.
The launches followed North Korea's October 3 missile test from Wonsan, which Pyongyang described as training for troops operating its hypersonic strategic weapons system.
Tensions rise
South Korea conducted its own first test launch of a hypersonic glide vehicle on Thursday, in an apparent demonstration of its advanced missile capabilities.
Japan also detected two suspected ballistic missiles, which fell outside its exclusive economic zone.
The latest launches come amid tensions following a September 21 land mine explosion in the Demilitarised Zone that injured three South Korean soldiers, two of them seriously.
Seoul accused North Korean troops of deliberately planting the mines following a joint investigation with the UN Command.
Pyongyang denied responsibility, accused Seoul of fabricating the findings and warned of retaliation against any military counteraction.
North Korea has not issued any public statement on Monday's launches.

articles.title: Russia’s Losses Reached 50,000 in September, NATO Estimates
articles.body:
In September, Russian forces lost more than 50,000 personnel in fighting in Ukraine, including up to 28,000 killed.
Bloomberg reports this, citing a senior NATO military official.
According to the source, the Russian command continues to send personnel into “kill zones” saturated with drones, minefields and artillery.
Ukrainian losses over the same period are estimated at around 5,000 personnel.
According to the Office of the President of Ukraine, Russian forces also suffered more than 40,000 killed and wounded per month in previous months.
Martin Jäger, head of Germany’s Federal Intelligence Service, noted that the hostilities have created a dynamic in which ending the war would come at a high political cost for the Kremlin.
In January, it was reported that one of Ukraine’s strategic goals in the war against Russia was to eliminate 50,000 Russian troops every month.
According to then-Defence Minister Mykhailo Fedorov, Ukraine’s Defense Forces eliminated 35,000 Russian troops in December 2025, with all these losses confirmed on video.
In July, Russian occupation forces suffered 42,860 confirmed personnel losses.
President Volodymyr Zelensky clarified in his address that 30,272 of those Russian troops were hit by drones.
BBC and Mediazona journalists have identified 258,989 Russian military personnel eliminated in the war against Ukraine.
Researchers estimate that these figures may account for 45% to 65% of the actual death toll, as the Russian authorities do not publish official casualty statistics.

articles.title: Ukraine Hits 8 Russian Ballistic Missile Launchers, Forcing Moscow to Alter Planned Attacks
articles.body:
- Category
- War in Ukraine
Ukraine Hits 8 Russian Ballistic Missile Launchers, Forcing Moscow to Alter Planned Attacks
Ukraine has struck eight Russian ballistic missile launchers since the beginning of September, destroying three and damaging five others. The attacks have already forced Russian forces to cancel or alter planned missile strikes against Ukrainian cities, disrupting Moscow’s ability to carry out ballistic attacks.
We bring you stories from the ground. Your support keeps our team in the field.
According to a UNITED24 Media correspondent, Ukrainian Defense Minister Yevhenii Khmara revealed the results during a briefing with journalists on October 10, describing the strikes as part of Ukraine’s strategy to counter Russia’s ballistic missile threat by targeting launch systems before they can fire.
The targeted weapons included Russia’s Iskander ballistic missile systems and S-400 launchers adapted to strike ground targets.
“During September and early October, the Defense Forces struck eight launchers used for ballistic attacks. Three were destroyed and five damaged,” Khmara said.
He emphasized that the operations had already produced operational results, forcing Russian troops to abandon or revise some scheduled missile attacks.
The strikes come as Ukraine faces a persistent shortage of interceptor missiles capable of countering Russian ballistic weapons.
According to figures shared during the briefing, Russia launched 76 ballistic missiles against Ukraine in September alone, some of which were intercepted. Khmara warned that existing and anticipated interceptor deliveries remain insufficient to fully protect Ukrainian cities from such attacks.
Ukraine is therefore prioritizing faster deliveries of Patriot interceptor missiles, particularly PAC-3 and PAC-2 GEM-T, while working with international partners to identify available stockpiles.
“We need dozens and hundreds of missiles, not single deliveries,” Khmara stressed, calling for accelerated transfers rather than waiting for lengthy procurement contracts. Meanwhile, Ukrainian forces are increasingly targeting the launchers themselves as an alternative way to reduce Russia’s missile threat.
Earlier, on October 8, Ukrainian forces struck the Sasta machine-tool plant in Russia’s Ryazan region, reportedly linked to the production of components for Iskander ballistic missile systems. The facility supplies specialized manufacturing equipment to Russia’s defense industry, including enterprises involved in missile production.
