articles.title: North Korean missile launches may be response to South's hypersonic test, Seoul says
articles.body:
North Korea's launch of multiple ballistic missiles towards the East Sea appears to be an apparent response to South Korea's successful test of a hypersonic glide vehicle last week, the South Korean military has confirmed.
South Korea's Joint Chiefs of Staff (JCS) detected the launches originating from the Pyongyang region.
At least one projectile flew more than 900 kilometres, Yonhap News Agency said.
JCS spokesperson Jang Do-young said the firing could also demonstrate technical advances under Pyongyang's five-year defence modernisation blueprint.
Jang declined to confirm whether the weapons tested were hypersonic systems or intermediate-range ballistic missiles, noting that further technical analysis is ongoing.
The launches followed South Korea’s inaugural test of a hypersonic glide vehicle on Thursday.
Regional reactions
Japan's defence authorities confirmed detecting two suspected ballistic missiles, reporting that the projectiles landed in waters outside its exclusive economic zone.
The US Pacific Command issued a statement confirming close consultations with regional allies: "Based on current assessments, this event does not pose an immediate threat to US personnel or territory, or to our allies."
The command reiterated Washington's ironclad commitment to defending regional partners.
The missile tests unfold amid friction along the inter-Korean border following a September 21 landmine detonation inside the Demilitarised Zone (DMZ) that injured three South Korean soldiers, two critically.
Seoul accused North Korean forces of deliberately laying the explosives following a joint inquiry with the UN Command.
Pyongyang rejected the findings as fabricated and warned it would retaliate against any countermeasures.
Pyongyang has not issued an official public statement regarding Monday's launches.

articles.title: US Asian ally tests Russian trade route to Europe
articles.body:
US Asian ally tests Russian trade route to Europe
A South Korean container ship has completed a trial round trip to Europe via Russia’s Northern Sea Route, demonstrating the potential of the Arctic passage as a commercial shipping corridor.
Seoul considers maritime cooperation with Russia important to its trade strategy, despite joining some Western sanctions against Moscow over the Ukraine conflict. Chinese shipping companies have also been exploring the strategic Arctic route.
The PanStar Acro returned to Busan on Sunday, 50 days after departing for Europe along Russia’s northern coast. The ship reached Felixstowe, Britain, on September 12 and Rotterdam, Netherlands, the following day. It also called at Gdansk, Poland, before returning to South Korea.
President Lee Jae-myung congratulated the crew on their safe return and thanked them for their work. The voyage, which cut travel time by approximately ten days in each direction compared with the traditional route through the Suez Canal, provided valuable navigation experience and data as South Korea prepares for an “Arctic route era,” Lee wrote on X.
Asian interest in the Northern Sea Route has grown amid turmoil in the Middle East. However, the Russian Arctic passage presents challenges, including a limited navigation season and the potential need for icebreaker escorts.
Earlier this month, Russian nuclear corporation Rosatom, which operates the Northern Sea Route through its subsidiary and maintains a fleet of nuclear-powered icebreakers, welcomed the PanStar Acro’s eastbound passage. The ship crossed the Arctic section in just 5.85 days, compared with 6.4 days on its westbound journey.
Timely Russian navigational guidance and information about weather and ice conditions “enabled route optimization and adherence to the planned schedule,” Rosatom said.
Russia used the Northern Sea Route for decades to supply its own hard-to-reach settlements in the north. With international traffic expected to rise due to climate change, Moscow is rapidly developing infrastructure required to support it.
According to Yonhap, the operator of the 2,758-TEU vessel had hoped to complete the journey faster but nevertheless considered the trial successful. The delay was relatively minor, and the ship encountered no major incidents.
South Korean vessels previously conducted trial voyages through the Northern Sea Route in 2013 and 2016, but the PanStar Acro became the first to complete a round trip to Europe. Seoul expects regular services along the Russian route to begin in 2030, with larger more profitable vessels using the passage by 2035 and Busan serving as a gateway port.
South Korea has joined some US-backed sanctions against Russia over the Ukraine conflict but has not directly sanctioned Rosatom. Seoul has also declined to supply weapons to Ukraine and recently experienced a diplomatic dispute with Kiev after Ukrainian leader Vladimir Zelensky disclosed an arrangement concerning the transfer to South Korea of two North Korean prisoners of war captured in Russia.
Meanwhile, Chinese carrier Sea Legend Shipping announced earlier this year the launch of regular seasonal deliveries from Ningbo-Zhoushan to European ports, including Felixstowe, Rotterdam, Gdansk, and Hamburg. The company said its “Arctic Express” service is focusing on time-sensitive cargo.

articles.title: Ukraine knocked out key Yandex data centers. The fallout is being felt across Russia.
articles.body:
Ukraine knocked out key Yandex data centers. The fallout is being felt across Russia.
Ukraine has struck three of the six data centers belonging to Yandex, a Russian technology company, in Sasovo (Ryazan region), Kaluga, and Vladimir. Kyiv called the strikes a response to Russian attacks on Ukrainian data centers, which Russian forces have been striking lately. The infrastructure of the company’s “iron heart,” as Yandex calls its data centers, has been damaged. Operations at two of them — in Sasovo and Vladimir — have been halted. At the data center in Kaluga, “several modules have been completely knocked out.” Outages have plagued the Russian internet since the strikes began: not only Yandex’s services but also the websites of other companies and even media outlets have been operating with restrictions. Users abroad have also complained about problems with Yandex’s apps. As of October 12, the company had not managed to restore their operation. Here’s a look at the consequences of the Ukrainian strikes that Yandex and its users have faced.
How the strikes on the data centers affected the company and its users
- Since the first attack on Yandex’s data centers on October 8, users have complained about outages in the company’s services, including Mail, Pay, Disk, Go, and others. The strikes also disrupted Yandex Cloud for its clients. In recent days, there have been reports (1,2,3) of problems accessing other companies’ websites and services: the app for the cafe chain Vkusno i Tochka, media websites, the Pulkovo airport, and continuous glucose monitoring services used by people with diabetes.
- Russians have been especially vocal in their complaints about problems with Yandex Pay, after some users reported on social media that all their funds had been frozen. “All my money’s on Yandex, so I have no money for food,” one affected user said. Yandex tried to reassure users, saying their funds were safe, though the company could not say when everything would be working again.
- The outages affected Yandex users outside Russia as well. People in Kyrgyzstan, Kazakhstan, and Uzbekistan were unable to order taxis and food, and similar problems were reported in Armenia, Belarus, and Serbia.
- Three of Yandex’s supercomputers are located in the data centers hit by the strikes. The company uses them, among other things, to train its artificial intelligence models, and their fate remains uncertain.
- Cybersecurity experts said Russian bot traffic dropped by almost half, to 49% of its usual level, after the strikes on Yandex’s data centers. According to Ukrainian President Volodymyr Zelensky, there has been “less hatred and provocations” on social media since the strikes because there are fewer bots.
How Yandex responded
- After the first strike, Yandex warned users of possible outages. On October 11, the company announced it had restored access to Alice (its AI assistant), Search, Maps, Mail, and other services, though not all features were working again.
- Yandex restricted downloads from its Yandex Disk cloud storage to “maintain the functionality” of other services, as engineers focus first on restoring the most popular services.
- After navigation outages, Yandex Pro advised drivers working with Yandex Taxi to use Google Maps or the navigation app Waze, which is also owned by Google.
- Yandex arranged to move customer data and services to data centers operated by cloud providers VK Cloud, Selectel, and K2Cloud.
- After the strikes, Yandex added a clause to its user agreement exempting the company from liability in cases of force majeure, including attacks by Ukrainian drones.
What company employees, analysts, and market participants are saying
- “Things are bad. I don’t think we’ll come out of this night without losses. Some [of the capacity] definitely won’t be restored at all,” one of The Bell’s sources at Yandex said after Ukraine’s first attack on the Sasovo facility.
- Replacing the damaged equipment is expected to take about six months, and Yandex will have to buy new equipment “on the most expensive market in recent years.” The additional cost will ultimately push up prices for customers’ cloud services.
- After the first strikes, Yandex shares on the Moscow Exchange fell more than 7.6%. Experts say the company’s business has a sufficient margin of safety, but its main risk is rising spending on protection, backup capacity, and infrastructure redistribution if the strikes continue. A second risk is disruption to Yandex’s cloud infrastructure and corporate solutions, which could affect customers’ businesses.
- Amid the attacks on Yandex, other data center owners have begun taking measures to protect their infrastructure, including purchasing equipment to defend against drones. Those added costs could make data center services even more expensive.
- Yadro, an X Holding subsidiary, could profit from protecting Russian data centers from drones. The holding’s deputy general director is Boris Korolev — the son of Sergei Korolev, first deputy director of Russia’s Federal Security Service (FSB). Yadro supplies mobile data processing centers, demand for which has grown since late summer, as the industry has discussed the inevitability of Ukrainian attacks on Russian data centers since around that time. Russia has more than 250 data centers in total, a significant portion of which are located in Moscow and neighboring regions.
What authorities and propagandists are saying
- The Kremlin has not commented on the strikes on Yandex. Russia’s digital development minister called the attack on Yandex “unprecedented,” and the ministry is discussing data center protection with the Defense Ministry. The State Duma, the lower house of Russia’s parliament, said the responsibility for protecting data centers lies with the companies themselves.
- Margarita Simonyan, editor-in-chief of RT, a Russian state propaganda outlet, complained on her Telegram channel about outages at Yandex. “They won’t stop sending me requests and confirmations to prove I’m not a robot. I’m not a robot!” she explained. Simonyan threatened to switch back to Google or move to China’s DeepSeek. She soon deleted the post.

The story you’re reading was written by one of our living, breathing journalists and translated from Russian using an AI model configured to follow our strict editorial standards. This translation process is the result of extensive testing and refinements to ensure our English-language coverage is timely and accurate. A Meduza editor reviews every draft before publication.

articles.title: Russia unveils new AI training hub for combat drones
articles.body:
Russia unveils new AI training hub for combat drones
The Russian Defense Ministry has revealed a new service providing drone developers with combat footage from FPV, multirotor, and fixed-wing drones to train military AI systems. The ministry said the platform will help the armed forces adapt to evolving AI-related challenges.
Russian President Vladimir Putin said in September that Russia will continue to actively integrate digital technologies and AI-based solutions into its weapons development programs. However, he warned of the risks of using AI in the military, noting that cases in which the technology makes decisions autonomously have been recorded.
The new service is protected by certified information-security systems, including modern encryption and authentication tools, the Defense Ministry said on Monday. The platform also uses a standardized classification system for machine-learning data, allowing developers to organize and process information in a common format.
Developers upload the results of their work to the platform, where the data is checked for completeness and to ensure it follows the standardized format. The Defense Ministry uses the data to build and train its own AI models.
More than 40 organizations involved in AI model training have joined the project, Deputy Defense Minister Dmitry Shcherbinin said. Some are already integrating their trained models into combat drone systems, he added.
In July, the ministry announced the development of a data repository for training neural networks. Defense Minister Andrey Belousov said it will allow drone manufacturers to train neural networks for their aircraft and process data directly onboard. He acknowledged the technical complexity of the work but said solutions are already being developed. Belousov also ordered upgrades to a hardware and software system used to assess the performance of drone crews more accurately.
The Defense Ministry has also been integrating AI into drones, air defense systems, and military command and control. Russia established a separate branch of the military dedicated to unmanned systems in November 2025. Deputy Chief Sergey Ishtuganov said the branch’s training units were working closely with drone manufacturers.
Earlier this year, Belousov said Russian drones use AI for image recognition, target acquisition, and navigation. He said neural networks need continuous training, prompting the creation of data centers across the country. He also identified air defense as another area for AI development, with a project to upgrade these systems due to be completed by the end of the year in cooperation with commercial companies.
Last year, Belousov announced trials of SVOD, a system that uses AI to analyze intelligence and recommend courses of action to commanders as part of a broader digital transformation of the military. In July, Konstantin Nechaev, the commander of Russia’s Center Group of Forces, said the system enabled automated fire strikes and had been in use for nearly a year.

articles.title: The Gulf has entered a new era of instability. If its leaders think they can rely on old alliances, they are wrong | Nesrine Malik
articles.body:
On Saturday, Houthi rebels launched a shocking and deadly attack on Saudi Arabia’s capital city, Riyadh. At the time of writing, the missile strike on King Khalid international airport has killed at least 13 people and left 300 injured, marking a significant turn in a regional conflagration that is only getting more intense. It was the single most deadly attack on any Gulf country since the US and Israel launched their war on Iran in February. In Saudi Arabia, a country that is unaccustomed to such fatalities, the death toll is bewilderingly high and likely to prompt a bloody response.
Over the past year, the Gulf has entered a new era of instability that is not temporary and cannot be reversed. This may feel like an overstatement – casualties have been relatively low, after all, compared with Gaza and Iran – but the gradual erosion of peace and security in places such as Saudi Arabia, Qatar and the UAE has changed the region more dramatically than its leaders would like to acknowledge.
The first audacious and unthinkable thing happened just over a year ago, when Iran fired missiles at an airbase in Qatar that hosts American troops, in retaliation for US strikes on Iranian nuclear facilities. Lighting up Doha’s skies and scattering shrapnel, it was a dismaying moment for the Qataris, who have tried to maintain good relations with Iran. But even then there was a degree of warning and coordination that signalled this was a face-saving measure on the part of the Iranians. Yet later in 2025, with no similar warning or choreography, Israel struck Doha, targeting Hamas members and killing five Palestinians and one Qatari. That was the beginning of the end of a longstanding norm and expectation – that there was a sanctity to Gulf lives and sovereignty, one secured by the management of the relationship with Iran and alliances with the US.
Then came Donald Trump and Benjamin Netanyahu’s war on Iran, which drew the Gulf once and for all into the fray. In retaliation for what Iran perceives to be political, military and logistical support for the offensive against it, Tehran struck Saudi Arabia, Qatar, the UAE, Bahrain, Kuwait and Oman. Iran targeted military sites, energy facilities, desalination plants – an entire infrastructure that underpins the economies of these countries. Much damage was inflicted by the suspension of normal life, the shuttering of schools for months, the closure of airports and airspace.
The most disastrous consequence of all, from the perspective of Gulf rulers, has been the way the attacks have disrupted the integration of these countries into the cosmopolitan international community as places for tourism, entrepreneurs, sports and entertainment. They spent billions in securing Formula One, golf and boxing franchises and tournaments, only for a flurry of cheap drones to put it all at risk.
The result is a fractious unravelling that has reactivated hostilities that had laid dormant. Yemen’s civil war began in 2014 when Iran-backed Houthi rebels, in aspiration to greater autonomy in the minority Shia homelands, took over the capital city, Sana’a. In 2015, a coalition of countries led by Saudi Arabia led a brutal campaign to dislodge the Houthis from territories they had gained, intensifying a grinding civil war that killed hundreds of thousands and triggered a humanitarian catastrophe. The war deescalated in 2022 with a de facto but unformalised division of the country between the Houthis and an internationally recognised, Saudi-backed government; the ceasefire was followed by rapprochement between Saudi Arabia and Iran.
But the 2026 war against Iran opened up strategic opportunities and stirred political loyalties, triggering a surge of Houthi advancement in Yemen. The closure of the strait of Hormuz, for example, shifted more commercial traffic along Yemen’s coastline, prompting the Houthis to make advances and seize territory in order to gain control of the now crucial Bab al-Mandab strait in the Red Sea. Tensions came to a head five months after the start of the war, with Saudi Arabia escalating strikes against the Houthis, and the Saudi-backed government bombing its own airport in Sana’a to prevent an Iranian plane from landing.
These developments are not just the result of a mischievous group seizing the moment, acting as spoiler in a bigger contest between Iran and the west. The Houthis are backed by Iran, but they are not empty proxies for Iran; they have domestic ambitions and sharp regional animosities, particularly against the House of Saud, which they see an imperious and arrogant master to whom they shall never submit. A senior Houthi official said that Saturday’s attack took place “so that the world understands” that Yemeni civilian infrastructure has been, and is being, targeted by the Saudis, gesturing towards that sense that Riyadh treats Yemeni lives as cheap.
From another perspective, what we are witnessing in the region is another consequence of Hamas’s 7 October attacks on Israel, and what followed in Gaza, Lebanon and Iran. The final piece that was stabilising the region’s tense equilibriums fell away when Trump decided that the safety and security of the US’s Gulf allies was secondary to his Iran “excursion”, as he called it. The limits of relying on the US security umbrella became clear both to allies and enemies.
Last month, the Trump administration refused to extend military assistance to Saudi Arabia to fight the Houthis, after a meeting of US officials with the Houthis, who assured them that they would not attack US ships in the Red Sea, only Saudi vessels. What is upon Saudi Arabia now is a long, intractable war with a resourceful and impassioned antagonist, one willing to sustain a high degree of pain in ways that Riyadh can’t match without orienting itself entirely towards war. If the 2015 campaign is anything to go by, it will claim thousands of lives with only a remote possibility of a decisive outcome.
And so Saudi, and the entire Gulf, are pulled further into the relentless storm. Trump cannot bring the Iran war to an end, Gaza remains an open wound, Israel continues to strike and occupy parts of Lebanon. The Houthi resurgence represents a new reality in a region that is bewildered and losing lives and capital, stuck between old alliances that no longer work and new hostilities that are too calamitous to confront.
- Nesrine Malik is a Guardian columnist

articles.title: US weapons supplies to Ukraine via PURL continue – NATO source
articles.body:
US weapons supplies to Ukraine via PURL continue – NATO source
A source has told European Pravda that US weapons and ammunition supplies to Ukraine through the Prioritised Ukraine Requirements List (PURL) mechanism are continuing, despite US President Donald Trump's demands that Kyiv stop striking Russian oil refineries and reports that PURL could be suspended as a means of pressuring Ukraine.
Source: European Pravda's Brussels correspondent, citing a NATO official speaking on condition of anonymity
Details: NATO confirmed that the mechanism for supporting Ukraine via PURL continues to operate despite Trump's remarks.
"Support for Ukraine via PURL continues to arrive," the NATO official stated.
The source provided no other information regarding the long- and medium-term plans for the PURL mechanism.
Background:
- European media outlets previously reported that Trump's administration is threatening to halt the PURL procurement system, which enables Kyiv's allies to procure US weapons for Ukraine, in order to force Ukraine to stop its strikes on Russian energy infrastructure.
- European Pravda reported that Trump accused Ukrainian President Volodymyr Zelenskyy of being unwilling to end the war and said "it's time for Ukraine to get a new president".
- This occurred after Trump announced an agreement with Kremlin leader Vladimir Putin regarding the supply of Russian diesel fuel to the US and global markets.
- Following this, Zelenskyy stated that President Trump's decision to unilaterally lift sanctions on Russia and allow it to export diesel fuel is "unfair and dishonest".

articles.title: EU Expands Sanctions on North Korea and Russian Firms Over Growing Military and Economic Ties
articles.body:

EU Expands Sanctions on North Korea and Russian Firms Over Growing Military and Economic Ties
The European Union has imposed new sanctions on three individuals and four entities over their support for North Korea’s nuclear and missile programs, as well as their cooperation with Russia.
Following this decision, the EU sanctions list regarding North Korea now includes 80 individuals and 25 entities.
We bring you stories from the ground. Your support keeps our team in the field.
Among those targeted is Ri Song Jin, a researcher at North Korea’s National Aerospace Technology Administration and an official of the country’s General Missile Administration. He worked in Russia as a technical specialist, training Russian forces in the use of North Korean missiles.
Sanctions were also directed at the Russian development company Samolet Group and its chief executive officer, Anna Akishina. The company brought in workers from North Korea for construction projects in Vladivostok, violating UN sanctions.
The list includes Vladimir Sokolov, the founder of the Russian holding company Black Horse. He is accused of facilitating trade and industrial cooperation with North Korea, including a joint investment project in the Primorsky Krai region.
The targeted entities include the shipping company Paekyangsan Shipping, whose vessel transported oil products from Russia to North Korea in violation of UN restrictions, and Golden Autumn Agroholding, a subsidiary of Black Horse.
The sanctions mandate an entry ban into the EU and a freeze on assets. The listed individuals and entities are also prohibited from receiving funds or economic resources, directly or indirectly.
The Council of the EU expressed concern over the deepening military and economic ties between Russia and North Korea, citing the deployment of North Korean troops to Russia, employment of North Korean citizens, joint business initiatives, and weapon exchanges for oil.
While the EU introduced new sanctions against North Korean and Russian individuals for illegal cooperation, Estonia simultaneously requested the removal of a Russian rare-earth supplier from the same sanctions package to protect key European industries.
Kerstin Lepik, spokesperson for Estonia’s permanent representation in Brussels, confirmed the decision to ERR. She stated that Estonia had asked for one Russian company and a related individual to be removed from the sanctions list approved by the ambassadors of the COREPER II member states.
Lepik explained that the company supplied materials to Estonia-based NPM Silmet that were considered strategically important for Europe. Industries dependent on NPM Silmet included electric vehicle manufacturing, wind turbines, electronics, automotive production, and aviation across the EU.
She added that NPM Silmet was actively seeking alternative sources for materials imported from Russia, and Estonia planned to reconsider adding the Russian company and the associated individual to the sanctions list the following year.

articles.title: Russia’s sabotage of Europe should bring Ukraine more weapons through US purchase scheme, with clear statement of where its red lines lie, NATO’s top European commander says
articles.body:
Russian sabotage assaults on Europe should end with more weapons flowing to Ukraine, NATO’s top commander in Europe says. NATO should respond to the attacks by increasing contributions to the alliance’s PURL weapons program or by sending Ukraine more air-defense interceptor missiles, Supreme Allied Commander Europe General Alexus Grynkewich said at the Warsaw Security Forum, Ukrinform reports.
The remark runs counter to a fresh scare. After US President Donald Trump’s diesel deal with Russia, European officials said that Washington had threatened to halt weapons for Ukraine through PURL, the Financial Times reports, unless Kyiv stopped hitting Russian refineries. Grynkewich’s call to expand the program ran the other way.
One of the main goals of Russia’s hybrid operations, from airspace violations to sabotage and cyberattacks, is to break the West’s will to keep backing Ukraine, he stated. The sharpest answer is to prove that assumption wrong, he argued, turning each attack into a reason to send more.
The PURL program that lets allies fund US-made weapons for Ukraine, which drew nearly $5.5 billion in pledges before May.
Name the culprit out loud, and watch Moscow lose its cover
Once responsibility for a specific attack is established, countries should publicly name who did it, Grynkewich noted, so Russia understands it has been exposed and that its network was never as untraceable as it believed.
Moscow bets it can escape blame because the West cannot work out who is behind an attack, in his telling. The response, he urged, should be to show that the West can.
One voice, not thirty-two, is what Russia actually fears
Coordination is the other half. Allies must craft a joint response rather than send Moscow chaotic, uncoordinated signals from individual states, he stressed, and must spell out clearly where their red lines lie.
That unity is itself a deterrent. A single, agreed answer tells Russia the alliance is harder to split than its hybrid campaign assumes, and that attacks meant to divide the West only harden its resolve, he contends.

articles.title: Bipartisan US senators say Trump’s Russian diesel deal conflicts with 2022 ban, as he presses Kyiv to spare Russian refineries
articles.body:
Seven US senators from both parties said the Trump administration's decision to authorize Russian diesel imports conflicts with a 2022 law banning Russian energy imports and accused it of failing to consult Congress, in a statement on 11 October.
The dispute comes as the war with Iran drives up US fuel prices, which US President Donald Trump has blamed on Ukraine's strikes on Russian refineries. Trump says Russian supplies will help bring prices down, while lawmakers warn that purchases could provide Moscow with revenue to continue its war against Ukraine.
The senators—Republicans Susan Collins, Lisa Murkowski, Thom Tillis, and John Curtis, and Democrats Jeanne Shaheen, Richard Blumenthal, and Ron Wyden—called on the administration to reverse course, saying the US should not provide Russian President Vladimir Putin with “a financial lifeline.”
What the 2022 law requires before the ban can end
The law, signed on 8 April 2022, allows the president to end the import ban only after submitting a certification to Congress. The certification must find that Russia has agreed to pull out its forces and stop the fighting on terms Ukraine's free and independent government accepts, no longer poses an immediate threat of attack to any NATO member, and recognizes Ukrainians' right to pick their own government.
The law also requires consultation with four congressional committees and a report at least 45 days before certification. The termination takes effect 90 days after certification unless a joint resolution of disapproval is enacted into law during that period. The senators allege the administration failed to meet the consultation and reporting requirements. Their statement does not establish whether a certification has been submitted.
Treasury’s license cites sanctions rules, not the 2022 law
The Treasury Department's Office of Foreign Assets Control issued General License No. 135 on 9 October, authorizing certain transactions involving Russian-origin diesel that would otherwise be restricted under US sanctions regulations. It runs until 7 April 2027 and cites sanctions regulations, not the 2022 import-ban law.
EU blacklists 1,569 Russian arms suppliers and their bosses in its biggest sanctions round ever, as Trump eases up on Moscow
Treasury Secretary Scott Bessent defended the deal on Fox News on 11 October, saying the administration would proceed under existing legal authority. He said lawmakers who argued that either the earlier law or the current Lindsey Graham sanctions law prohibited the deal were wrong, and argued the agreement would lower prices, Reuters reported.
How much diesel Trump says Russia will supply
Trump said on Truth Social that Russia would immediately supply more than 300,000 tons of diesel to US and global markets, followed by 500,000 tons in November and 1 million tons after that. He said Russia would deliver another 3 million tons “within a short period of time,” depending on the condition of its diesel refineries. The promised volumes have not been independently verified.
Russia partially lifted its diesel export ban on 10 October, allowing 500,000 tons onto the global market at this stage, the Russian government said, according to state news agency TASS.
A House bill to block Russian oil purchases
Pennsylvania Republican Rep. Brian Fitzpatrick plans to introduce the Ronald Reagan Peace Through Strength Act to block Russian oil purchases and use a discharge petition to force a House vote, Axios reported. The procedure can force consideration of a bill if 218 House members sign. Republican Rep. Don Bacon said he would support the bill and called Trump's decision a serious mistake, according to Ukrainska Pravda.
Barrasso defends the deal. Zelenskyy calls it an investment in war
On CBS's Face the Nation on 11 October, Senate Majority Whip John Barrasso, a Republican from Wyoming, called the deal “another point of leverage” for Trump to use against Putin. Asked whether the decision violated US law, Barrasso said the president was balancing competing priorities and had to make tough decisions.
Ukrainian President Volodymyr Zelenskyy wrote on Telegram on 9 October:
“Allowing Russia to sell petroleum products is an investment in a war that must be ended, not prolonged.”
Trump also expects Ukraine to stop striking Russian refineries under his proposed energy ceasefire, a White House official told Axios. Zelenskyy said Kyiv would halt such strikes if Moscow did the same.

articles.title: Saudi MBS 'shuttling between bunker palaces' amid Houthi attacks
articles.body:
Breadcrumb
Saudi's MBS 'shuttling between bunker palaces' amid Houthi attacks
Saudi Crown Prince Mohammed bin Salman is reportedly moving between heavily guarded palaces equipped with bunkers in Riyadh as Yemen's Houthis intensify their missile and drone attacks on the Saudi capital.
The kingdom's de facto ruler has not been seen in public since last Tuesday and is travelling between fortified royal residences accompanied by a handpicked security team, according to the Wall Street Journal.
The reported movements come as the Houthis continue to bombard Riyadh with drones, cruise missiles and ballistic missiles, forcing the closure of King Khalid International Airport until 17 October following repeated strikes.
On Saturday, a ballistic missile struck one of the airport's terminals, killing 13 people and injuring hundreds. Another missile hit the airport on Sunday, killing one person, while four others were killed in attacks on Wednesday and Thursday.
The strikes have raised concerns over Saudi Arabia's ability to defend its capital, amid reports that the kingdom is running low on interceptor missiles used to shoot down incoming ballistic and cruise missiles.
According to the Wall Street Journal, Saudi Arabia's air defence stockpiles have been depleted by repeated attacks, leaving the kingdom increasingly vulnerable to further strikes.
Saudi Arabia, like much of the region, has expended large quantities of interceptor missiles defending against Iranian ballistic and cruise missiles launched following the outbreak of the US-Israeli war on Iran.
Saudi air defences under strain
Dr Burcu Ozcelik, a senior research fellow at the Royal United Services Institute (RUSI), told The New Arab that Saudi Arabia faced significant challenges in countering Houthi attacks, particularly low-flying drones and cruise missiles that are harder to detect.
The kingdom's dwindling stockpile of interceptor missiles has further complicated its defensive efforts.
"It would be a mistake to say the Kingdom’s air defence systems are failing completely, they are under strain and stretched. But there are also reports of successful interceptions," Ozcelik said.
A report by the Associated Press in September revealed that Saudi officials had asked Britain, France, Pakistan and Egypt to deploy air defence systems to the country amid concerns over dwindling interceptor stocks.
The US has also deployed additional Patriot missile defence systems to Saudi Arabia and Qatar to protect energy infrastructure, according to Axios.
Other countries, including Greece, Britain and France, have provided air defence support, while Turkey and Pakistan, both partners in the Mecca Defence Pact, are also assisting Riyadh.
Ozcelik said Saudi Arabia was facing an asymmetric threat similar to tactics previously employed by Iran and its regional allies during the wider conflict.
Iran launched thousands of ballistic missiles and drones across the region, including against Gulf states, striking energy facilities and US military bases.
"What we are seeing is the familiar playbook the IRGC used against the Gulf - even a small number of missile or drones that gets through sophisticated air defences can create disproportionate damage and disruption," Ozcelik said.
"That's the asymmetric warfare logic that is working to the Houthis advantage."
Saudi Arabia vows decisive response
The Saudi-led coalition fighting the Houthis has vowed to "respond decisively" to the attacks, having already resumed its air campaign against the group in support of Yemeni government offensives.
The renewed Saudi-led air campaign preceded the latest escalation in Houthi attacks on Saudi airports, with the group initially concentrating its strikes on energy infrastructure.
The repeated attacks have heightened security concerns in the Saudi capital, with the reported movements of Mohammed bin Salman between fortified palaces highlighting the growing pressure on the kingdom's leadership as the conflict intensifies.

articles.title: Iran offers to mediate Saudi-Houthi talks as attacks mount
articles.body:
Breadcrumb
Iran offers to mediate Saudi-Houthi talks amid mounting attacks
Iran has offered to help launch talks between Saudi Arabia and Houthi rebels as increasing attacks on the kingdom and renewed airstrikes on Yemen threaten to deepen the regional conflict.
Iranian Foreign Minister Abbas Araghchi made the offer during a phone call with his Saudi counterpart, Prince Faisal bin Farhan, on Sunday evening, according to a statement from Iran's foreign ministry.
Araghchi expressed Tehran's readiness to provide all forms of assistance to facilitate dialogue between Riyadh and the Iran-backed Houthis and support efforts to reach a political settlement.
The two ministers also discussed the latest regional developments, with Araghchi expressing concern over rising tensions and warning that continued reliance on military action would further complicate the situation.
He stressed that the region's crises could not be resolved through military means and urged greater emphasis on political solutions.
Separately, Saudi Arabia's foreign ministry confirmed the call on Sunday, saying the two ministers had discussed the latest regional escalation and efforts to address it.
However, the Saudi statement provided no further details about the diplomatic initiatives discussed or whether any agreements had been reached.
The diplomatic contact came amid intensifying hostilities between Saudi Arabia and the Houthis, including repeated missile and drone attacks targeting Saudi airports.
A recent Houthi attack on King Khalid International Airport in Riyadh killed at least 12 people and injured 309 others, while Abha airport in southern Saudi Arabia has also been targeted.
On Sunday evening, the Saudi-led coalition reported another attack on King Khalid International Airport, saying an unidentified projectile struck Terminal 4 and sparked a fire.
Coalition spokesman Turki al-Maliki said on X that emergency crews were working to contain the blaze. He subsequently announced that Saudi air defences had intercepted and destroyed a cruise missile near the airport.
Meanwhile, airstrikes targeted two districts of Yemen's capital, Sanaa, around midnight on Monday, according to the Houthis.
The group's media centre said the strikes hit the Hamdan and Thourah districts and blamed Saudi Arabia for the attacks, although it provided no further details.
The strikes come amid renewed military operations by the Saudi-led coalition and Yemeni government forces against Houthi positions in Sanaa, Taiz and areas surrounding the strategically important Bab al-Mandeb Strait.
The intensifying confrontation coincides with growing threats to maritime security elsewhere in the region.
India's foreign ministry said on Monday that two Indian sailors were missing after a drone struck the commercial tanker MT PETRO DOLPHIN near the Strait of Hormuz on Sunday.
The vessel was carrying 11 Indian crew members when it was attacked.
A second tanker, the Marshall Islands-flagged MT VALTHERA, was also struck by an unidentified projectile, causing a fire on board. All 11 Indian sailors aboard that vessel were reported safe.
India condemned the attacks on commercial shipping, warning that they risked further destabilising an already volatile region.
The latest developments have also prompted calls for greater security cooperation among Gulf states.
Anwar Gargash, a diplomatic adviser to the United Arab Emirates leadership, called on Monday for joint Gulf action to counter attacks by Iran and its allied groups.
He warned that attacks on Saudi Arabia threatened the security of the UAE and other Gulf countries, stressing that their security was indivisible.

articles.title: Anduril Unveils Steelfin Missile as a Low-Cost Alternative to the PAC-3, With Plans to Produce Several Thousand Missiles Per Year
articles.body:
Anduril Industries has presented the Steelfin family of anti-aircraft interceptor missiles, which it positions as a low-cost alternative to the PAC-3 missiles used in the Patriot air defense system.
The War Zone reported this.
The developer aims to ensure the new missiles are compatible with existing air defense infrastructure.
According to the media, the Steelfin missiles are being developed to launch from the M903A2 launcher used for the PAC-3 family of interceptor missiles.
Anduril spokesperson Steve Milano told The War Zone that the Steelfin configuration, designed to perform PAC-3 missions, will provide about 80% of PAC-3’s capabilities at less than half the cost of a PAC-3 missile.
The company also plans to ramp up production to several thousand interceptors per year, using a common production line for different missile versions.
The modular design will allow for the replacement of engines, warheads, and other components depending on the mission. The missiles will feature a two-stage design. The first stage will be a booster that determines range and flight characteristics, while the second stage will be the interceptor itself.
The company is developing the Steelfin family to intercept cruise and ballistic missiles, as well as hypersonic targets. Anduril is also exploring integrating the missiles with the Mk 41 ship-based vertical launch system and the Typhon ground-based system.
According to Anduril representative Steve Milano, a more powerful Steelfin configuration will be able to perform the tasks of the THAAD missile defense system at a significantly lower cost.
The company has already conducted ballistic tests of prototype models and plans to begin flight tests of various configurations in 2027.
Militarnyi previously reported that the American company Lockheed Martin had developed a new PAC-3 Edge interceptor missile for the Patriot air defense system. It is designed to counter hypersonic and other modern missile threats.

articles.title: Russia’s supply base in occupied Luhansk Oblast burned overnight—NASA’s fire map caught it
articles.body:
Ukrainian strikes hit a site housing Russian troops in Khrustalnyi, a city in Russian-occupied Luhansk Oblast, overnight on 12 October, according to local reports. Satellite fire data recorded blazes at a former motor depot there, in an area Russia once used as a logistics base for its offensive in the region.
Russia keeps attacking in Ukraine’s Donetsk Oblast and strikes Ukrainian cities and power plants every day. Its offensive depends on troops, ammunition, and fuel moved through occupied Ukraine, so strikes there reach the supply chain behind the front.
Fires at a former motor depot in occupied Khrustalnyi
Ukrainian forces launched heavy strikes around Khrustalnyi in eastern Ukraine overnight, the Ukrainian monitoring channel Exilenova+ reported. It counted three separate fires and one large blaze, and said local residents reported a hit on a site where Russian troops were based. Ukraine’s military had not officially commented on the strike by the publication time of this article on 12 October.
NASA’s Fire Information for Resource Management System (FIRMS), which tracks active fires by satellite, shows blazes at a former motor transport enterprise and an industrial zone in Khrustalnyi, Ukrainian military outlet Militarnyi reported. Three fire hotspots appeared there at 01:10 and spread by 02:07, the outlet said.
Ukraine also hit the site on 16 June 2022, striking an ammunition depot there, and local residents then heard secondary detonations, Militarnyi said. The site served as an important logistics base for Russia’s 2nd Army Corps in its offensive on Sievierodonetsk and Lysychansk, two cities in Luhansk Oblast, the outlet added.
Explosions at a Crimean airfield Russia used to launch drones overnight
Drones attacked occupied Crimea from the evening of 11 October into the night, and Russian air defenses, including mobile fire groups, fired across the peninsula, Krym.Realii, Radio Liberty’s Crimea service, reported. Explosions sounded in Simferopol, Feodosiia, and Yevpatoriia, among other places, the Crimean monitoring Telegram channel Crimean Wind said, according to the outlet.
Subscribers told the channel about a series of explosions and a glow at Russia’s Hvardiiske military airfield in Simferopol district as air defenses fired. Krym.Realii said neither Ukraine’s nor Russia’s military had commented and that it could not verify the reports independently.
Ukraine says it struck a Bastion in Crimea, the launcher Russia pairs Zircon and Oniks missiles on
Overnight, Russia also launched attack drones at Ukraine from several directions, including Hvardiiske in occupied Crimea, Ukraine’s Air Force reported.
Ukraine’s General Staff said in August that a 3 August strike on the Hvardiiske airfield destroyed nine aviation fuel tanks and damaged two aircraft hangars.
Ukraine keeps hitting Russian rear areas in occupied territory
On 10 and 11 October alone, the General Staff reported hitting a Russian repair base and supply depots in occupied Luhansk Oblast, along with Russian troop concentrations near Lysychansk and two other towns there.
Ukraine has also kept up its campaign of so-called middle strikes, drone attacks on Russian supply lines in occupied territory beyond the front. French mapper Clément Molin counted 770 confirmed drone hits on Russian trucks in September, up from 630 in August, with the strikes concentrated on supply routes running through occupied southern Ukraine into Crimea.
Strikes on troop sites and airfields far behind the front leave Russia fewer safe places in occupied territory to house troops and launch drones, adding to the battlefield losses Ukraine’s drones already inflict.

articles.title: EU Adopts Record Sanctions Expansion Targeting 1.6K Russian Defense Firms and Executives
articles.body:
EU foreign ministers on Monday formally adopted the bloc’s largest-ever expansion of its Russia sanctions blacklist, targeting nearly 1,600 people and companies linked to the country’s military-industrial complex.
The measures, initially agreed by EU envoys last week, add 826 Russian companies and 743 executives to the blacklist.
“Over half address the production chain for the ballistic missiles Russia uses to kill Ukrainian civilians every day,” EU foreign policy chief Kaja Kallas said.
The companies supply components for Russian missiles, drones and aircraft, including explosives, ammunition, semiconductors and computers, according to the EU.
The bloc said they represent the “core” of the Russian military industry, employing more than a quarter-million people and generating an annual turnover of at least 20 billion euros ($22.3 billion).
The EU also sanctioned 74 State Duma lawmakers and three members of Russia’s Central Election Commission over their involvement in parliamentary elections held in Russian-occupied Ukrainian territories.
Separately, three people and four entities in North Korea were sanctioned over Pyongyang’s growing military and economic cooperation with Moscow.
Those listed face EU asset freezes, while EU citizens and companies are barred from making funds available to them. Sanctioned individuals also face travel bans across the 27-member bloc.
The latest additions bring the total number of people and entities under EU sanctions over Russia’s war in Ukraine to nearly 4,600.

Trump's 'energy ceasefire' sparks confusion as Russia strikes Ukraine
US President Donald Trump sowed confusion on Sunday, announcing an "energy ceasefire" between Ukraine and Russia that sparked astonishment in Kyiv, silence from Moscow and support from Ukraine's Western allies.
But the ceasefire appeared shaky at best as Ukrainian President Volodymyr Zelensky said Russia struck multiple Ukrainian power plants on Sunday, including one in the capital and another in Kharkiv, leading to power outages and outrage.
Trump's announcement came two days after he declared a temporary easing of US sanctions on Russian diesel, prompting outrage by European allies and Kyiv, who said it would only embolden Russian President Vladimir Putin.
"Effective immediately, there is an ENERGY CEASEFIRE in the War between Russia and Ukraine," Trump said early Sunday on Truth Social. "Both parties have agreed. Do not break it!"
Zelensky appeared to express surprise at the announcement, saying he was seeking further details, but added that "Ukraine supports the ceasefire, and it is important that Russia support it as well."
Russia has yet to confirm its agreement.
Zelensky later said that multiple Ukrainian power stations had been hit and that "Ukrainian skies have been infested with Russian 'shaheds' all day," referring to a type of drone originally designed by Iran that is now used extensively by Russia.
Since launching a full-scale invasion of its neighbor in 2022, Russia has systematically hit Ukrainian energy infrastructure, leading to energy and heating shortages—prompting Ukraine to hit back at Russian oil refineries it says fund the war.
More recently, Trump's war in Iran has led to oil shortages and ensuing price spikes, creating major headwinds for his Republican Party ahead of midterm elections early next month.
'Up to our people'
The ceasefire appeared to garner support on Sunday from Ukraine's key western allies, including the UK, France, Canada and the European Commission.
Several leaders called on Russia to uphold the deal.
But that support was in contrast to broad criticism of the US-Russia diesel deal earlier in the week, which has led to mounting tensions between Trump and Zelensky.
Zelensky said the diesel deal was a "weak decision," while several of Ukraine's European allies expressed outrage and pledged to increase pressure on Moscow.
Seven US senators—including four Republicans—released a statement Sunday blasting the diesel deal with Russia, saying it was illegal.
Canadian Prime Minister Mark Carney added to the chorus on Sunday after a call with Zelensky, saying the diesel deal "is in direct opposition to the efforts of Ukraine, Canada and our allies to create peace and stability in Europe."
Asked about the criticism on Saturday, Trump said it was "time for Ukraine to get a new president" who would finally settle the war.
Zelensky pushed back, telling ABC News that "it's up to our society, up to our people to choose one or another leader."
He said that fuel prices were rising because of the US-Israeli war on Iran and the blocked Strait of Hormuz.
"Everybody understands it," he said.
Support for Zelensky
Germany's foreign minister said Sunday that Berlin continued to "fully support" Zelensky.
"Europe needs stability and that means that we are very clearly continuing to stay by the side of Ukraine and its government," Johann Wadephul said in Berlin.
EU chief Ursula von der Leyen also backed the Ukrainian leader "as he leads the fight for his people's freedom."
UK Prime Minister Andy Burnham also said his country "strongly supports President Trump's call today for a sustained energy ceasefire to start now."
In Kyiv, several residents expressed concern about Trump's call for Zelensky to be replaced.
"I believe our president is the best, and Americans should think about their own president," said 40-year-old Olesia Goncharuk.
"We Ukrainians decide our own fate and our own freedom, and we are free people," she told AFP.

articles.title: Ukraine Strikes Russian Troop Deployment Site in Khrustalnyi, Luhansk Region
articles.body:
The Ukrainian Defense Forces struck Russian military positions near the temporarily occupied town of Khrustalnyi in the Luhansk region.
NASA’s FIRMS satellite monitoring data detected fires near a former motor transport facility and an industrial zone.
Three separate fires were detected at the strike site. They started at 01:10 a.m., and by 02:07 a.m., the fires had spread.

In addition, the Ukrainian Defense Forces are targeting storage facilities holding surface-to-air missiles for air defense systems, as well as other depots used by Russian forces to supply their troops in Ukraine.
In March 2026, the Ukrainian Defense Forces destroyed a storage facility containing surface-to-air missiles near the Russian-occupied town of Dovzhansk in the Luhansk region.
The facility is located at coordinates 48.101990, 39.670564, approximately 150 kilometers from the current line of contact.
Ukraine’s Defense Forces are carrying out massive strikes in the area of occupied Khrustalnyi in Luhansk Oblast. Three separate fire hotspots and a large-scale blaze have been reported.

articles.title: EU adopts record sanctions on Russia's defense industry
articles.body:
The European Union has adopted its biggest-ever sanctions package against Russia over its war on Ukraine, listing almost 1,600 individuals and entities linked to the Russian military-industrial complex, the EU Council said.
"In response to Russia's continued and increasingly large-scale aggression against Ukraine, and in particular its recent brutal military campaign aimed at deliberately destroying civilian infrastructure and causing severe suffering to the civilian population, the EU Council today adopted additional restrictive measures against 1,569 individuals and entities linked to the Russian military-industrial complex. The list includes 826 Russian companies and 743 executives of these enterprises," it said.
The council said this is the largest package of sanctions listings adopted at one time in the EU's history. The total number of individuals and entities under sanctions within the regime supporting Ukraine's territorial integrity has reached almost 4,600.
"Today the EU decided to impose the largest sanctions package since 2022. Almost 1,600 sanctions listings target the Russian military-industrial complex. More than half of them concern the production chain of the ballistic missiles that Russia uses every day to kill Ukrainian civilians. The bombing of bridges in Kyiv, grain ships and the National Academy of Sciences are not the actions of a country that wants peace. Now is not the time to ease pressure on Moscow, but to increase it," EU High Representative for Foreign Affairs and Security Policy Kaja Kallas said.
The council said the package specifically targets mid-tier suppliers, which form the 'core' of Russia's military industry, generating annual turnover of at least EUR 20 billion and employing more than 250,000 people.
The listed companies supply key components for some of Russia's most advanced weapons systems, including missiles, drones and aircraft. These components include electronics, including semiconductors, microchips and computers; communications equipment, including radars, antennas and receivers; aviation, satellite and missile systems; explosives and ammunition; and optical and navigation systems, it said.
The council said the listings were adopted under the EU framework of restrictive measures against actions that undermine or threaten the territorial integrity, sovereignty and independence of Ukraine. Those listed under this sanctions regime are subject to an asset freeze, and making funds or economic resources available to them or for their benefit, directly or indirectly, is prohibited. Listed individuals are also subject to a travel ban to the EU, it said.
Notes: I used "said" in place of the source's "констатували", "деталізували" and "зазначили". I dropped the timestamp. The source headline's "рос ВПК" is shorthand, so the headline uses "defense industry" instead. I put 'core' in single quotes as a quoted term inside running text.

articles.title: Zelenskyy: Increased pressure on Russia's military-industrial complex - necessary signal if we’re serious about ending Russia's war
articles.body:
Ukrainian President Volodymyr Zelenskyy thanked European Council President António Costa, European Commission President Ursula von der Leyen, and all EU member states for adopting a new package of EU sanctions against Russia's military-industrial complex.
"It is becoming increasingly clear that Russia does not want to agree to the energy truce proposed by the United States and intends to continue its terrorist air attacks against our people and communities," Zelenskyy wrote on X on Monday.
According to the president, Russians attacked six energy facilities in Ukraine just today. Thirty-three people were injured in strikes across the country.
"This is what happens when Russia sees the prospect of increased revenue for its war machine. Therefore, stepping up pressure on Russian entities—particularly those involved in the production of ballistic missiles and Shahed drones—sends the right and necessary signal if we are serious about ending Russia's war," Zelenskyy emphasized.
Earlier, EU High Representative Kaja Kallas announced that the EU Foreign Affairs Council had approved sanctions targeting 1,600 items linked to the Russian military-industrial complex.

articles.title: Anduril bets on mass-produced missile interceptors
articles.body:
- Anduril unveiled Steelfin, a family of two-stage surface-to-air interceptors aimed at cruise, ballistic and hypersonic missiles, with flight tests planned next year.
- The company plans to build several thousand a year and says Steelfin will fit existing launchers including Patriot, Mk 41 and Typhon.
Anduril Industries has unveiled Steelfin, a family of surface-to-air interceptor missiles designed to shoot down cruise, ballistic and hypersonic missiles at a fraction of the cost of today’s interceptors, with flight tests set to begin next year.
The company announced Steelfin on Oct. 12, the first day of the Association of the U.S. Army’s annual meeting in Washington. Anduril says it plans to build on the order of several thousand Steelfin missiles a year in the short term. It did not give a unit price, name a customer or say which U.S. service is backing the program, saying only that it has been developing Steelfin for years while investing alongside multiple customers. The company has completed ballistic testing with representative air vehicles but has not yet flown a Steelfin missile.
The first stage is a solid rocket booster that can be swapped for different motors depending on how far and how fast the missile needs to fly, and how tightly it must pack into a launcher. The second stage is a common “terminal interceptor” that carries the airframe, electronics, software and flight controls shared across the family, with open interfaces so Anduril can drop in different seekers and mission systems without redesigning the missile.
Anduril says the approach lets it build versions for every layer of air and missile defense, from short-range point defense of a single site to upper-tier ballistic missile defense, while aiming for a fraction of the cost of current interceptors in each class. The company did not say what those benchmark costs are, but a single Patriot PAC-3 MSE interceptor costs about $4 million, and the Missile Defense Agency is pursuing a separate low-cost interceptor effort with a target price below $750,000 per round.
Because the variants share parts, Anduril says they can run down the same production line with the same tooling and workers, letting it shift output to whichever version is in demand. The company also says the common interfaces let it buy commercial components and use multiple suppliers.
Steelfin is designed to fire from launchers the U.S. military already fields, including the M903A2 launcher used by the Patriot air defense system, the U.S. Navy’s Mk 41 Vertical Launch System aboard cruisers and destroyers, the U.S. Army’s Typhon mid-range missile launcher, and newer containerized launchers. Anduril says it will work with existing fire control systems such as the U.S. Navy’s Aegis and the U.S. Army’s Integrated Battle Command System, known as IBCS, rather than requiring a new command network.
The launch comes as U.S. air defense stocks have been drawn down by combat in the Middle East. This month alone, Raytheon received contracts worth up to $6.3 billion for SM-3 Block IB interceptors and up to $24.4 billion for SM-6 missiles to replenish U.S. Navy inventories. Anduril already makes smaller counter-drone interceptors such as Roadrunner and Anvil, but Steelfin is its first family aimed at cruise and ballistic missiles.

articles.title: Russian diplomat expelled from Bulgaria in 2021 amid investigation into arms depot explosions now serves as assistant military attaché in Serbia, RFE/RL finds
articles.body:
Russian diplomat expelled from Bulgaria in 2021 amid investigation into arms depot explosions now serves as assistant military attaché in Serbia, RFE/RL finds
RFE/RL’s Balkan Service and the investigative project Sistema have identified a diplomat at the Russian Embassy in Serbia who was declared persona non grata in Bulgaria in 2021 during an investigation into explosions at weapons depots.
Alexander Krasiy, an assistant military attaché, held the same position at the Russian Embassy in Bulgaria before moving to Serbia. In April 2021, Bulgaria’s Foreign Ministry said it was expelling a Russian diplomat but did not name him. The news agency Zona News and Bulgarian National Television identified him as Krasiy.
The decision came amid an investigation into explosions at four weapons depots and production facilities between 2011 and 2020. Bulgarian prosecutors suspected six Russians of involvement. According to prosecutors, the explosions may have been linked to the attempted poisoning of Bulgarian arms dealer Emilian Gebrev and were intended to “halt deliveries of military supplies to Georgia and Ukraine.”
After his expulsion, Krasiy resurfaced in Serbia. In 2021, he was photographed among instructors and participants in a professional development course at the University of Defense in Belgrade. He received accreditation as an assistant military attaché in 2026.
The journalists said Krasiy may have ties to Russia’s military intelligence agency, the GRU. Leaked records show that when he applied for a “COVID pass” during the pandemic, he listed his home address as a dormitory at the “Conservatory” — a nickname for the GRU’s Military Diplomatic Academy. Many graduates went on to become Russian intelligence officers and saboteurs, including Anatoly Chepiga.
According to The Telegraph, Russian intelligence services used Serbia as a base to prepare an unsuccessful sabotage attempt at Leipzig Airport in August 2026. The suspected organizer, Oleg Levushkin, left Europe through Serbia, while his accomplice, Maxim Lapunov, entered Europe through Belgrade. Investigators believe the explosives intended to blow up a Ukrainian aircraft may also have reached Germany through Serbia.
In September 2026, Agentstvo included Krasiy on a list of 29 Russian Embassy employees in Serbia with confirmed or possible ties to intelligence services. The outlet said Russia’s embassy and trade mission in Serbia employ a total of 78 people, while just 18 Russian diplomats work in neighboring Bulgaria, which has a comparable population.
Krasiy is not the first Russian diplomat to continue working in Serbia after being expelled from the EU. In 2023, RFE/RL found that at least three Russian diplomats expelled from the EU after the start of the war had received accreditation in Serbia. Two of them were found to have ties to Russian intelligence services.

articles.title: Israeli soldiers say ordered to drop heavy bombs on inhabited Gaza buildings without evacuation: Report
articles.body:
Four Israeli military intelligence soldiers acknowledged they received instructions to use “heavy bombs” against inhabited buildings in the Gaza Strip without evacuating residents first, in strikes that killed and injured hundreds of Palestinians, according to a media report on Monday.
The soldiers gave their accounts to the Israeli newspaper Haaretz, as Israel continues its genocide in Gaza, which began in October 2023.
The Israeli army has repeatedly claimed that it warns civilians in Gaza to evacuate before strikes, a practice Israeli officials, including Prime Minister Benjamin Netanyahu, have frequently boasted.
However, soldiers’ testimonies contradict these claims, as they revealed a complete change in open-fire regulations since the start of the war on Gaza, where approximately 2.4 million Palestinians live.
One intelligence soldier, identified only as A, who was tasked with tracking Hamas commanders in Gaza, said: “We knew almost nothing about Hamas and its military wing at the field level.
“In October 2023, we started almost from scratch to identify where their members and operatives were,” he said.
He added that the criteria for defining a target were quickly loosened, alongside “a sharp change in the concept of proportionality and the use of heavy weapons” and a significant easing of the policy governing the killing of civilians considered “collateral damage.”
Expanded targeting policy
Haaretz said the testimonies of the four soldiers portrayed “a fundamentally different concept of warfare, in which even relatively minor targets could be considered sufficient justification for attacks to harm civilians.”
The newspaper said the large number of civilians classified by the military as “collateral damage” was not simply the result of failures or mistaken identification, but stemmed from a policy of expanding the use of firepower “to the maximum extent.”
Haaretz said similar accounts had been presented during the three years of the war and that efforts to compensate for the intelligence failures of Oct. 7, 2023, “contributed to unprecedented tolerance for civilian casualties.”
The newspaper cited an Oct. 31, 2023 Israeli airstrike on a large residential complex in the Jabalia refugee camp in northern Gaza as one example. The stated target was Ibrahim Biari, a Hamas battalion commander in Jabalia.
“We knew Biari was underground, beneath large buildings, but we did not know beneath which building,” said a soldier identified only as D.
“So they chose buildings that were still inhabited and decided to destroy all the buildings above the tunnel where he was located. We did not carry out an evacuation because it was important to kill him without allowing him to escape,” he said.
Soldier A, who said he took part in the mission, said members of the targeting cell understood that the number of civilians likely to be harmed “was extremely high.”
“In the military intelligence estimates of potential collateral damage, there was talk of 250 to 300 people, so the decision was passed up for direct approval by the chief of staff,” he said.
“After the strike, as time passed, we understood that the number of dead was around 250,” he added, referring to Palestinian civilians.
“I remember being shocked when several densely populated buildings were flattened, killing hundreds, in order to kill a battalion commander who only a few weeks earlier would not even have been considered a target,” he said.
Responding to the Jabalia massacre, the Israeli army claimed that the strike had been “replanned several times to reduce harm to civilians,” saying the expected number of civilian casualties “was not in the hundreds.”
The army claimed that after the strike, “the damage was found to have exceeded its initial assessment.”
OPINION: Gaza’s displaced face a deadly choice: collapsing buildings or flooded tents
Civilian bloodshed
Nadav Weiman, executive director of Breaking the Silence, a left-wing Israeli organization, denounced the army’s conduct in Gaza.
“We cannot allow the killing of 300 civilians to assassinate a battalion commander,” he said. “Nor can we kill 20 civilians to kill every Hamas truck driver and then claim publicly that we did everything possible to prevent harm to innocent people.
“It is time for those who issued these orders to take responsibility instead of trying to get rid of the soldiers who courageously decided to tell the public the truth,” Weiman said.
In November 2024, the International Criminal Court issued arrest warrants for Netanyahu and former Defense Minister Yoav Gallant over war crimes and crimes against humanity in Gaza.
The International Court of Justice, the UN’s principal judicial organ, is also hearing a case brought by South Africa and joined by several countries accusing Israel of genocide against Palestinians in Gaza.
Haaretz said another case described by the soldiers involved the Oct. 13, 2023 targeting of Hamas commander Ali Qadi.
According to the newspaper, an intelligence soldier in the Gaza Division had warned that Qadi “was behaving unusually,” but the division’s intelligence officer disregarded the warning.
“A few days after the war began, Qadi became a target and was subjected to heavy fire,” soldier A said.
“He was in the house with his family, and they decided to kill him. The army quickly announced that he had been killed, but in reality Qadi was the only person who survived the attack. Everyone who was killed had no connection to the target,” he said.
Without evacuation
Another soldier, identified as B, who served in a drone unit, said that after the war began, the division was authorized to operate under expanded parameters, meaning attacks expected to injure up to 20 noncombatants “did not require approval from a senior official outside the targeting cell.”
A third soldier, identified as C, who served in military intelligence, said that several months after the ground offensive began on Oct. 27, 2023, his unit was asked to prepare an entry zone into Gaza City for a maneuvering division.
He said several high-rise buildings in the area were considered a threat to Israeli troops and that an intelligence assessment estimated that about 25% of residents were still inside their homes.
“When we tried to ask how many residents remained and whether that was reasonable, we were told that those residents were targets for the forces on the ground. I could not understand or believe that we were talking about such numbers,” he said.
He added that the forces planning to enter the area could have waited considerably longer before approving the attack.
“So in the early stages we attacked without a full evacuation. Defending the soldiers was given priority, which is understandable, but the numbers (of civilian casualties) kept growing and became unreasonable,” he said.
The Israeli army has killed more than 74,300 Palestinians and injured over 175,400 others in a brutal war since October 2023 that has left the entire enclave in ruins.

articles.title: Kremlin agrees with Trump on need for Ukraine leadership change
articles.body:
Kremlin agrees with Trump on need for Ukraine leadership change
Ukraine needs a new leader with the political will to end the conflict with Russia, Kremlin spokesman Dmitry Peskov has said. His comments came after US President Donald Trump stepped up pressure on Ukrainian leader Vladimir Zelensky, whose presidential term expired more than two years ago, to hold new elections.
Speaking to RIA Novosti on Monday, Peskov said Trump believes it is high time for Ukraine to elect a new leader because “Ukraine’s president must make very responsible and very difficult decisions to stop this war.”
“Either Zelensky takes on this responsibility and shows such political will, or he does not,” Peskov continued, adding that he has so far failed to do so.
Asked whether Russia wants a particular Ukrainian leader, Peskov replied: “What matters to us is that someone in the Kiev regime demonstrates the political will to recognize the realities on the ground and move toward a peaceful settlement.”
The comments come after Trump suggested on Saturday that it is time for Ukraine to get “a new president,” accusing Zelensky of repeatedly rejecting opportunities for peace. He added that he believes Russia wants an agreement and Zelensky does not.
Zelensky’s presidential term expired in May 2024, but he has since refused to hold new elections, citing martial law. Moscow has since declared him illegitimate, while suggesting that his questionable status is a major obstacle to signing a binding peace agreement. Former Defense Minister Mikhail Fedorov argued that Zelensky fears a new election due to potential competition from former army chief Valery Zaluzhny. Fedorov is also viewed as a potential candidate.
An unnamed White House official told Axios that “Trump is really mad” at Zelensky over the attacks on Russian oil refineries. A Financial Times report claimed that the Trump administration threatened to suspend intelligence sharing and block US weapons sales through the NATO-coordinated PURL procurement mechanism unless the Ukrainian strikes stop.
On Sunday, Trump announced that Russia and Ukraine had reached an energy ceasefire. Zelensky replied that the announcement was “news for me,” but expressed readiness to stop attacking Russian refineries if the country stops its strikes on Ukraine’s energy infrastructure. Russia has yet to comment.
Zelensky has also argued that elections in Ukraine can only be organized if Russia agrees to a 60-day ceasefire.
Moscow has opposed the idea of a temporary ceasefire, arguing that it would only serve to allow Kiev time to rebuild its battered forces and receive more weapons from the West.
The US pressure intensified after Trump’s phone call on Friday with Russian President Vladimir Putin, after which the sides reached a major deal on diesel exports to the US to alleviate the global fuel shortage.

articles.title: EU approves largest expansion of sanctions list against Russia
articles.body:
European Union foreign ministers approved a 22nd package of sanctions against Russia, adding about 1,600 legal entities and individuals to the sanctions list.
It’s the largest single expansion of the sanctions list since the full-scale war between Russia and Ukraine began, EU foreign policy chief Kaja Kallas said.
More than half of the new individuals and entities on the list are tied to the production of ballistic missiles, she said. “We are making it significantly harder, slower and more expensive for Russia to produce the weapons it uses to kill Ukrainians,” she added.
The investigative project Systema earlier reported that organizations in Russia’s military-industrial complex, along with their executives and employees, would face sanctions under the 22nd package. For some of these organizations, the sanctions are not being introduced for the first time, but are being expanded.

articles.title: Zelenskyy: Ukraine skipped strikes on Russian energy
articles.body:
- Zelenskyy said Ukraine did not strike Russian energy facilities overnight into Oct. 12 after Trump announced an energy ceasefire.
- He said Russia kept attacking Ukrainian gas and power infrastructure, and Moscow has not confirmed agreeing to the ceasefire.
Ukrainian President Volodymyr Zelenskyy said Ukraine did not strike any energy facilities inside Russia overnight into Oct. 12, after President Donald Trump announced an immediate halt to attacks on energy targets, but that Russia kept hitting Ukraine’s gas and power infrastructure.
Zelenskyy made the comments in a live interview with Fox News on Monday. Trump said on Truth Social on Sunday that Russia and Ukraine had agreed to stop attacking each other’s energy facilities. Moscow has not confirmed accepting any such deal, and the exact scope of the proposal is still unclear.
“We didn’t attack any energy objects on the territory of Russia because President Trump said that there will be an energy ceasefire between Ukraine and Russia. And we didn’t attack, but Russia attacked our gas stations, energy infrastructure, infrastructure and other things,” said Ukrainian President Volodymyr Zelenskyy.
He said Kyiv was ready to observe the ceasefire but doubted Moscow was, describing the overnight strikes as Vladimir Putin’s answer to Trump and saying Russia had signaled it knew nothing about an energy ceasefire.
Ukraine’s charge d’affaires in Washington, Denys Sienik, said Russian forces hit a power plant in Kyiv, cutting electricity and water, and then struck a thermal power plant in Kharkiv after Trump’s announcement. Sienik said Russia had attacked electricity generation and transmission facilities more than 200 times over the past week. Russia has not commented on those claims.
A White House official told Axios that Trump’s proposal initially focused on stopping attacks on oil refineries, with a broader halt covering power plants and electrical grids possibly to follow. Ukraine’s long-range drone campaign against Russian refineries has been a point of friction with Washington, and Trump has argued the strikes push up fuel prices. Zelenskyy rejected a refinery-only arrangement, saying an energy ceasefire has to cover Ukraine’s power grid, and tied any pause on refinery strikes to Russia doing the same.
“If Russia will not attack our energy, we will not attack the energy,” said Zelenskyy.
He also disputed Trump’s view that Ukrainian strikes are behind higher diesel prices, pointing instead to disruptions in the Strait of Hormuz. On Friday, Trump announced a deal with Russia to release Russian diesel to the United States and global markets, which critics in Congress say gives Moscow more revenue for the war.
Zelenskyy also responded to Trump’s suggestion over the weekend that Ukraine needs a new president. He said he was ready to hold elections but that Ukraine would need at least 60 days of security for its infrastructure to prepare, given ongoing Russian drone and missile attacks. Russian Foreign Minister Sergey Lavrov rejected the idea of a 60-day pause on Monday, arguing that European countries would use it to rearm Ukraine.
“I don’t think he deserves a respite,” Lavrov said, according to the BBC.
Zelenskyy said he last spoke with Trump in person at the U.N. General Assembly in New York in late September. Russia has not said whether it will stop striking Ukrainian energy facilities.
