articles.title: Chinese Cars in Norway Stored Military Exercise Footage and Access Codes
articles.body:
Norwegian military personnel discovered that rented Chinese-made cars automatically recorded and stored video footage during military exercises.
The Norwegian newspaper DN reported the incident.
The cars continued to be used throughout the exercises because few alternative vehicles were available.
Norwegian outlet Nettavisen drew attention to the supplier’s links to China’s Zhejiang Geely Holding Group.
The Norwegian Armed Forces use rental vehicles from First Rent A Car Norway AS, which operates under the Hertz brand, for daily activities, military exercises, and operational tasks.
The company is part of Volvo Cars’ corporate structure. China’s Zhejiang Geely Holding Group is Volvo Cars’ majority owner.
In 2024, the Norwegian Armed Forces’ logistics organization signed nationwide framework agreements with two suppliers for vehicle rentals: First Rent A Car Norway AS and RAC Norway AS. The maximum combined value of the contracts is NOK 350 million.
First Rent A Car’s link to the Chinese automotive group runs through Volvo Cars. An official European Commission decision on the acquisition of First Rent A Car states that Volvo Cars gained full control of the company, while Zhejiang Geely Holding Group controlled Volvo.
As of 2026, Geely remains Volvo Cars’ majority owner. Geely Sweden Holdings owns about 78.65% of Volvo Cars’ shares, and the China-based Zhejiang Geely Holding Group ultimately owns it.
The military’s use of modern civilian vehicles also raises separate security concerns. In its Risiko 2025 assessment, Norway’s National Security Authority warned that a modern car can contain more than 200 electronic sensors.
If external actors gain access to such data, they could use it for surveillance, tracking movements, or intelligence-gathering.
In its National Threat Assessment 2026, Norway’s counterintelligence service, the Police Security Service, stated that Chinese intelligence and security agencies had expanded their capacity to conduct operations in Norway, including in cyberspace and through human intelligence sources.
In May, a Chinese national was arrested in Norway on suspicion of complicity in espionage. The suspected target may have been the Andøya spaceport, which is strategically important to the country.
In August 2025, the Israel Defense Forces (IDF) banned Chinese-made vehicles from entering military bases. The restrictions were introduced as a precautionary measure to reduce the risk of sensitive information being collected on military premises.
In November 2025, the IDF began removing Chinese-made official vehicles from officers’ use over information-security concerns.
The collection of information through civilian electronic devices is also a concern for other NATO countries. In April, the German Armed Forces (Bundeswehr) restricted the use of personal smartphones, tablets, and smartwatches when handling classified information due to the threat of espionage by Russia and China.

articles.title: Here’s what Trump’s latest U-turn really means for Russia and Ukraine
articles.body:
Here’s what Trump’s latest U-turn really means for Russia and Ukraine
The latest turn in Russia-US relations has shocked Kiev, outraged the EU, provoked discontent among a considerable number of politicians in the US, and left many observers around the world perplexed.
The Trump administration’s sudden decision to suspend sanctions on Russian diesel supplies appears to contradict its recent actions, including the adoption of tough new sanctions legislation intended to increase pressure on Moscow, and while some attribute the reversal to US President Donald Trump’s unpredictability, others see the beginnings of a new policy, or evidence of a fundamental change in the administration’s approach to Ukraine.
To understand what’s happening, however, we must look beyond the peculiarities of the US president’s public behavior. Trump’s extravagance, which frequently borders on the absurd, often conceals a relatively clear set of objectives, but whether those objectives are sensible is another question.
The most likely explanation for his latest reversal lies in domestic American politics, as the congressional midterm elections are less than a month away, and the Republican Party faces difficult prospects. Trump maintains an air of indifference, but losing control of both houses of Congress would condemn him to two years of political confrontation and considerable frustration.
He probably understands that there’s little prospect of fundamentally improving the economic situation, particularly consumer prices, before voters go to the polls, so for now, the emphasis is on psychological impact.
Russia isn’t the first country Washington has approached about increasing fuel supplies to international markets, and the more agreements Trump can announce, the more opportunities he has to proclaim that the White House is working tirelessly to protect ordinary Americans from rising prices.
The expectation, presumably, is that voters will forget how much of the present difficulty stems from Trump’s own actions in the Persian Gulf.
We shall soon discover whether this approach works, but there’s nothing particularly irrational about it, and Trump is pursuing a deliberate political objective. The fact that his latest decision contradicts previous statements doesn’t trouble him because he’s long operated on the assumption that words have value at the moment they’re spoken, but impose few obligations thereafter.
What does this mean for Russia, beyond the welcome prospect of additional budget revenues?
Colleagues from the Vatfor project have identified an important development, in that for the first time since the beginning of the conflict, the US president has made a significant decision regarding Russia without making Ukraine the determining consideration.
Until now, the Ukrainian question has been inseparable from virtually every aspect of Washington’s policy towards Moscow, but this time, not only has it been set aside, the decision directly contradicts Kiev’s interests at a particularly difficult moment.
Hence the indignation of the Ukrainian leadership, as from its perspective, the Americans have behaved unfairly.
There are probably several reasons for this change, but the principal one appears to be Ukrainian leader Vladimir Zelensky’s unwillingness to accommodate Washington’s demands that Ukraine stop attacking Russian energy infrastructure.
The strikes have become one of Kiev’s principal instruments of warfare, and American requests to curtail them have largely gone unanswered.
Trump, meanwhile, has become fixated on Russian oil supplies as a means of addressing rising fuel prices, and their importance shouldn’t be exaggerated, even if additional Russian supplies alone are unlikely to transform the global market. Nevertheless, Trump has evidently decided that Zelensky bears responsibility for aggravating the situation.
Once the US president reaches this conclusion, persuading him otherwise becomes extremely difficult. Therefore, for the moment, Kiev’s objections have simply been disregarded.
The more consequential question concerns American intelligence assistance, because to stop, or at least substantially reduce, Ukrainian attacks on Russian targets, Washington would have to restrict the intelligence it provides to Kiev, and much of this information amounts, in practical terms, to targeting assistance.
Trump already demonstrated willingness to use this instrument when around a year and a half ago, he temporarily suspended intelligence cooperation for several days to put pressure on the Ukrainian leadership.
A longer interruption would be a different matter and it would represent a genuine change in Washington’s approach to the conflict, effectively distancing the US from its Ukrainian partner, but whether Trump is prepared to take this step is uncertain.
There is, after all, an extensive informal coalition interested in maintaining the present course, and it includes the US defense industry, increasingly influential technology companies, European governments, and their political allies in Washington.
Trump encountered these forces during his previous attempt to advance his preferred settlement following the Anchorage summit, and that initiative ultimately produced little, so it remains to be seen whether the present effort will fare any better.
If Washington proves unwilling to exert sustained pressure on Kiev, the latest initiative could gradually lose momentum, and this is especially likely after the congressional elections, when the immediate political value of announcing presidential achievements will diminish.
The decisive question, therefore, is whether the US leadership can compel its partners to move in the direction it considers necessary, and if it can, an opportunity for further negotiations on a settlement could emerge.
There’s also a second conclusion which is particularly important for Russia, because Washington’s latest actions offer a glimpse of how Russia-US relations could develop after the military phase of the conflict ends.
The enormous collection of sanctions imposed on Russia is unlikely to disappear, and removing them would be exceptionally difficult, both procedurally and politically, given too many restrictions have become embedded in law and institutional practice.
Instead, the sanctions will probably remain formally in place, while decisions about their enforcement are taken according to circumstances; thus, when a particular restriction conflicts with US interests, Washington could suspend its application, but when the circumstances change, it can be restored.
In other words, sanctions will become instruments to be activated or deactivated according to immediate political and economic requirements, rather than permanent expressions of an immutable policy, and this is an important distinction between the American and European approaches.
The Americans generally display a greater degree of pragmatism as they are perfectly capable of proclaiming principles with great conviction, abandoning them when circumstances demand it, and returning to the same principles when doing so becomes convenient. European governments, by contrast, have increasingly bound themselves to political commitments from which retreat is both institutionally complicated and publicly embarrassing.
For Moscow, understanding this difference will be essential when constructing its future relationship with Washington now that the confrontation over Ukraine has reached a stage at which its consequences extend far beyond the immediate military and territorial questions.
Whatever the eventual outcome, it will help determine the structure of future political relations between Russia and the various components of the Western world, and while that structure is already beginning to emerge, its geometry remains unsettled, and the lines are still moving.

articles.title: Shin Bet's answer to 7 October failures is an 'Islam school'
articles.body:
Breadcrumb
Shin Bet's answer to 7 October intelligence failures is to 'study Islam', not Israeli occupation
Israel's domestic intelligence agency, Shin Bet, is planning to establish a school of Islamic studies following its failure to anticipate the Hamas-led attacks on 7 October 2023, focusing on religious ideology rather than the decades of Israeli occupation, dispossession and violence that shaped the emergence of Hamas and other Palestinian factions.
The initiative, reported by the Israeli news website Walla, raises questions about Israel's attempts to explain its intelligence failures by a lack of understanding of Islam, rather than examining the political realities that gave rise to Hamas and the institutional failures that allowed the attack to take place.
The project is being spearheaded by Shin Bet chief David Zini and will provide specialised education on Islam, its different schools of thought and Palestinian society to intelligence personnel working across various departments.
The school will operate alongside Shin Bet's existing Arabic-language training programme, which also provides instruction to some Israeli military personnel.
According to Walla, the project will involve academics, researchers, specialist institutions and current and former senior intelligence officials, with its curriculum tailored to the operational challenges facing the agency.
The initiative follows internal investigations into Israel's intelligence failures preceding 7 October, when Palestinian fighters breached the Gaza perimeter and attacked Israeli military positions and communities.
Despite possessing extensive intelligence about Hamas's preparations, Israeli security agencies failed to anticipate the scale and timing of the assault.
Walla reported that one conclusion drawn by Israel's intelligence establishment was that officials lacked sufficient understanding of Islam, Palestinian culture and Hamas's ideological foundations, particularly in Gaza.
Investigators reportedly identified shortcomings in their understanding of the movement's development following the release of Hamas leader Yahya Sinwar from Israeli prison in 2011, as well as the continuing influence of the organisation's founder, Sheikh Ahmed Yassin.
Sheikh Yassin was assassinated in an Israeli airstrike in 2004, while Sinwar was killed by Israeli forces in Gaza in October 2024.
A senior Israeli intelligence official told Walla: "We did not realise the extent to which Hamas hates Israel, how unwilling it is to accept any compromise, or how strong and prepared it was before 7 October, even though the warning signs were clearly visible."
However, framing Hamas primarily through its religious ideology risks reducing a movement rooted in the Palestinian experience of occupation to a question of Islamic beliefs.
Hamas was established in 1987 during the First Palestinian intifada uprising against Israeli occupation, nearly two decades after Israel occupied the West Bank, East Jerusalem and Gaza in 1967.
Although the movement emerged from the Palestinian branch of the Muslim Brotherhood and draws on Islamist ideology, its formation and development were closely related to the Palestinian struggle against Israeli military rule, territorial dispossession and the denial of national self-determination.
Hamas has previously offered Israel a long-term truce if it withdraws from the entirety of the West Bank and Gaza, while signalling its acceptance of a Palestinian state only on those territories.
Its political and armed activities have arguably been shaped by continued occupation, repeated Israeli military offensives, the blockade of Gaza and the failure of successive political efforts to secure Palestinian statehood.
Treating Islam as the central explanation for Hamas's actions therefore risks confusing the movement's ideological identity with the political and historical conditions that produced it.
The focus on Islam also comes amid the Netanyahu government's growing cultivation of far-right political movements in Europe, including parties and figures associated with Islamophobia and hostility towards Muslim immigration.
Israeli officials, particularly Diaspora Affairs Minister Amichai Chikli, have increasingly sought alliances with European nationalist parties around a shared opposition to alleged "radical Islam". The outreach has included France's National Rally, Spain's Vox and Austria's Freedom Party, as Israeli leaders increasingly portray the country as a defender of Western civilisation against an alleged Islamist threat.
Hamas's 7 October assault on Israel took place in a year when Israeli violence in the West Bank and East Jerusalem had already killed more Palestinians in any full year since the UN began recording fatalities in 2005.
Israeli military raids, particularly in Jenin and Nablus, had intensified, while illegal settlement expansion and settler attacks placed growing pressure on Palestinian communities.
In Gaza, Israel had launched another major military offensive in May 2023, carrying out hundreds of airstrikes. The escalation left 33 Palestinians dead, including at least 12 civilians, according to the UN, and damaged thousands of homes.
These developments came against the backdrop of Israel's blockade of Gaza, imposed in 2007, which had devastated the territory's economy and severely restricted the movement of its population.
Just a day before the 7 October attack, The New Arab reported that 2023 had already become the deadliest year for Palestinian children in the occupied West Bank, with Israeli forces killing 47 children since January, surpassing the 45 killed throughout 2022.
Tensions had also intensified at the Al-Aqsa Mosque compound in occupied East Jerusalem, while the prospect of Saudi-Israeli normalisation threatened to further marginalise the Palestinian national question.
Israel's occupation overlooked in 7 October reckoning
Hamas named its operation "Al-Aqsa Flood", citing Israeli actions at the holy site, the blockade, Palestinian prisoners and the occupation among its stated grievances.
The focus on religion risks obscuring a more immediate explanation for Israel's failure to anticipate the attack, as its intelligence agencies had already possessed detailed warnings about Hamas's plans.
Israeli investigations into the 7 October attack have exposed failures that went far beyond a lack of cultural or religious understanding.
Israeli intelligence reportedly possessed detailed information about Hamas's plans, including a document outlining an assault remarkably similar to the one eventually carried out, but senior officials dismissed the scenario as unrealistic.
In September 2026, an investigation published by Haaretz revealed that Israeli Prime Minister Benjamin Netanyahu had also reportedly received a direct warning from UAE President Mohammed bin Zayed around 10 days before the attack that Hamas was preparing a major offensive.
According to the report, Netanyahu reassured the Emirati leader that Israel was prepared for any scenario but failed to pass the warning to senior Israeli security officials. An Emirati source subsequently confirmed the reported conversation to The Times of Israel, although Netanyahu's office denied it had taken place, calling the allegations an "absolute lie".
Warnings from Israeli surveillance personnel stationed near Gaza were also reportedly ignored, raising questions about institutional complacency and the failure to act on intelligence already available, rather than simply a lack of understanding of Hamas's ideology.
Despite these revelations, three years after the attack, Israel has still not established an independent state commission of inquiry into the political, military and intelligence failures surrounding 7 October, amid opposition from Netanyahu and disputes over how such an investigation should be conducted.

articles.title: Putin does not read Truth Social, and his "Shaheds" operate according to different instructions - Zelenskyy on the "energy truce"
articles.body:
Putin does not read Truth Social, and his "Shaheds" operate according to different instructions - Zelenskyy on the "energy truce"
Kyiv • UNN
Zelenskyy said that after the U.S. president's post, Russian drones flew over Ukraine. The Russian Federation attacked an energy facility in Kharkiv.
President of Ukraine Volodymyr Zelenskyy said that Russian drones flew over Ukraine immediately after the publication by the President of the United States regarding an "energy truce." And immediately after this publication, Russia launched a targeted strike on a power plant in Kharkiv, causing additional damage to Ukraine's energy system. The Head of State said this during an address to the Warsaw Security Forum on October 12, reports UNN.
Details
"Yesterday, we were all genuinely surprised when, immediately after the sudden but very important post by the President of the United States stating that he had managed to secure an energy truce between Russia and Ukraine, Russian jet-powered drones were flying in our airspace at that very moment. Large areas of Kyiv were left without water and electricity, while repair crews were working to restore power after a Shahed strike on a power plant. And immediately after this post, Russia launched a targeted strike on a power plant in Kharkiv, causing additional damage to our energy system," Zelenskyy said.
"It was obvious that Putin does not read Truth Social, and that his Shahed drones operate according to different instructions," Zelenskyy noted.
"However, this post concerns something that affects the lives of millions of people, and that is precisely why it is extremely important. First and foremost, it is important for Ukraine, because Russia is trying to use yet another winter and another period of cold weather against our country, attacking power plants, power grids, and all components of our energy infrastructure every day," the President emphasized.
Additional information
Volodymyr Zelenskyy said that Ukraine is ready to respond if Russia does not agree to an energy truce this winter.

articles.title: Air defense downs 89 of 122 Russian targets, impacts at 15 locations
articles.body:
Ukraine's Defense Forces neutralized 89 Russian targets overnight into Monday; however, impacts of enemy air attack assets were recorded across 15 locations, the Air Force of the Armed Forces of Ukraine reported.
"According to preliminary data, as of 09:00, air defense shot down or suppressed 89 Russian UAVs of the Shahed type (55 of them jet-powered), Gerberas, and other drone types," the statement reads.
In total, overnight into October 12 (from 18:00 on October 11), the enemy attacked with an Kh-59 guided air missile from the airspace over the Black Sea, as well as 121 strike UAVs including Shahed (76 of them jet-powered), Gerbera, Banderol/Dan-T, and Parodiya decoy drones from the directions of Orel, Kursk, Primorsko-Akhtarsk (Russia), occupied Donetsk region, and occupied Crimea (Hvardiyske).
The air attack was repelled by aviation, anti-aircraft missile troops, electronic warfare and unmanned systems units, and mobile fire groups of the Ukrainian Defense Forces.
Meanwhile, impacts of Russian air attack assets were recorded at 15 locations, and falling debris from downed targets was reported at four locations.
The attack remains ongoing, with about ten Russian UAVs currently in Ukrainian airspace, the command added.

articles.title: ‘This deal doesn’t help’: Europe slams Trump’s plan to buy Russian diesel
articles.body:
European governments rebuked U.S. President Donald Trump’s plan to import hundreds of thousands of tons of Russian diesel, and vowed to keep isolating Moscow and supporting Ukraine as it heads into a brutal wartime winter.
Trump said over the weekend he would import 300,000 tons of Russian diesel, weeks ahead of U.S. midterm elections in which the Republicans are polling badly and in which energy prices and cost-of-living concerns are expected to play a major role.
“This deal doesn't help neither the price of oil products nor the unity of the transatlantic community,” Lithuanian Foreign Minister Kęstutis Budrys said at a gathering of the bloc’s foreign ministers on Monday morning, adding “it is not the European way.”
Irish Foreign Minister Helen McEntee called Trump’s announcement of a deal with Moscow “concerning,” while German Minister of State for Europe Gunther Krichbaum said every dollar spent on Russian energy funded the purchase of weapons used against Kyiv.
The EU’s top diplomat, Kaja Kallas, reminded Washington that “Russia has started this war. We should not forget this.”
On Monday, Zelenskyy suggested that Washington had other motives for pursuing an energy agreement with Moscow, arguing that the Russian fuel involved would make little difference to global supplies.
Speaking at the Warsaw Security Forum, Zelenskyy said proposed Russian diesel deliveries were insignificant compared with global monthly consumption of roughly 120 million tons.
"I don't think that this will have a tangible impact," Zelenskyy said. "I believe that there are different rationales behind this decision."
Advertisement
Zelenskyy also suggested Washington should consider an alternative arrangement with Kyiv. "Why doesn't America then conclude a diesel deal with Ukraine?" he asked. "Let's propose a diesel deal with Ukraine."
He also revealed that Kyiv had not been informed beforehand of Trump's announcement that he had secured an energy ceasefire. "No, we did not know about that," Zelenskyy said. "We've learned that from the media as well."
On their way into their meeting, the EU's foreign ministers remained united in their insistence that increasing pressure on Moscow was the only way forward.
“Obviously our position has not changed — pressure on Russia, sanctions, support to Ukraine, Russia’s isolation is the way to peace,” Latvian Foreign Minister Baiba Braže said.
The British Foreign Office’s minister of state Stephen Doughty said London was “not planning to follow suit with” purchasing Russian energy and would ratchet up “economic pressure” on Moscow.
“Pressure, pressure, pressure on Russia,” Lithuania’s Budrys said.
Advertisement
What ceasefire?
Trump’s claim that Ukraine and Russia had agreed to an “energy ceasefire” drew confusion from Kyiv and its allies over the weekend, with Zelenskyy saying the truce and its terms were “news” to him but that he would support it nonetheless — provided Moscow followed suit.
Just hours after Trump’s announcement, however, Russian bombs fell on Ukrainian power plants, causing widespread blackouts.
Kyiv is bracing for its fifth winter since Russia launched its full-scale invasion in February 2022, which Polish Prime Minister Donald Tusk said last month could prove “tragically critical” for Ukraine due to Russia’s near-constant strikes on infrastructure.
At the opening session of the Warsaw Security Forum on Monday, Tusk slammed "anyone who is trying to introduce any symmetries, who suggests it is Ukraine responsible for the war," saying doing so "gives a valuable present, gift, to the aggressor, to Putin."
Kallas said any ceasefire shouldn’t “only apply to the refineries, where Ukraine has one and Russia has plenty,” adding that would “definitely [be] in the benefit of the Russians.”
She also called on Washington to join Brussels and London in imposing harsh sanctions on Russia. “Of course the U.S. is our biggest ally,” she said, “but our message is clear: If we want to end this war, the only way we can do this is putting more pressure on Russia.”
Advertisement
Ukraine’s financial needs are set to come up at a meeting of European heads of state and government on Thursday in Brussels. The IMF estimated that Kyiv will face a financing gap of $30 billion to $35 billion next year.
"Ukraine will be front and center at this week's European Council," European Commission President Ursula von der Leyen said in a statement Sunday night after a phone call with Zelenskyy, adding the war was entering a "new, grimmer phase."
Zoya Sheftalovich contributed reporting from Brussels. Nick Vinocur contributed reporting from Warsaw.

articles.title: Ukraine’s FM: Russia’s war budget makes the case for using frozen assets now
articles.body:
Ukraine's Foreign Minister Andrii Sybiha speaks during a briefing marking Ukrainian Defence Industry Day in Kyiv, on April 13, 2026. | Tetiana Dzhafarova/AFP via Getty Images
Andrii Sybiha is Ukraine’s minister of foreign affairs
Europe can no longer remain immobilized on Russian assets. Now is the time to use them for Ukraine’s defense and recovery.
This decision, which is long overdue, would be a game changer that could shift the balance in Ukraine’s favor — particularly if taken alongside strong sanctions pressure. But to achieve this, we have to be faster and more decisive than Russia.
Advertisement
According to the latest reports, Russia plans to spend a record €180 billion on its military in 2027 — more than 40% above its 2026 defense allocation. And that is only part of the picture. The country’s draft federal budget allocates a combined €669 billion to defense and security for the 2027–2029 period.
These figures make clear Russia wants war. Moscow is increasing the pressure, intensifying its terror against Ukrainian civilians and raising the cost of defense for both Ukraine and Europe. But as the cost of war grows, it should grow faster for the aggressor.
The higher the price for Moscow, the sooner peace will be restored. Half-hearted pressure on Russia and half-measures in support of Ukraine will only prolong conflict and increase the overall price tag. Decisive steps can bring it to a close.
Local residents stand amid the rubble of a five-storey residential building following a Russian attack that killed seven people, including three children, in Zaporizhzhia on October 10, 2026. | Daria Nazarova/AFP via Getty Images
At the end of August, Sweden, the Netherlands, Spain and Poland addressed the European Commission, urging renewed discussion on the full use of immobilized Russian assets. We are grateful to them. But it is now time to turn this discussion into a legal process: launch a permanent platform, engage experts and develop the decision.
Europe has taken the hardest step already. In 2022, the G7 immobilized some €300 billion in Russian central bank reserves, roughly €210 billion of them in the EU. In 2024, the G7 borrowed $50 billion for Ukraine against the future windfall profits on those reserves. And in December 2025, the bloc made the immobilization open-ended.
What remains undecided is the only step that matters: using the assets themselves.
Advertisement
Every argument for and against this has been heard, and the debate now revolves around its scope and how to mitigate associated risks.
The prevailing view is that the decision to use these assets must not expose any single country to disproportionate risk — above all Belgium, where most of the assets sit at Euroclear. We agree. To that end, Ukraine’s Finance Ministry proposed a clear plan to the European Commission: placing the assets under collective EU control, so that the decision to use them — and the liability for doing so — is European, not Belgian.
An outside view of the headquarters of the Euroclear Group financial institute in Brussels, April 9, 2025. | Nicolas Maeterlinck/Belga Mag/AFP via Getty Images
Belgium’s exposure is a reason to share the risk, not to do nothing.
Another common argument is that any decision must cover immobilized assets in every jurisdiction, not only those at Euroclear. Again, we agree — with one caveat: This can be done but on parallel tracks. Europe should not make its own decision contingent on protracted global coordination when its security is in peril.
Skeptics raise four objections of principle against the full use of these assets: that using them breaks the rule of law, that it undermines the euro as a reserve currency, that it gives away leverage in peace talks, and that Russia would retaliate by seizing Western assets.
Let’s take these arguments in turn.
Advertisement
On rule of law: Under the International Law Commission’s 2001 Articles on State Responsibility, a state that commits an internationally wrongful act owes full reparations, and injured states may take countermeasures to induce compliance. And in November 2022, the U.N. General Assembly recognized that Russia must bear the legal consequences of its aggression, including reparations.
The same articles also require countermeasures to be reversible, and Ukraine’s position honors that: The legal title stays in an EU-governed vehicle, Ukraine receives financing rather than ownership, and the arrangement unwinds the day Russia pays what it owes.
On the euro: This has already been tested. When the reserves were immobilized in February 2022, the euro’s share of global reserves did not move. Reserve holders understood then what they understand now — that this principle applies to a state waging a war of aggression in breach of the U.N. Charter, not to anyone else. Moreover, the euro’s credibility as a reserve currency rests on Europe’s ability to defend order and principles.
Members of the General Assembly vote on a draft resolution during a special session in the General Assembly Hall at United Nations Headquarters on November 14, 2022 in New York City. | Michael M. Santiago/Getty Images
On leverage: These assets have been immobilized for more than four years and have not moved Moscow any closer to peace. A country budgeting €669 billion for a war of aggression is not bargaining for its reserves. What deters Russia is Ukraine’s capacity to keep fighting — and that is precisely what a European solution on these assets would fund. The leverage is not in holding the money, it is in spending it.
Finally, on seizing Western assets in Russia: Putin has been doing this since 2022. This September alone, Moscow took control of the Russian businesses of Nestlé, Auchan, Leroy Merlin, FM Logistic and Metro, following Danone and Carlsberg. That is why, as early as March 2022, we urged companies to leave. The confiscation of European property has already happened — and keeping the assets immobilized did not deter this.
Let us be clear about what we are not proposing. We are not proposing outright confiscation — the legal title will not transfer. We are not proposing a Belgian decision — the risk will be shared at the EU level. And we are not proposing a precedent for anyone else. The conditions — a war of aggression condemned by the U.N. General Assembly — are met by only one state.
Advertisement
Russia must be the one to pay for the damage it has caused and continues to cause, not European taxpayers.
We should be sending the right signal to Moscow: That it will not outlast our resolve.
We should be sending the right signal to skeptical audiences across Europe ahead of a major election year: That the rising cost of Ukraine’s defense will be covered at the expense of Russia.
Last but not least, we should be sending the right signal to the Ukrainian people: that they are not alone in confronting the aggressor.
The full use of Russian assets would bring tangible and immediate results, strengthening Ukraine on the frontline and bringing peace closer. After four years, Europe should no longer be immobilized on major decisions. It needs political will, collective commitment and a solid legal formula.
We urge EU leaders to make this vital decision without delay. And we look forward to the European bravery in taking this critical step.

articles.title: Ignoring Russian nukes is ‘suicidal’ – Jeffrey Sachs (VIDEO)
articles.body:
Ignoring Russian nukes is ‘suicidal’ – Jeffrey Sachs (VIDEO)
European leaders who threaten nuclear-armed Russia while assuming there will be no consequences are displaying “suicidal” incompetence and ignore basic realities, Columbia University Professor Jeffrey Sachs has said.
In an interview with Afshin Rattansi on ‘Going Underground’ published on Monday, Sachs described the dismissal of Russian warnings that a direct conflict with NATO could escalate into nuclear war as “unbelievably reckless.”
Smaller European NATO nations that engage in hostile rhetoric act “a little bit like Israel... even radically more so,” believing the US will protect them in an actual conflict, he said.
“This is actually not how the world works and they are so reckless and stupid to talk in these terms,” Sachs stressed.
The West’s broader confrontation with Russia, which Sachs maintains was provoked by NATO’s 2008 declaration that Ukraine would eventually become a member, reflects “not only war profiteering” but also “a tremendous amount of incompetence and cowardice and unwillingness of these politicians to admit basic truths.”
Sachs also criticized US President Donald Trump for failing to follow through on an agreement he reached last year with Russian President Vladimir Putin to wind down the Ukraine conflict.
He lamented the UN’s inability to fulfill its role as guardian of world peace, arguing that Washington routinely disregards international rules.
“Essentially, the United States says: ‘We don’t obey any rules,’” he said.

articles.title: NATO’s top general lays out plan to fight Russia — with or without America
articles.body:
NATO Supreme Allied Commander Europe General Alexus G. Grynkewich at the Warsaw Security Forum on October 12, 2026 in Warsaw, Poland. | Omar Marques/Getty Images
NATO’s top commander U.S. Gen. Alexus Grynkewich on Monday vowed to block, blunt and break any Russian attack as part of a new “Theory of Victory,” and underlined that alliance troops would fight even if U.S. forces were engaged elsewhere.
Speaking at the Warsaw Security Forum, Grynkewich outlined how the 32-member alliance would respond to an invasion of NATO territory as concerns grow that Russia could be capable of attacking a NATO member by the end of the decade.
“Our alliance exists to preserve peace,” he said, “but let there be no doubt: should war come, we will block, blunt any attack, and then, if it does not cease, we will break the forces conducting aggression against us.”
Advertisement
The rare intervention by the four-star general to discuss a military blueprint underscores NATO’s effort to deter Russia. It is also aimed at sending a message of NATO unity after a grueling year for the alliance, which was rocked by Donald Trump’s threats to annex Greenland and infighting over the U.S.-Israeli war in Iran.
Under the three-part blueprint, NATO would initially use land-based troops — buttressed by air, naval, cyber and space capabilities — to stop an assault, targeting attacking forces and preventing them from seizing territory, Grynkewich said.
NATO would then use sensors and autonomous systems among other capabilities to “overwhelm enemy formations … and their advance,” he said, before using “highly effective precision munitions” and unmanned systems if necessary to “break the [enemy] warfighting system” and “everything that supports” it.
Lithuanian Defense Minister Robertas Kaunas said the theory laid out by Grynkewich “will send a strong message to our adversaries that we are going to defend ourselves.”
NATO's Supreme Allied Commander Europe said he does “not assess that conflict is imminent or inevitable.” But “we will … ensure any attack against any ally proves utterly futile.”
The speech describes a more forceful response if a foe attacks, but its credibility depends on allies having the forces, infrastructure, and coordination to implement the plan.
Advertisement
Asked whether the plan factored in a scenario where the U.S. was engaged elsewhere, Grynkewich said: “It absolutely does account for that, and in fact, it must.”
Under Trump, the U.S. has sought to refocus its military on other priorities such as the Indo-Pacific, homeland security and the Western Hemisphere. U.S. ambassador to NATO Matthew Whitaker said in Warsaw on Monday that Europe only ranks fourth among Washington’s strategic concerns.
“No one should question the commitment of the United States to this alliance,” Grynkewich argued, but added that “ultimately, it's a political decision about who's providing troops where.”
Camille Grand, NATO's former assistant secretary-general for defense investment, said the plan was “a very deliberate effort” to signal that the alliance would be ready to fight with or without large-scale involvement of U.S. forces.
“For my country, fighting with Russians is with or without Americans,” said a separate senior European defense official, who was granted anonymity to speak freely. “We expect them to come, but if they won’t, we will fight anyway.”
Advertisement
Grand added that the blueprint is also an indication that NATO is ready to take a bolder approach toward Moscow by threatening the destruction of its war machine even deep behind the front lines.
That comes as Moscow sent a letter to NATO last month threatening to use its nuclear arsenal if the alliance tried to isolate its Kaliningrad exclave.
Grynkewich warned that NATO would be ready to respond — even with its nuclear arsenal.
“Should an adversary threaten escalation by saber-rattling, or should one actually decide to escalate during conflict, it will not fracture our alliance,” he said. “We should take comfort in our ability to deliver mass effects and the implicit warning that we could match any enemy move up the escalation ladder.”

articles.title: Russia Pulled Rare S-400 Launchers From Strategic Kapustin Yar Range—Ukraine Found and Hit Them
articles.body:

Russia Pulled Rare S-400 Launchers From Strategic Kapustin Yar Range—Ukraine Found and Hit Them
Ukrainian forces destroyed three and damaged five Russian Iskander and S-400 launchers used for ballistic missile attacks during September and early October 2026, according to Defense Minister Yevhenii Khmara.
New footage released by Ukraine’s Security Service also appears to support earlier assessments that the vehicles hit were rare 51P6A launchers pulled out of storage at the Kapustin Yar test range and reassigned for strikes against Ukraine, according to Defense Express on October 12.
OSINT researcher AS-22 examined satellite imagery of Kapustin Yar and found that roughly 30 such launchers were visible there in 2022, but only 14 remained by 2025. That would mean 16 had been removed from storage and likely reassigned to operational use.
We bring you stories from the ground. Your support keeps our team in the field.
One of the easiest ways to distinguish the 51P6A from more common S-400 launchers is its chassis. The vehicle is mounted on the Belarusian-made MZKT-7930 Astrolog platform, while standard S-400 launchers more commonly use the Russian-built BAZ-64022 chassis.
Defense Express notes that the 51P6A launchers observed near Ukraine were reportedly moving individually, without the radar vehicles normally associated with S-400 air-defense batteries.
That pattern supports the theory that they were being used not in the system’s traditional air-defense role, but as launch platforms for PM-48U surface-to-surface ballistic missiles.
Ukraine’s Defense Intelligence had estimated by late August that Russia possessed up to 17 S-400 launchers specifically assigned to PM-48U operations.
The same 51P6A launchers had also appeared at Kapustin Yar when Russia first publicly discussed specialized ballistic missiles for the S-400 in fall 2023.
The PM-48U itself represents an unusual adaptation of Russia’s existing air-defense missile inventory for ground-strike missions.
The exact launch and guidance architecture used with the 51P6A remains unclear, but the absence of accompanying radar vehicles near some of the launchers suggests that Russia is operating them differently from a conventional S-400 battery.
Previously, reports emerged that Russia used its newest 9M723-2 ballistic missile, commonly referred to as the Iskander-1000, against Kyiv for the first time during a combined attack on the Ukrainian capital this summer.

articles.title: One essential ingredient for AI safety? Democracy | Matthew Botvinick
articles.body:
AI safety is having a moment. After years as a topic for techies and futurists, the potential risks from artificial intelligence systems – from cyberattacks to hyper-persuasion to rogue behavior – are suddenly under discussion both in the corridors of power and around kitchen tables.
In fact, the conversation now reaches beyond classical safety concerns, getting into AI’s impact on economic life and the environment, as well as possible responses, from alignment research to government regulation.
This expanding public discussion is coming none too soon, as recent news about AI security breaches makes clear. However, something important is still missing. For all its vibrancy, the public debate has not yet focused on one of the most important requirements for AI safety: constitutional democracy.
To see why democracy matters for AI safety, imagine that we have already built a powerful AI system that is “safe” in all the now-familiar senses: it cannot escape human control, cannot launch cyberattacks or make bioweapons, and cannot power killer robots. Now picture that system in two different political contexts, one democratic, the other authoritarian.
Placed inside a healthy democracy – a constitutional republic, with free and fair elections, protected civil liberties, and robust rule of law – AI could bring massive benefits, advancing science and medicine, expanding education and bolstering economic prosperity. Under the right conditions, AI could strengthen democracy itself, helping citizens make their voices heard, improving policymaking and making government services more efficient and accountable.
Now consider the authoritarian scenario. Here, everything flips. AI becomes a tool for government surveillance and censorship, for propaganda and for political suppression and entrenchment. No imagination is required to conjure this scenario. It is already playing out in China, Russia, Iran, Venezuela, several Gulf states and elsewhere.
Placing these two scenarios side by side reveals an elemental truth: there can be no such thing as safe AI unless we secure the future of constitutional democracy and the rule of law. It doesn’t matter how “safe” your AI is if you live under authoritarian rule; you will not be safe. In short, AI safety requires political freedom.
Once this fact sinks in, it becomes clear that we must reverse the retreat of democracy that has occurred around the world over the past two decades, including, here at home, the steady erosion of constitutional checks under administrations of both parties.
Of course, preserving democracy has always been a worthwhile goal. With the AI era looming, it has become an urgent one.
To complicate matters, AI itself will put new pressure on democratic institutions. As AI starts to affect jobs, the resulting economic insecurity may create openings for demagogues of every stripe.
By creating national security crises – cyberattacks, for example – AI will multiply opportunities for governments to invoke emergency powers, powers that, once claimed, are rarely relinquished. And as AI is integrated into executive-branch functions, traditional checks and balances may be disturbed, and the risk of political surveillance will grow.
In the longer term, if AI replaces a majority of jobs – an outcome that economists such as Daniel Susskind and Anton Korinek are concerned about – ordinary citizens will face a serious risk of losing their leverage over those who govern them. To see why, we need only look at present-day petrostates, where governments that do not depend on taxing their citizens’ work often disregard those same citizens’ rights.
A solid first step toward countering these risks would be to update our legal codes, setting limits on executive power by reforming emergency and surveillance law, and ensuring due process by narrowing the circumstances in which the state secrets privilege may be invoked.
In the US, this would mean, for example, revisiting the National Emergencies Act and International Emergency Economic Powers Act, and closing the “data broker” loophole in intelligence work. As executive agencies begin to leverage AI, we should also furnish Congress and the courts with equally powerful AI tools, so that their oversight can keep pace.
The principle here is not new. As James Madison wrote, “Ambition must be made to counteract ambition,” only here in a digital setting.
Longer-term, to avoid widespread political disempowerment, we will need to renew our traditions of self-government, involving citizens more directly in policymaking and government oversight. If we play our cards right, AI itself may help, making information easier to access and helping citizens reason together – town halls for a digital age.
Buttressing political freedom in these ways would be important in its own right. Today, however, it is also a form of AI safety work.
Who is best positioned to drive the needed reforms? Policymakers, civic organizations and ordinary citizens must all participate.
But there is another key player: the AI industry. While the major AI labs are willing to weigh in on specific policy issues, most have recently gone quiet on the topic of democracy itself.
Over the past year, a number of AI-industry leaders have justifiably stressed the need to equip military and intelligence agencies with AI, so that democracies can compete abroad. But the same leaders have been conspicuously absent from the debate over the health of democracy at home.
The tech sector was not always so reserved. In 2013, Apple, Google, Microsoft, Facebook, Twitter, Yahoo, LinkedIn and AOL joined forces to publish an open letter to the president and Congress, stating that government surveillance methods had “tipped too far in favor of the state and away from the rights of the individual – rights that are enshrined in our constitution”.
In 2018, Microsoft publicly asked Congress to limit government use of facial recognition technology, writing: “We must ensure that the year 2024 doesn’t look like a page from the novel 1984.” And as recently as 2021, companies including Alphabet, Amazon, Apple, Facebook, IBM, Microsoft and Twitter published an open letter opposing proposed changes to state voting laws, declaring: “We stand for democracy.”
More recently, however, many tech companies have fallen silent. This is understandable. These companies answer to their investors, and in the current environment, speaking out can put shareholder value at risk.
That, however, should not be the end of the story. The leading AI labs all describe AI safety as core to their mission. If they mean what they say, then – for the reasons I’ve highlighted – they bear a duty to stand up for basic constitutional principles, despite the commercial risks.
Journalists, researchers and ordinary citizens can help them recognize that duty by insistently pointing out the connection between safety and freedom.
It is good that people outside the AI industry are suddenly talking about AI safety. AI will affect everyone, and everyone should be involved in shaping how it is built and used.
But we need to make political freedom a centerpiece of the discussion. We need to build public awareness that AI safety fundamentally depends on democracy. Only by bearing this point firmly in mind can we avoid the dangers of AI and reap its potentially immense benefits.
- Matthew Botvinick is the author of the forthcoming book AI and Political Freedom and a senior fellow at Yale Law School. He has held multiple research positions in the AI industry, including at Google DeepMind and currently Anthropic, but writes here exclusively in his Yale role

articles.title: Ukraine’s Zelenskyy accuses Russia of violating Trump’s ‘energy ceasefire’
articles.body:
Ukraine’s Zelenskyy accuses Russia of violating Trump’s ‘energy ceasefire’
The European Union also announced that it officially added almost 1,600 new sanctions on Russia’s military industrial complex.
Ukraine’s President Volodymyr Zelenskyy has accused Russia of violating the “energy ceasefire” that United States President Donald Trump unilaterally announced at the weekend and promised to respond if the attacks continue.
Speaking at the Warsaw Security Forum via video link on Monday, the Ukrainian leader urged the US to step in to ensure that Moscow abides by the truce in the four-and-a-half-year Russia-Ukraine war, noting that there have already been “Russian violations of the energy ceasefire announced by President Trump”.
Zelenskyy said Ukraine was “horribly surprised” that despite Trump’s announcement, Russia struck several energy facilities, including a power plant in Kharkiv.
“We are waiting for the details of the conditions between the Americans and Russians, and we are waiting to see what specific steps the Americans are ready to take,” he said.
“This energy ceasefire, it can work, and it can become a major step toward ending the war if the Americans truly step in now and make sure Russians respect it … If Russia does not agree to an energy ceasefire, we will respond,” Zelenskyy told the Warsaw Security Forum.
Kremlin spokesperson Dmitry Peskov said talks for a possible “energy ceasefire” were ongoing, but rejected Zelenskyy’s proposal for a 60-day truce to allow elections to take place.
“In the Kremlin, both President Putin and officials at other levels have repeatedly stated we do not want a ceasefire,” Peskov said. “We want long-term peace and are prepared to do everything possible to achieve it.”
Trump’s announcement on Sunday that the two countries had agreed to an “energy ceasefire” caused confusion. It came two days after Trump declared a temporary easing of US sanctions on Russian diesel, prompting outrage from European allies and Kyiv, who said it would only embolden Russian President Vladimir Putin.
Both Ukraine and Russia have been launching mutual attacks on each other’s energy infrastructure for months, adding to upward pressure on global energy prices that have risen amid the US-Israel war on Iran.
Zelenskyy initially denied any knowledge of the agreement and said it was “news to him”, according to Axios.
Trump has previously taken to his Truth Social account to announce truces or other arrangements before either Kyiv or Moscow confirmed them.
“An energy ceasefire and other steps to reduce escalation and guarantee security are truly needed here in reality, not just on Truth Social,” Zelenskyy added.
European leaders expressed encouragement at the proposed ceasefire, but agreed with Zelenskyy that it had not taken effect.
“I have not noted, over the last 48 hours, any energy ceasefire coming from the Russian side,” French President Emmanuel Macron told reporters at a Paris auto show.
At the Warsaw Security Forum, Polish Prime Minister Donald Tusk said that “Russia is not interested in a ceasefire, de-escalation, or peace … that is why I will go to Brussels to urge all European partners to consider increasing sanctions.”
In Brussels, the European Union announced that it has officially added almost 1,600 new sanctions on Russia’s military-industrial complex, including individuals and entities involved in the war, in a bid to maintain pressure on Moscow.
“This is the single largest expansion of our sanctions list since Russia started its war,” EU foreign policy chief Kaja Kallas wrote online. “Europe is again showing a united front … We are making it significantly harder, slower and more expensive for Russia to produce the weapons it uses to kill Ukrainians.”
Meanwhile, Russia attacked Ukrainian gas production facilities belonging to its state oil and gas company Naftogaz in the Kharkiv region overnight, which caused a fire, the company said on Monday.
“The attack damaged critical equipment. Our employees are doing everything possible to repair the damage as quickly as possible and prevent risks to the stable operation of the energy system,” Naftogaz acting CEO Sergii Fedorenko wrote on Telegram.
A day earlier, Zelenskyy had said that Ukraine was ready to halt attacks on Russian oil refineries if Moscow ceased its own attacks on Ukrainian energy infrastructure.

articles.title: UK PM accuses Russia of Brexit meddling (VIDEO)
articles.body:
UK PM accuses Russia of Brexit meddling (VIDEO)
UK Prime Minister Andy Burnham claims that Russia “clearly” interfered in the 2016 Brexit referendum which led to Britain leaving the EU, without providing evidence to back up the rehashed allegations.
Speaking on ‘The Rest is Politics’ podcast on Sunday, the prime minister said he sought answers about Russia’s alleged involvement after taking office this summer.
“I asked the question coming to Downing Street: Well, was there interference in the 2016 referendum from Russia? I’ve had the clear answer that yes, there was.”
Burnham did not identify who provided the assessment, what evidence supports it, or whether any alleged interference affected the result. Defending the timing of his unsubstantiated claim – ten years after Brexit – Burnham argued that voters need to understand that some political movements were “instigated via our enemies, namely Russia.”
Britain voted to leave the EU in the June 23, 2016 referendum, with 51.89% backing Leave against 48.11% for Remain, with 72.2% turnout. The vote was driven largely by demands to reclaim sovereignty, control immigration, cut EU regulations and budget contributions, and pursue independent trade deals, amid widespread dissatisfaction with the political establishment.
Allegations of Russian interference through media activity and bots allegedly boosting pro-Leave sentiment have surfaced before, but Burnham is the first sitting prime minister to publicly make the claim. Previous governments denied that Russia influenced the vote, citing “no evidence of successful interference” or any impact on the result.
Russia has dismissed the allegations as baseless speculation and part of a pattern of Western accusations. Moscow has not yet commented on Burnham’s claims.
Russian interference?
Western governments have repeatedly pointed the finger at Russia over elections and political developments, including recent contests in Germany, France, Moldova, and Georgia. On the podcast, Burnham recalled a conversation with German Chancellor Friedrich Merz, whose CDU was defeated by the right-wing Alternative for Germany (AfD) in three major state elections in recent weeks. According to Burnham, Merz also raised the issue of Russian involvement, citing the AfD’s alleged ties to Moscow.
Russia firmly rejects the allegations of political interference. Officials maintain that Russia respects the sovereignty of other states and does not interfere in their internal affairs, describing the accusations as part of domestic political struggles and anti-Russia campaigns.
Russia, meanwhile, has accused the West of meddling abroad. Foreign Minister Sergey Lavrov said earlier this year that Western governments interfere through color revolutions, military force, and “electoral neocolonialism” – using politically biased election monitoring, media campaigns, and external pressure to influence other countries’ political processes and challenge unfavorable results.
Russia has accused Britain of interference in the Ukraine conflict, citing extensive weapons deliveries, military training, and intelligence support for Kiev, as well as former Prime Minister Boris Johnson’s alleged role in derailing the 2022 peace talks. Moscow argues that London’s actions make it a de facto party to the conflict and obstruct peace efforts. Lavrov said in August that British involvement in missile strikes on Russia gave the country grounds to regard the UK as a party to the conflict, “with all ensuing consequences.”
Brexit reversal looming?
Burnham’s decision to revisit alleged ‘Russian interference’ comes as his government considers closer ties with Brussels. At the Labour Party’s annual conference last month, he argued that Brexit has done “more harm than good,” and suggested that rejoining the EU could feature in the party’s next election manifesto, opening the door to reversing the vote.
Economic assessments have generally found that Brexit has hurt Britain’s economy, which has experienced weak growth since leaving the EU. Recent estimates suggest that GDP is 6% to 8% lower than it would have been had the country remained.
A YouGov poll last month suggests that 59% of Britons support rejoining the EU, with 32% opposed. However, support for closer ties without rejoining the EU, single market, or customs union is higher, at 73%.
Critics of reversing Brexit, including Reform UK leader Nigel Farage, argue that rejoining the EU would force Britain to surrender control over immigration, regulation, and trade policy while taking on new financial obligations.
Commenting on Burnham’s allegations of Russia meddling in an interview with The Guardian on Monday, Farage called the prime minister “a liar,” dismissing the claims as part of a longstanding “Russia hoax.”
“The prime minister is a liar. Yes, a liar... There was no Russian interference. And the Russia hoax has run all the way through this,” he said, citing previous denials under Boris Johnson and Foreign Office minister Stephen Doughty’s assertion that any attempted meddling failed.

articles.title: Zelenskyy: If Russia wants us to stop hitting refineries, it must stop strikes on our energy system
articles.body:
Zelenskyy: If Russia wants us to stop hitting refineries, it must stop strikes on our energy system
President Volodymyr Zelenskyy has stated that Ukraine has only one oil refinery, which is why when it comes to an energy ceasefire, stopping Russian strikes on power stations and the energy grid is key, and the American team has been well informed about this.
Source: European Pravda, citing Zelenskyy during an address at the Warsaw Security Forum on 12 October
Details: The president referenced Russia's recent strikes against power generation facilities carried out following US President Donald Trump's post on Truth Social regarding a so-called "energy ceasefire".
Quote: "It was clear that Putin does not read Truth Social, and his Shahed drones follow a different set of instructions. But this post is actually about something that affects the lives of millions of people, and that makes it very, very important."
Details: Zelenskyy assured that if Russia does not agree to an energy ceasefire this winter, Ukraine "will respond".
Quote: "We in Ukraine immediately supported this idea [of an energy ceasefire], as we did, by the way, as we did on and on for months when we ourselves put forward the idea of the energy ceasefire… The American team knows very well what this means for us. We do not have major oil reserves, large oil export capacities or dozens of oil refineries. We import large amounts of diesel fuel and other oil products."
Details: Zelenskyy added that Russia launched its campaign of strikes against Ukrainian power plants and the electricity grid several years ago, and every winter, including this one, the Russians attempt to make these attacks even more intense.
Quote: "We have power cuts every single day. For Russia, of course, the petrol shortages and burning oil refineries because of our strikes and response are painful. And these are not the same volumes that could be lost because of the crisis in Hormuz. But if Russia wants us to stop our long-range strikes against its oil refineries and oil exports, then Russia must stop its strikes against our energy system and critical infrastructure and stop killing our people. This is only fair."
Background:
- A White House official told Axios that an "energy ceasefire", as understood by the US president, means that Russia and Ukraine will stop attacks solely on each other's oil refineries.
- On 11 October, Trump in his social media Truth Social claimed that Ukraine and Russia had agreed to an immediate energy ceasefire.
- Barak Ravid, a journalist at American news portal Axios, stated that Zelenskyy had been unaware of the "energy ceasefire" between Ukraine and Russia announced by Trump but is willing to agree to it.

Zelensky says Ukrainian military ‘received all relevant orders’ over energy truce announced by Trump
Volodymyr Zelensky said the Armed Forces of Ukraine have “received all relevant orders” related to the energy truce Donald Trump announced on October 11.

“Ukraine is ready not to strike Russian energy facilities, and we are counting on similar readiness from Russia and an agreement by the US president on this issue,” Zelensky said in his evening video address.
Zelensky said Ukraine had offered numerous steps toward de-escalation, but Putin “responded to all of them with one thing: his own “no.”” “We very much hope that he will finally tell America, Ukraine, and the whole world something different,” he added.

articles.title: Ukraine Expects to Need 10,000 Jet Engines of One Type per Month
articles.body:
Ukraine has identified jet engine production as one of the critical areas for developing its domestic defence industry.
Ukraine’s Minister of Defence Yevhen Khmara shared this with journalists at an event attended by a Militarnyi correspondent.
For one type of these engines, estimated demand in 2027 could reach around 10,000 units per month.
Demand for jet propulsion systems spans several weapons classes, from interceptor drones and middle-strike weapons to deep-strike systems and cruise missiles.
The Ministry of Defence says Ukraine already has a number of relevant designs and manufacturers that the state is supporting and assisting. In total, around 20 Ukrainian manufacturers are involved.
Volodymyr Zelensky has also announced plans to significantly expand domestic production of propulsion systems. Following a meeting of the Supreme Commander-in-Chief’s Staff on September 25, the president announced new decisions on establishing production of various types of jet engines in Ukraine.
A shortage of jet engines is one of the factors limiting the scaling up of high-speed interceptor drones.
In October, Zelensky reported that the Bars jet-powered interceptor was delivering some of the best results against Russian jet-powered drones, but Ukraine still imports a significant share of the necessary engines.
Meanwhile, Ukraine’s defence industry is developing its own propulsion systems for other weapons classes. In March, Fire Point announced that it had completed development of its own jet engine for the Flamingo cruise missile.

articles.title: Russia is plotting to assassinate defense industry executives in Europe, Western intelligence agencies warn, FT reports
articles.body:
Russia is plotting to assassinate defense industry executives in Europe, Western intelligence agencies warn, FT reports
Western intelligence services have warned the heads of European defense companies that Russia is stepping up efforts to physically eliminate them, the Financial Times reported, citing five sources it spoke with.
The Kremlin has ordered an expansion of sabotage and “hybrid” operations in Europe to “fatally weaken support for Kyiv,” the FT’s sources said. Assassination attempts on civilians in Europe are becoming an increasingly prominent part of those plans, the newspaper wrote.
FT sources said Moscow is targeting CEOs and other senior executives at defense companies, as well as leaders of smaller firms, particularly those that produce drones or drone components.
In response, companies have increased personal security for senior executives. Germany’s domestic intelligence agency, the BfV, has stepped up its work with employees and management at German defense companies, including recommending they hire private security details.
Russian military intelligence is believed to be responsible for planning and carrying out the sabotage. FT sources said the GRU has recently adapted its methods: its operatives now work more closely with organized crime groups, rely on cross-border agent networks, and split reconnaissance, logistics, planning, and execution across different cells or individuals rather than relying on lone agents recruited online.
Even so, one FT source said the actions of Russian agents “were still amateurish” in many cases and are easy to thwart.
One intelligence official who spoke with the journalists believes Russia’s main goal “is still psychological.” “Just by making people feel they might be a target, they are having their effect. They want individuals to think twice before doing business with Ukraine,” the official said.
In summer 2024, it was reported that Russia had been planning the assassination of Armin Papperger, the head of the German arms company Rheinmetall, which, among other things, produces artillery shells and military equipment for Ukraine. Later, NATO confirmed that it had known about these plans — as well as other instances of sabotage and subversion that Russia is believed to be behind.

articles.title: Trump again says Russia and Ukraine agreed to an energy ceasefire. For Zelensky, it came as ‘news.’

Trump again says Russia and Ukraine agreed to an energy ceasefire. For Zelensky, it came as ‘news.’
U.S. President Donald Trump announced on Sunday that Russia and Ukraine have agreed to a ceasefire in the energy sector.
“Effective immediately, there is an ENERGY CEASEFIRE in the War between Russia and Ukraine. Both parties have agreed. Do not break it!,” Trump wrote on the social network Truth Social.
He gave no further details.
Financial Times correspondent Christopher Miller writes that Ukraine “has no information” about the energy ceasefire Trump announced. “Just now our repair teams are restoring electricity and water supplies in Kyiv [after Russian strikes],” a senior Ukrainian official close to Volodymyr Zelensky told the FT. “Nobody has heard [about the ceasefire].”
For Zelensky himself, the ceasefire Trump announced came as “news,” he said in a brief interview with Axios. “If President Trump negotiated it with Putin, please tell us when the ceasefire begins. We are ready, and we will accept it,” Zelensky added.
Trump had already announced an energy ceasefire between Russia and Ukraine on September 14. At the time, he said that “Ukraine has agreed not to hit Russian Energy targets” and that “Russia has agreed to do, likewise.” However, the Financial Times later wrote that Trump had apparently jumped the gun with his announcement. Sources who spoke to the FT, familiar with the Kremlin’s position, said Vladimir Putin does not want to conclude an energy deal before winter because he believes attacks on energy facilities during the cold season could force Kyiv into making concessions.

articles.title: Built by Ukraine’s ex-defense minister and unit that wrecked $12 billion of Russian gear, new interceptor downs two jet drones over Kyiv
articles.body:
A month from idea to first kill. A new interceptor drone built by former Defense Minister Mykhailo Fedorov's team with Pavlo Yelizarov, the commander of Lasar's Group unit, soldiers, and engineers, has shot down two Russian jet-powered Geran-5 drones heading for Kyiv, Fedorov says, just one month after development began.
Russia's jet-powered Gerans fly far faster than the propeller Shaheds that Ukraine learned to shoot down, and they remain the hardest targets for its air defenses, which catch only about 55 percent of them. The new drone is fast enough to catch a jet drone before it reaches a city, Fedorov noted, adding that the two Geran-5 kills are the first confirmed for the interceptor.
Crews from Lasar's Group in Ukraine's National Guard ran the combat trials and downed the two drones within days. Fedorov announced the drone on 12 October, Yelizarov's birthday.
A former minister and a legendary commander behind the kill
Yelizarov joined Ukraine's Defense Forces in 2022 and, in January 2026, became deputy commander of the Air Force, responsible for small-scale air defense and systems for intercepting Russian drones, Forbes Ukraine reports. He founded Lasar's Group, which destroyed $12 billion worth of Russian equipment.
Fedorov, who ran the Digital Transformation and Defense ministries before moving to the private sector, says the interceptor is one of several projects his team continues to develop in Ukraine, combining engineering, military experience, and resources.
The next goal: a drone that hunts Shaheds on its own
The drone is not finished evolving. Testing continues as the team refines the technology and raises production, Fedorov said, with the next step a fully autonomous version that can detect and intercept Russian drones without an operator.
The developers also plan to scale the interceptor's use to protect more Ukrainian cities, he added. The push fits a wider drive: Ukraine aims to build up to 400 interceptors a month to chase the faster Gerans.

articles.title: Seventeen nations join NATO nuclear exercise in Italy
articles.body:
NATO’s annual nuclear deterrence exercise begins on Tuesday and is being hosted by Italy this year, with seventeen nations taking part, according to the alliance.
Steadfast Noon is described as a long-planned, routine training activity, part of the effort to maintain readiness and test the procedures that contribute to deterrence and defence. The overall scale is in line with previous iterations, and no live weapons are used at any point.
NATO Secretary General Mark Rutte said: “NATO is a defensive Alliance. This exercise helps us ensure a safe, secure, effective, and credible capability to preserve peace, prevent coercion and deter aggression. It also sends a clear message of unity and resolve.”
The alliance adds that the exercise is not linked to current world events and is not directed against any country.
Flying is expected to run from Aviano in Pordenone province and Ghedi in Brescia province, along with other locations across the area of responsibility, over roughly ten days, according to Il Sole 24 Ore. Aviano hosts United States Air Force units, and Ghedi is an Italian Air Force base operating the F-35A.
Seventeen participating nations is an increase on the fourteen that took part last year and the thirteen the year before. France does not take part, having never joined NATO’s Nuclear Planning Group, and the United States contributes flight crews and maintenance personnel.
Last year’s edition was led by the Netherlands from Volkel, supported by Kleine Brogel in Belgium and RAF Lakenheath in Suffolk, and drew around seventy aircraft from fourteen allied nations across a mix of conventional and dual-capable types. Italy has hosted the exercise six times before, in 2010, 2013, 2014, 2018, 2021 and 2023.
The Italian Air Force has said that no live ammunition is to be used.

articles.title: Trump calls for Ukraine to choose a new president as relations with Zelensky hit their lowest point since Oval Office clash
articles.body:
Trump calls for Ukraine to choose a new president as relations with Zelensky hit their lowest point since Oval Office clash
Relations between Volodymyr Zelensky and Donald Trump have fallen to their “lowest point” since the two clashed in the Oval Office in early 2025, The Wall Street Journal reports. The newspaper based its assessment on remarks Trump made to reporters October 10, when he said Ukraine might need a new president:
You know what I suggest? I suggest [Ukrainians] get a new leader who could make a deal because he could’ve made many deals and for some reason he never does […] I think it’s time for Ukraine to get a new President.
Axios also calls the situation a “serious crisis.” The outburst, according to the WSJ, could undermine arrangements Europe has spent the past year and a half building, as it has tried to persuade Trump to maintain U.S. support for Ukraine and keep pressure on Russia.
Trump made the statement a day after reaching an agreement with Vladimir Putin to allow Russian diesel fuel to reach the U.S. and world markets. In the same conversation with reporters, Trump said that the U.S. had warned Zelensky that he “could do whatever [he] want[s] to Russia” but should not strike oil refineries, calling that a “world problem.” “And what does he do? He goes and hits the diesel fuel. He better damn well stop,” Trump said. Trump had previously insisted that Ukraine halt its strikes on Russian oil refineries, which he claims are driving up fuel prices in the U.S., according to Axios.
The U.S. Treasury Department has already granted Russia a license allowing it to supply diesel fuel to the global market despite U.S. sanctions. The license is valid until April 7, 2027. Zelensky called the decision “an obvious weakness”:
Gifts to Putin will not bring peace or any benefit to the civilized world. Russia will “repay” the diesel with further terror and perfidy. Allowing Russia to sell petroleum products is an investment in a war that must be ended, not prolonged. What is needed is real de-escalation with Russia on a reciprocal basis.
Trump’s suggestion that Ukraine needs a different leader “shocked and stunned” Kyiv, Bild, Welt, and Politico journalist Paul Ronzheimer wrote on X. A close adviser to Zelensky told him: “We understood that during the [U.S.] midterm election campaign we would once again find ourselves in the spotlight. But we never expected THIS.”
According to Ronzheimer, Kyiv’s biggest fear is a halt to intelligence sharing, which could affect the Ukrainian military’s combat capability. That already happened once, after Trump and Zelensky’s Oval Office clash in February 2025.
Zelensky said October 11 that strikes on Russian oil refineries would stop if “Russia stops striking our energy infrastructure”: “Any de-escalation steps must be mutual and come with real guarantees.” Putin does not want to stop Russian strikes, Zelensky believes.
After Trump suggested Ukraine change leaders, people in Zelensky’s own circle rallied behind him. Ukrainian Foreign Minister Andrii Sybiha wrote: “President [Volodymyr Zelensky] leads our nation in a time of war — a war for independence, freedom, and dignity. He has the support of the Ukrainian people, and they have the right to decide. Statements from abroad only confirm that he is doing his job well. He deserves support.”
Estonian Prime Minister Kristen Michal, who criticized the deal between Putin and Trump, pledged Kyiv support for strikes on Russian oil refineries.
This is a big mistake, because deals with dictators lead to hell. Innocent people are being killed for gas and fuel money. And in all likelihood, the expected fuel will not materialize.
This kind of agreement contradicts the West’s long-term strategy of limiting the flow of money to Putin. The U.S. has been urging its allies to give up Russian fuel, and so have we. The long-term tactic of depriving Russia of money is correct, and it needs to continue.
Next week, Estonia and the European Council should discuss whether we can quickly invest more in Ukraine so that it can blow Russian oil refineries to pieces.
Elon Musk, the owner of SpaceX, which provides the Ukrainian military with Starlink satellite internet, voiced support for Trump. Commenting on Trump’s remarks about Ukraine’s strikes on Russian oil refineries, he wrote: “Zelensky has gone too far.” In another post, Musk added that it’s ”time for Ukraine to get a new leader.”

articles.title: Russia's September casualties in war against Ukraine exceeded 50,000 – Bloomberg citing NATO
articles.body:
Russia's September casualties in war against Ukraine exceeded 50,000 – Bloomberg citing NATO
NATO has estimated that Russia suffered more than 50,000 casualties in its war against Ukraine in September, of whom 28,000 were killed. This figure is significantly higher than the losses suffered by Ukraine's Armed Forces.
Source: Bloomberg, citing a NATO military official
Details: Bloomberg noted that Russian troops are attempting to advance into Ukrainian territory by sending soldiers into "kill zones", where they face drones, landmines, artillery fire and other defensive measures designed to repel attacks.
Meanwhile, an anonymous source cited by Bloomberg said that Ukraine's defence forces had suffered around 5,000 casualties over the same period.
Background: In the summer, NATO estimated that Russia had lost more than 1.4 million troops in its war against Ukraine.
